Both $\begin{bmatrix}I&F\\0&H\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\C&I\end{bmatrix}$ are block triangular, so their determinants are $\det I\cdot\det H=\det H$ and $\det A\cdot\det I=\det A$. Taking determinants of the identity above gives $\det M\cdot\det H=\det A$. ∎

solutions.title: Schur complement and continuity
solutions.body:
If $A$ is invertible, block elimination gives $M=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\CA^{-1}&I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\0&D-CA^{-1}B\end{bmatrix}$, so $\det M=\det A\cdot\det S$ with $S=D-CA^{-1}B$, and the standard block-inverse formula gives $H=S^{-1}$. Hence $\det M\det H=\det A$.

If $A$ is singular, replace $A$ by $A+tI$ for small $t\ne0$: then $A+tI$ is invertible and (for $|t|$ small) $M_t$ is still invertible; the lower-right block $H_t$ of $M_t^{-1}$ depends continuously on $t$. The identity $\det M_t\det H_t=\det(A+tI)$ for all small $t\ne0$ passes to the limit $t\to0$. ∎

prompt:
Show that
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n-1}\sin(\log n)}{n^\alpha}$$
converges if and only if $\alpha>0$.
answer: For $\alpha>0$, $f(t)=\sin(\log t)/t^\alpha$ has $|f'(t)|\le(1+\alpha)t^{-\alpha-1}$, so the paired terms $f(2k-1)-f(2k)$ are absolutely summable and $f(n)\to0$. For $\alpha\le0$ the terms do not tend to $0$: each interval $[e^{2\pi k+\pi/4},e^{2\pi k+3\pi/4}]$ has length $>1$ and contains an $n$ with $\sin(\log n)\ge\frac{\sqrt2}2$.

solutions.title: Pair the terms; the terms do not vanish for $\alpha\le0$
solutions.body:
Let $f(t)=\dfrac{\sin(\log t)}{t^\alpha}$ for $t\ge1$.

**$\alpha>0$: convergence.** We have
$$f'(t)=\frac{\cos(\log t)-\alpha\sin(\log t)}{t^{\alpha+1}},\qquad |f'(t)|\le\frac{1+\alpha}{t^{\alpha+1}}.$$
By the mean value theorem, $|f(2k-1)-f(2k)|\le\sup_{[2k-1,2k]}|f'|\le\frac{1+\alpha}{(2k-1)^{\alpha+1}}$, and $\sum_k(2k-1)^{-\alpha-1}<\infty$ because $\alpha+1>1$. So the partial sums
$$S_{2N}=\sum_{k=1}^N\bigl(f(2k-1)-f(2k)\bigr)$$
converge. Moreover $|f(n)|\le n^{-\alpha}\to0$, so $S_{2N+1}=S_{2N}+f(2N+1)$ has the same limit. Hence the series converges.

**$\alpha\le0$: divergence.** Then $|f(n)|\ge|\sin(\log n)|$ for $n\ge1$, so it suffices to show that $\sin(\log n)\not\to0$. For each integer $k\ge0$ consider
$$I_k=\bigl[e^{2\pi k+\pi/4},\ e^{2\pi k+3\pi/4}\bigr].$$
Its length is $e^{2\pi k+\pi/4}(e^{\pi/2}-1)>1$, so it contains an integer $n_k$, and $\log n_k\in[2\pi k+\frac\pi4,2\pi k+\frac{3\pi}4]$ gives $\sin(\log n_k)\ge\frac{\sqrt2}2$. Thus infinitely many terms have absolute value $\ge\frac{\sqrt2}2$; the terms do not tend to $0$ and the series diverges. ∎

prompt:
a) Let the mapping $f:M_n\to\mathbb R$ from the space $M_n=\mathbb R^{n^2}$ of $n\times n$ matrices with real entries to the reals be linear, i.e.
$$f(A+B)=f(A)+f(B),\qquad f(cA)=cf(A)\tag{1}$$
for any $A,B\in M_n$, $c\in\mathbb R$. Prove that there exists a unique matrix $C\in M_n$ such that $f(A)=\operatorname{tr}(AC)$ for any $A\in M_n$. (If $A=(a_{ij})_{i,j=1}^n$ then $\operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum_{i=1}^na_{ii}$.)

b) Suppose in addition to (1) that
$$f(AB)=f(BA)\tag{2}$$
for any $A,B\in M_n$. Prove that there exists $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ such that $f(A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A)$.
answer: a) $c_{ji}=f(E_{ij})$, since $\operatorname{tr}(AC)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}c_{ji}$; uniqueness from $\operatorname{tr}(E_{ij}C)=c_{ji}$. b) $f(E_{ij})=f(E_{ii}E_{ij})=f(E_{ij}E_{ii})=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $f(E_{ii})=f(E_{ij}E_{ji})=f(E_{ji}E_{ij})=f(E_{jj})$, so $f=\lambda\operatorname{tr}$.

solutions.title: Evaluate on matrix units
solutions.body:
Let $E_{ij}$ be the matrix with $1$ in position $(i,j)$ and $0$ elsewhere; they form a basis of $M_n$, and $E_{ij}E_{kl}=\delta_{jk}E_{il}$.

**a)** For any $C=(c_{ij})$, $\operatorname{tr}(AC)=\sum_{i}\sum_j a_{ij}c_{ji}$. Define $C$ by $c_{ji}=f(E_{ij})$. Then by linearity
$$f(A)=f\Bigl(\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}E_{ij}\Bigr)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}f(E_{ij})=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}c_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(AC).$$
Uniqueness: if $\operatorname{tr}(AC)=\operatorname{tr}(AC')$ for all $A$, then with $D=C-C'$ and $A=E_{ij}$ we get $0=\operatorname{tr}(E_{ij}D)=d_{ji}$ for all $i,j$, so $C=C'$.

**b)** For $i\ne j$: $E_{ij}=E_{ii}E_{ij}$ while $E_{ij}E_{ii}=0$, so by (2) $f(E_{ij})=f(E_{ii}E_{ij})=f(E_{ij}E_{ii})=f(0)=0$. For any $i,j$: $E_{ij}E_{ji}=E_{ii}$ and $E_{ji}E_{ij}=E_{jj}$, so $f(E_{ii})=f(E_{jj})$; call this common value $\lambda$. Then
$$f(A)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}f(E_{ij})=\lambda\sum_ia_{ii}=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).\ \blacksquare$$

solutions.title: Use the matrix $C$ from part a)
solutions.body: For b), write $f(X)=\operatorname{tr}(XC)$. Then (2) says $\operatorname{tr}(ABC)=\operatorname{tr}(BAC)=\operatorname{tr}(ACB)$ (cyclicity), i.e. $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A(BC-CB)\bigr)=0$ for all $A$. By the uniqueness in a), $BC-CB=0$ for every $B$: $C$ commutes with all matrices. Taking $B=E_{ij}$: $E_{ij}C=CE_{ij}$; comparing entries, $(E_{ij}C)_{il}=c_{jl}$ and $(CE_{ij})_{il}=c_{ii}\delta_{jl}$, so $c_{jl}=0$ for $l\ne j$ and $c_{jj}=c_{ii}$. Thus $C=\lambda I$ and $f(A)=\operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}A$. ∎

prompt: Let $X$ be an arbitrary set, and let $f$ be a one-to-one function mapping $X$ onto itself. Prove that there exist mappings $g_1,g_2:X\to X$ such that $f=g_1\circ g_2$ and $g_1\circ g_1=\mathrm{id}=g_2\circ g_2$, where $\mathrm{id}$ denotes the identity mapping on $X$.
answer: Split $X$ into orbits of $f$; on an orbit $\{f^k(x_0)\}$ (indexed by $\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z/m$) set $g_2(f^k(x_0))=f^{-k}(x_0)$ and $g_1(f^k(x_0))=f^{1-k}(x_0)$ — two "reflections" whose composition is the shift.

solutions.title: Reflections on each orbit
solutions.body:
Write $f^k$ for the $k$-th iterate ($k\in\mathbb Z$; $f^0=\mathrm{id}$, $f^{-k}=(f^{-1})^k$), which makes sense because $f$ is a bijection. For $x\in X$ let $T(x)=\{f^k(x):k\in\mathbb Z\}$ be its orbit. Two orbits are equal or disjoint, so $X$ is a disjoint union of orbits, each mapped onto itself by $f$. It is enough to define $g_1,g_2$ on each orbit separately.

Choose (axiom of choice) a base point $x_0$ in each orbit $T$. Every element of $T$ is $f^k(x_0)$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. If $T$ is infinite, $k$ is unique; if $T$ is finite with $m$ elements, then $f^k(x_0)=f^l(x_0)$ iff $k\equiv l\pmod m$. Define on $T$
$$g_2\bigl(f^k(x_0)\bigr)=f^{-k}(x_0),\qquad g_1\bigl(f^k(x_0)\bigr)=f^{1-k}(x_0).$$
These are well defined: if $k\equiv l\pmod m$ then $-k\equiv-l$ and $1-k\equiv1-l\pmod m$. Now
- $g_2(g_2(f^k(x_0)))=f^{k}(x_0)$ and $g_1(g_1(f^k(x_0)))=f^{1-(1-k)}(x_0)=f^k(x_0)$, so $g_1\circ g_1=g_2\circ g_2=\mathrm{id}$;
- $g_1(g_2(f^k(x_0)))=g_1(f^{-k}(x_0))=f^{1+k}(x_0)=f\bigl(f^k(x_0)\bigr)$, so $g_1\circ g_2=f$.

(Geometrically: on a finite orbit $f$ is a rotation of a regular $m$-gon and on an infinite orbit it is the shift $k\mapsto k+1$ of $\mathbb Z$; both are compositions of two reflections, $k\mapsto-k$ followed by $k\mapsto1-k$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous function. Say that $f$ "crosses the axis" at $x$ if $f(x)=0$ but in any neighbourhood of $x$ there are $y,z$ with $f(y)<0$ and $f(z)>0$.

a) Give an example of a continuous function that "crosses the axis" infinitely often.

b) Can a continuous function "cross the axis" uncountably often? Justify your answer.
answer: a) $f(x)=x\sin\frac1x$, $f(0)=0$ (crosses at every $\frac1{k\pi}$). b) **Yes**: on the Cantor set $C$, let $f=0$ on $C$ and $f=(-1)^k\operatorname{dist}(x,C)$ on the intervals removed at stage $k$; $f$ is continuous and crosses the axis at every point of the uncountable set $C$.

solutions.title: Signed distance to the Cantor set
solutions.body:
**a)** Let $f(x)=x\sin\frac1x$ for $x\in(0,1]$ and $f(0)=0$; $f$ is continuous since $|f(x)|\le x$. Its zeros in $(0,1]$ are $x_k=\frac1{k\pi}$, $k\ge1$, and near each $x_k$ the factor $\sin\frac1x$ changes sign while $x>0$, so $f$ takes both signs in every neighbourhood of $x_k$. Thus $f$ crosses the axis at infinitely many points (also at $0$).

**b) Yes.** Let $C\subset[0,1]$ be the Cantor set: $C_0=[0,1]$, and $C_k$ is obtained from $C_{k-1}$ (a union of $2^{k-1}$ closed intervals of length $3^{-(k-1)}$) by removing the open middle third of each interval; $C=\bigcap_kC_k$. Call the $2^{k-1}$ removed open intervals the intervals *of stage $k$*; $[0,1]\setminus C$ is the disjoint union of all of them. $C$ is closed and uncountable: $C$ consists of the numbers $\sum_{j\ge1}b_j3^{-j}$ with $b_j\in\{0,2\}$, and $(b_j)\mapsto\sum b_j3^{-j}$ is injective on such digit sequences, so $C$ is in bijection with the set of all $0$–$1$ sequences.

Define
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\(-1)^k\operatorname{dist}(x,C),&x\text{ in an interval of stage }k.\end{cases}$$
*Continuity.* $x\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(x,C)$ is continuous (1-Lipschitz). On each removed open interval $f=\pm\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,C)$ with a fixed sign, hence continuous there. At $c\in C$: $|f(x)-f(c)|=|f(x)|\le\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le|x-c|$. So $f$ is continuous on $[0,1]$.

*Crossing.* Let $c\in C$ and $\delta>0$. Choose $K$ with $3^{-K}<\delta$. The point $c$ lies in one of the closed intervals $J$ of $C_K$, which has length $3^{-K}$, so $J\subset(c-\delta,c+\delta)$. The middle third of $J$ is an interval of stage $K+1$, and the middle third of the left third of $J$ is an interval of stage $K+2$; both lie in $J$. On them $\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,C)>0$ and $f$ has the signs $(-1)^{K+1}$ and $(-1)^{K+2}$, i.e. both signs occur in $(c-\delta,c+\delta)$. Since $f(c)=0$, $f$ crosses the axis at every point of $C$ — uncountably many points. ∎

prompt: Let $V$ be a $10$-dimensional real vector space and $U_1$ and $U_2$ two linear subspaces such that $U_1\subseteq U_2$, $\dim_{\mathbb R}U_1=3$ and $\dim_{\mathbb R}U_2=6$. Let $\mathcal E$ be the set of all linear maps $T:V\to V$ which have $U_1$ and $U_2$ as invariant subspaces (i.e., $T(U_1)\subseteq U_1$ and $T(U_2)\subseteq U_2$). Calculate the dimension of $\mathcal E$ as a real vector space.

solutions.title: Block upper-triangular matrices
solutions.body:
Choose a basis $v_1,v_2,v_3$ of $U_1$, extend it by $v_4,v_5,v_6$ to a basis of $U_2$, and by $v_7,\dots,v_{10}$ to a basis of $V$. A linear map $T$ lies in $\mathcal E$ iff
- $Tv_1,Tv_2,Tv_3\in U_1=\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, and
- $Tv_4,Tv_5,Tv_6\in U_2=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_6)$

(invariance only needs to be checked on a basis of each subspace; then $T(U_1)\subseteq U_1\subseteq U_2$ handles $v_1,v_2,v_3$ for $U_2$ too). So in this basis the matrix of $T$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks of sizes $3,3,4$:
$$\begin{bmatrix}*_{3\times3}&*_{3\times3}&*_{3\times4}\\0&*_{3\times3}&*_{3\times4}\\0&0&*_{4\times4}\end{bmatrix},$$
and every such matrix occurs. $\mathcal E$ is the subspace of matrices with these free entries: columns $1$–$3$ have $3$ free entries each, columns $4$–$6$ have $6$ each, columns $7$–$10$ have $10$ each:
$$\dim\mathcal E=3\cdot3+3\cdot6+4\cdot10=9+18+40=67.$$
**Answer: $67$**

solutions.title: Count the forced zeros
solutions.body:
Of the $100$ entries of a $10\times10$ matrix (in the adapted basis above), the forced zeros are: in the $3$ columns of $v_1,v_2,v_3$ the $7$ rows $4$–$10$, i.e. $21$ zeros; in the $3$ columns of $v_4,v_5,v_6$ the $4$ rows $7$–$10$, i.e. $12$ zeros. All other entries are free, so $\dim\mathcal E=100-21-12=67$.

**Answer: $67$**

prompt:
Prove that the following proposition holds for $n=3$ (5 points) and $n=5$ (7 points), and does not hold for $n=4$ (8 points).

"For any permutation $\pi_1$ of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ different from the identity there is a permutation $\pi_2$ such that any permutation $\pi$ can be obtained from $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ using only compositions (for example, $\pi=\pi_1\circ\pi_1\circ\pi_2\circ\pi_1$)."
answer: The proposition says $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle=S_n$. $n=3$: pair a transposition with a 3-cycle (Lagrange). $n=4$: fails for $\pi_1=(12)(34)$, since $S_4/V_4$ has order $6$ but no element of $S_4$ has order divisible by $6$. $n=5$: explicit partners for one representative of each of the $6$ cycle types, e.g. $(12)$ & $(12345)$, $(123)$ & $(12)(345)$, $(12)(34)$ & $(135)(24)$, $(1234)$ & $(45)$, $(123)(45)$ & $(34)$.

solutions.title: Reduce to generation, then check each cycle type
solutions.body:
**Reformulation.** In a finite group every element has finite order, so $g^{-1}=g^{k-1}$ where $k$ is the order of $g$. Hence the set of all compositions of $\pi_1,\pi_2$ is the subgroup $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle$, and the proposition says: for every $\pi_1\ne\mathrm{id}$ there is $\pi_2$ with $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle=S_n$.

It suffices to check one permutation of each cycle type: if $\pi_1=\sigma x\sigma^{-1}$ and $\langle x,y\rangle=S_n$, then $\langle\pi_1,\sigma y\sigma^{-1}\rangle=\sigma\langle x,y\rangle\sigma^{-1}=S_n$. We use the rule $\sigma(a\,b)\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma(a)\,\sigma(b))$ and the fact that the transpositions $(1\,k)$, $k=2,\dots,n$, generate $S_n$ (every permutation is a product of transpositions and $(a\,b)=(1\,a)(1\,b)(1\,a)$).

**$n=3$.** If $\pi_1$ is a transposition, take $\pi_2=(1\,2\,3)$; if $\pi_1$ is a $3$-cycle, take $\pi_2=(1\,2)$. In both cases $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle$ contains elements of orders $2$ and $3$, so by Lagrange its order is divisible by $6=|S_3|$.

**$n=4$ fails.** Let $x=(1\,2)(3\,4)$ and $V=\{\mathrm{id},(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$, a normal subgroup of $S_4$ with $|S_4/V|=6$. Suppose $\langle x,y\rangle=S_4$. Since $x\in V$, the quotient $S_4/V$ is generated by $yV$, so $yV$ has order $6$. But the order of $yV$ divides the order of $y$, and elements of $S_4$ have orders $1,2,3,4$ — none divisible by $6$. Contradiction; so no $\pi_2$ exists for $\pi_1=(1\,2)(3\,4)$.

**$n=5$.** The non-identity cycle types are $(12)$, $(123)$, $(12)(34)$, $(1234)$, $(123)(45)$, $(12345)$.
1. $x=(1\,2)$, $y=(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$: conjugating $x$ by $y,y^2,y^3$ gives $(2\,3),(3\,4),(4\,5)$; the adjacent transpositions generate $S_5$. Symmetrically, for $x=(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ take $y=(1\,2)$.
2. $x=(1\,2\,3)$, $y=(1\,2)(3\,4\,5)$: $y^3=(1\,2)$ and $y^4=(3\,4\,5)$. Conjugating $(1\,2)$ by $x$ and $x^2$ gives $(2\,3),(3\,1)$. Conjugating $(1\,3)$ by $(3\,4\,5)$ and its square gives $(1\,4),(1\,5)$. So all $(1\,k)$ lie in the subgroup: it is $S_5$.
3. $x=(1\,2)(3\,4)$, $y=(1\,3\,5)(2\,4)$: $y^3=(2\,4)$, $y^4=(1\,3\,5)$. Then $x(2\,4)x^{-1}=(1\,3)$; $(1\,3\,5)$ conjugates $(1\,3)$ to $(3\,5)$; $x$ conjugates $(3\,5)$ to $(4\,5)$. The transpositions $(1\,3),(3\,5),(5\,4),(4\,2)$ form a path through all five points, and they generate $S_5$ (e.g. $(1\,5)=(1\,3)(3\,5)(1\,3)$, and so on along the path).
4. $x=(1\,2\,3\,4)$, $y=(4\,5)$: conjugating $(4\,5)$ by $x,x^2,x^3$ gives $(1\,5),(2\,5),(3\,5)$; the transpositions $(k\,5)$ generate $S_5$.
5. $x=(1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$, $y=(3\,4)$: $x^3=(4\,5)$, $x^4=(1\,2\,3)$. Conjugating $(3\,4)$ by $(1\,2\,3)$ and its square gives $(1\,4),(2\,4)$; together with $(3\,4),(4\,5)$ we have all $(k\,4)$, which generate $S_5$.

So the proposition holds for $n=3$ and $n=5$ and fails for $n=4$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f(x)=2x(1-x)$, $x\in\mathbb R$. Define $f_n=\underbrace{f\circ\dots\circ f}_{n}$.

a) Find $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\displaystyle\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx$.

b) Compute $\displaystyle\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx$ for $n=1,2,\dots$.
answer: $f_n(x)=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\left(x-\frac12\right)^{2^n}$, so $\displaystyle\int_0^1f_n=\frac12-\frac1{2(2^n+1)}$ and the limit is $\frac12$.

solutions.title: Closed form for the iterates
solutions.body:
**b)** Note $f(x)=\frac12-2\left(x-\frac12\right)^2$. We claim
$$f_n(x)=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\left(x-\tfrac12\right)^{2^n}\qquad(n\ge1).$$
For $n=1$ this is the identity above. If it holds for $n$, then
$$f_{n+1}(x)=f_n(f(x))=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\Bigl(-2\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^2\Bigr)^{2^n}=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\,2^{2^n}\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^{2^{n+1}}=\frac12-2^{2^{n+1}-1}\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^{2^{n+1}}.$$
Integrating,
$$\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\left[\frac{(x-\frac12)^{2^n+1}}{2^n+1}\right]_0^1=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\cdot\frac{2\cdot2^{-(2^n+1)}}{2^n+1}=\frac12-\frac1{2(2^n+1)}.$$
(Check: $n=1$ gives $\frac13=\int_0^12x(1-x)\,dx$.)

**a)** Letting $n\to\infty$: $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1f_n=\frac12$.

**Answer: a) $\frac12$; b) $\frac12-\frac1{2(2^n+1)}$.**

solutions.title: Monotone convergence for part a)
solutions.body:
Fix $x_0\in(0,1)$ and let $x_n=f_n(x_0)$. Then $x_1=2x_0(1-x_0)\in(0,\frac12]$, and for $t\in(0,\frac12]$ we have $f(t)-t=t(1-2t)\ge0$ and $f(t)\le\frac12$. So $(x_n)_{n\ge1}$ is nondecreasing and bounded by $\frac12$; its limit $l>0$ satisfies $l=2l(1-l)$, i.e. $l=\frac12$. Thus $f_n\to\frac12$ pointwise on $(0,1)$, with $0\le f_n\le\frac12$ on $[0,1]$, and by dominated convergence $\int_0^1f_n\to\frac12$.

**Answer to a): $\frac12$.**

prompt:
The function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable and satisfies $f(0)=2$, $f'(0)=-2$ and $f(1)=1$. Prove that there exists a real number $\xi\in(0,1)$ for which
$$f(\xi)\cdot f'(\xi)+f''(\xi)=0.$$
answer: $g=\frac12f^2+f'$ has $g'=ff'+f''$ and $g(0)=0$; find $\eta\in(0,1)$ with $g(\eta)=0$ (Rolle for $h=\frac x2-\frac1f$ if $f$ has no zero, otherwise IVT between the first and last zero of $f$), then apply Rolle to $g$ on $[0,\eta]$.

solutions.title: An auxiliary function $g=\frac12f^2+f'$
solutions.body:
Let $g(x)=\frac12f(x)^2+f'(x)$. It is differentiable with $g'=ff'+f''$, and $g(0)=\frac12\cdot4-2=0$. So it suffices to find $\eta\in(0,1)$ with $g(\eta)=0$: Rolle's theorem on $[0,\eta]$ then gives $\xi\in(0,\eta)\subset(0,1)$ with $g'(\xi)=0$.

**Case 1: $f$ has no zero in $[0,1]$.** Then $h(x)=\frac x2-\frac1{f(x)}$ is differentiable on $[0,1]$ and $h(0)=-\frac12=\frac12-1=h(1)$. By Rolle there is $\eta\in(0,1)$ with
$$0=h'(\eta)=\frac12+\frac{f'(\eta)}{f(\eta)^2}=\frac{g(\eta)}{f(\eta)^2},$$
so $g(\eta)=0$.

**Case 2: $f$ has a zero in $[0,1]$.** The zero set is closed and, as $f(0)=2$, $f(1)=1$, contained in $(0,1)$. Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be the smallest and largest zeros. Since $f>0$ on $[0,z_1)$,
$$f'(z_1)=\lim_{x\to z_1^-}\frac{f(x)-0}{x-z_1}\le0,$$
and since $f>0$ on $(z_2,1]$, $f'(z_2)=\lim_{x\to z_2^+}\frac{f(x)}{x-z_2}\ge0$. So $g(z_1)=f'(z_1)\le0\le f'(z_2)=g(z_2)$. As $g$ is continuous ($f'$ is differentiable), the intermediate value theorem gives $\eta\in[z_1,z_2]\subset(0,1)$ with $g(\eta)=0$.

In both cases we are done. ∎

*Remark.* $f(x)=\frac2{x+1}$ satisfies the hypotheses and $ff'+f''\equiv0$.

prompt:
Let $P$ be an algebraic polynomial of degree $n$ having only real zeros and real coefficients.

a) Prove that for every real $x$ the following inequality holds:
$$(n-1)\bigl(P'(x)\bigr)^2\ge nP(x)P''(x).\tag{2}$$

b) Examine the cases of equality.
answer: With $a_i=\frac1{x-x_i}$: $(n-1)\frac{P'^2}{P^2}-n\frac{P''}{P}=\sum_{i<j}(a_i-a_j)^2\ge0$. For $n\ge2$, equality at $x$ holds iff $x$ is a multiple zero of $P$ or all zeros of $P$ coincide ($P=c(x-a)^n$, equality for every $x$); for $n=1$ both sides vanish identically.

solutions.title: Logarithmic derivative
solutions.body:
If $n=1$ then $P''\equiv0$ and both sides of (2) are $0$, so equality always holds. Let $n\ge2$ and $P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n(x-x_i)$ with real $x_i$ (with multiplicity) and $c\ne0$.

**At a zero $x=x_i$:** the right side is $0$ and the left side is $(n-1)P'(x_i)^2\ge0$, with equality iff $P'(x_i)=0$, i.e. iff $x_i$ is a multiple zero.

**At $x$ with $P(x)\ne0$:** put $a_i=\frac1{x-x_i}$. Then
$$\frac{P'}{P}=\sum_ia_i,\qquad \frac{P''}{P}=\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)'+\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2=-\sum_ia_i^2+\Bigl(\sum_ia_i\Bigr)^2=2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j.$$
Hence
$$(n-1)\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2-n\frac{P''}{P}=(n-1)\sum_ia_i^2+2(n-1)\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j-2n\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j=(n-1)\sum_ia_i^2-2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j=\sum_{i<j}(a_i-a_j)^2\ge0.$$
Multiplying by $P(x)^2>0$ gives (2).

**b) Equality** at such an $x$ holds iff all $a_i$ are equal, i.e. $x_1=\dots=x_n$. So, for $n\ge2$: equality holds at $x$ iff $x$ is a multiple zero of $P$, or all zeros of $P$ coincide. In the latter case $P=c(x-a)^n$, and indeed $(n-1)n^2c^2(x-a)^{2n-2}=n\cdot c(x-a)^n\cdot n(n-1)c(x-a)^{n-2}$ for all $x$: (2) is an identity exactly for these polynomials. ∎

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
For $P(x)\ne0$ and $a_i=\frac1{x-x_i}$ as above, $\frac{P'}{P}=\sum a_i$ and $\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2-\frac{P''}{P}=-\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)'=\sum a_i^2$. By Cauchy–Schwarz, $\bigl(\sum a_i\bigr)^2\le n\sum a_i^2$, i.e.
$$\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2\le n\Bigl(\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2-\frac{P''}{P}\Bigr)\iff nP P''\le(n-1)P'^2,$$
with equality iff all $a_i$ are equal, i.e. all zeros coincide. At zeros of $P$ argue as in the first solution. ∎

prompt:
Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous function with the property that for any $x$ and $y$ in the interval,
$$xf(y)+yf(x)\le1.$$
a) Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\le\frac\pi4$.

b) Find a function, satisfying the condition, for which there is equality.
answer: a) Substituting $x=\sin\theta$ and $x=\cos\theta$: $2\int_0^1f=\int_0^{\pi/2}\bigl(\cos\theta f(\sin\theta)+\sin\theta f(\cos\theta)\bigr)d\theta\le\frac\pi2$. b) $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$.

solutions.title: Two trigonometric substitutions
solutions.body:
**a)** Let $I=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$. The substitutions $x=\sin\theta$ and $x=\cos\theta$ ($\theta\in[0,\frac\pi2]$) give
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}f(\sin\theta)\cos\theta\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/2}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta.$$
Adding and applying the hypothesis with $x=\sin\theta$, $y=\cos\theta$ (both in $[0,1]$):
$$2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\bigl(\sin\theta\,f(\cos\theta)+\cos\theta\,f(\sin\theta)\bigr)d\theta\le\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,d\theta=\frac\pi2 .$$
So $I\le\frac\pi4$.

**b)** Let $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, continuous on $[0,1]$. For $x,y\in[0,1]$ write $x=\sin\theta$, $y=\sin\varphi$ with $\theta,\varphi\in[0,\frac\pi2]$; then $f(x)=\cos\theta$, $f(y)=\cos\varphi$ and
$$xf(y)+yf(x)=\sin\theta\cos\varphi+\cos\theta\sin\varphi=\sin(\theta+\varphi)\le1 .$$
Its integral is the area of a quarter of the unit disc, $\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx=\frac\pi4$, so equality holds. ∎

prompt: Let $V$ be a real vector space, and let $f,f_1,f_2,\dots,f_k$ be linear maps from $V$ to $\mathbb R$. Suppose that $f(x)=0$ whenever $f_1(x)=f_2(x)=\dots=f_k(x)=0$. Prove that $f$ is a linear combination of $f_1,f_2,\dots,f_k$.
answer: $\Phi=(f_1,\dots,f_k):V\to\mathbb R^k$ has $\ker\Phi\subseteq\ker f$, so $f=L\circ\Phi$ for a linear $L$ on $\Phi(V)$; extend $L$ to $\mathbb R^k$, $L(t)=\sum c_it_i$, giving $f=\sum c_if_i$.

solutions.title: Factor through $\mathbb R^k$
solutions.body:
Let $\Phi:V\to\mathbb R^k$, $\Phi(x)=(f_1(x),\dots,f_k(x))$, a linear map. The hypothesis says $\ker\Phi\subseteq\ker f$.

Define $L:\Phi(V)\to\mathbb R$ by $L(\Phi(x))=f(x)$. This is well defined: if $\Phi(x)=\Phi(x')$ then $x-x'\in\ker\Phi\subseteq\ker f$, so $f(x)=f(x')$. It is linear because $f$ and $\Phi$ are. The image $W=\Phi(V)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^k$; extend a basis of $W$ to a basis of $\mathbb R^k$ and define $L$ to be $0$ on the added vectors. This gives a linear functional on $\mathbb R^k$, which has the form $L(t_1,\dots,t_k)=c_1t_1+\dots+c_kt_k$. Hence for all $x\in V$
$$f(x)=L(\Phi(x))=c_1f_1(x)+\dots+c_kf_k(x).\ \blacksquare$$

solutions.title: Induction with a dual system of vectors
solutions.body:
Induction on $k$; the case $k=0$ (then $f\equiv0$) is trivial. Discarding some $f_i$ that are linear combinations of the others does not change the common kernel, so we may assume $f_1,\dots,f_k$ are linearly independent.

For each $j$ there is $a_j\in V$ with $f_i(a_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $f_j(a_j)=1$: otherwise $f_j$ vanishes on $\bigcap_{i\ne j}\ker f_i$, and by the induction hypothesis (with $k-1$ functionals) $f_j$ would be a combination of the others, contradicting independence; then normalize. Now for any $x\in V$ the vector $z=x-\sum_jf_j(x)a_j$ satisfies $f_i(z)=f_i(x)-f_i(x)=0$ for all $i$, so $f(z)=0$, i.e.
$$f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^kf(a_j)\,f_j(x).\ \blacksquare$$

prompt:
Let
$$\mathcal P=\Bigl\{f:\ f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^3a_kx^k,\ a_k\in\mathbb R,\ |f(\pm1)|\le1,\ \bigl|f(\pm\tfrac12)\bigr|\le1\Bigr\}.$$
Evaluate
$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal P}\ \max_{-1\le x\le1}|f''(x)|$$
and find all polynomials $f\in\mathcal P$ for which the above "sup" is attained.
answer: The supremum is $24$, attained exactly for $f=\pm T_3=\pm(4x^3-3x)$. Key formula: $f''(1)=\frac{16}3f(1)-\frac{28}3f(\tfrac12)+\frac{20}3f(-\tfrac12)-\frac83f(-1)$ (and symmetrically for $f''(-1)$).

solutions.title: Express $f''(\pm1)$ through the four values
solutions.body:
Write $A=f(-1)$, $B=f(-\frac12)$, $C=f(\frac12)$, $D=f(1)$ for $f=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+a_3x^3$. Then
$$D+A=2a_0+2a_2,\quad C+B=2a_0+\tfrac12a_2\ \Rightarrow\ a_2=\tfrac23(A+D-B-C),$$
$$D-A=2a_1+2a_3,\quad C-B=a_1+\tfrac14a_3\ \Rightarrow\ a_3=\tfrac23\bigl(D-A-2C+2B\bigr).$$
Since $f''(x)=6a_3x+2a_2$ is linear, $\max_{[-1,1]}|f''|=\max(|f''(1)|,|f''(-1)|)$, and
$$f''(1)=6a_3+2a_2=\tfrac{16}3D-\tfrac{28}3C+\tfrac{20}3B-\tfrac83A,$$
$$f''(-1)=-6a_3+2a_2=\tfrac{16}3A-\tfrac{28}3B+\tfrac{20}3C-\tfrac83D.$$
For $f\in\mathcal P$, $|A|,|B|,|C|,|D|\le1$, so by the triangle inequality
$$|f''(\pm1)|\le\tfrac{16+28+20+8}3=24 .$$
**Equality.** $|f''(1)|=24$ forces $|A|=|B|=|C|=|D|=1$ with the signs of $D,C,B,A$ equal to $\varepsilon\cdot(+,-,+,-)$ for a common $\varepsilon=\pm1$, i.e. $(A,B,C,D)=\varepsilon(-1,1,-1,1)$. A cubic is determined by its values at four points (Lagrange interpolation), and the Chebyshev polynomial $T_3(x)=4x^3-3x$ takes the values $T_3(-1)=-1$, $T_3(-\frac12)=1$, $T_3(\frac12)=-1$, $T_3(1)=1$. Hence $f=\varepsilon T_3$. Likewise $|f''(-1)|=24$ forces $(A,B,C,D)=\varepsilon(1,-1,1,-1)$, i.e. again $f=\pm T_3$.

Conversely $\pm T_3\in\mathcal P$ and $|T_3''(x)|=|24x|$ has maximum $24$ on $[-1,1]$.

**Answer: the supremum is $24$, attained exactly for $f(x)=\pm(4x^3-3x)$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $0<c<1$ and
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac xc,&x\in[0,c],\\[2mm]\dfrac{1-x}{1-c},&x\in[c,1].\end{cases}$$
We say that $p$ is an $n$-periodic point if
$$\underbrace{f(f(\dots f}_{n}(p)))=p$$
and $n$ is the smallest number with this property. Prove that for every $n\ge1$ the set of $n$-periodic points is non-empty and finite.
answer: $f^n$ consists of $2^n$ affine pieces, each mapping its interval onto $[0,1]$, so $f^n$ has exactly $2^n$ fixed points. At most $2+4+\dots+2^{n-1}=2^n-2$ of them have a smaller period, so at least $2$ (and finitely many) are $n$-periodic.

solutions.title: Count fixed points of the iterates
solutions.body:
Let $f^n$ denote the $n$-th iterate.

**Claim.** $[0,1]$ is the union of $2^n$ closed intervals $J$ with disjoint interiors such that on each $J$ the map $f^n$ is affine and maps $J$ bijectively onto $[0,1]$.

For $n=1$ take $[0,c]$ and $[c,1]$. If the claim holds for $n$, take a piece $J$ for $f^n$; since $f^n|_J$ is an affine bijection onto $[0,1]$, the preimages of $[0,c]$ and $[c,1]$ split $J$ into two closed subintervals, and on each of them $f^{n+1}=f\circ f^n$ is a composition of affine bijections onto $[0,1]$. This gives $2^{n+1}$ pieces.

**Fixed points of $f^n$.** Let $J=[s,t]$ be a piece. Its length is $<1$ (there are $2^n\ge2$ pieces), so $f^n|_J$ has slope $\pm\frac1{t-s}$ with absolute value $>1$; therefore $f^n(x)-x$ is strictly monotone on $J$. If $f^n$ increases on $J$, then $f^n(s)-s=-s\le0$ and $f^n(t)-t=1-t\ge0$; if it decreases, $f^n(s)-s=1-s\ge0$ and $f^n(t)-t=-t\le0$. Either way $f^n$ has exactly one fixed point in $J$. A fixed point cannot be a common endpoint of two pieces: such an endpoint $e$ lies in $(0,1)$ while $f^n(e)\in\{0,1\}$. Hence $f^n$ has exactly $2^n$ fixed points.

**Conclusion.** Every $n$-periodic point is a fixed point of $f^n$, so there are finitely many. A fixed point of $f^n$ that is not $n$-periodic is a fixed point of some $f^k$ with $1\le k\le n-1$; there are at most $2+2^2+\dots+2^{n-1}=2^n-2$ such points. So at least $2^n-(2^n-2)=2$ fixed points of $f^n$ are $n$-periodic; in particular the set is non-empty. ∎

prompt:
Let $A_n=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, where $n\ge3$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the family of all non-constant functions $f:A_n\to A_n$ satisfying the following conditions:

(1) $f(k)\le f(k+1)$ for $k=1,2,\dots,n-1$,

(2) $f(k)=f(f(k+1))$ for $k=1,2,\dots,n-1$.

Find the number of functions in $\mathcal F$.
answer: $\binom n3$. Every $f\in\mathcal F$ is $f(i)=k$ for $i\le m$, $f(m+1)=l$, $f(i)=i-1$ for $i\ge m+2$, with $1\le k<l\le m\le n-1$; these correspond to the $3$-subsets $\{k<l<m+1\}$ of $A_n$.

solutions.title: Structure of the functions
solutions.body:
**The functions.** For $1\le k<l\le m\le n-1$ define
$$f_{k,l,m}(i)=\begin{cases}k,&i\le m,\\ l,&i=m+1,\\ i-1,&i\ge m+2.\end{cases}$$
It is nondecreasing ($k<l$, and $l\le m<m+1=f(m+2)$) and non-constant. Condition (2): for $i\le m-1$, $f(f(i+1))=f(k)=k$ since $k\le m$; for $i=m$, $f(f(m+1))=f(l)=k=f(m)$ since $l\le m$; for $i=m+1$, $f(f(m+2))=f(m+1)$; for $i\ge m+2$, $f(f(i+1))=f(i)$. So $f_{k,l,m}\in\mathcal F$.

**Every $f\in\mathcal F$ is of this form.** Let $f\in\mathcal F$ and $k=f(1)$.
1. *A value taken twice is a fixed point.* If $f(i)=f(i+1)=v$ then by (2) $f(v)=f(f(i+1))=f(i)=v$. Such a pair exists: otherwise $f$ is strictly increasing, hence the identity, but the identity violates (2) ($k\ne k+1$).
2. *If $f(v)=v$ then $f\equiv v$ on $\{1,\dots,v\}$.* Indeed if $f(j)=v$ for some $j\ge2$, then $f(j-1)=f(f(j))=f(v)=v$; descend from $j=v$. In particular $v=f(1)=k$: **$k$ is the only fixed point**, $f\equiv k$ on $\{1,\dots,k\}$, and by 1 (a value taken twice by a nondecreasing function is taken at two consecutive places) every value other than $k$ is taken at most once.
3. Let $m=\max\{i:f(i)=k\}$. Then $k\le m\le n-1$ ($f$ is non-constant), $f\equiv k$ on $\{1,\dots,m\}$ by monotonicity, and $f$ is strictly increasing on $\{m+1,\dots,n\}$ with values $>k$.
4. *$f(i)<i$ for $i>m$.* $f(i)=i$ is impossible ($i>k$ would be a second fixed point). If $f(i)>i$ for some $i>m$, strict increase gives $f(n)\ge f(i)+(n-i)>n$, impossible.
5. *$f(i)=i-1$ for $i\ge m+2$.* Here $f(i)>f(m+1)>k$. If $f(i)\le m$ then $f(i-1)=f(f(i))=k$, contradicting $i-1\ge m+1$. So $m+1\le f(i)\le i-1$, and $f(f(i))=f(i-1)$ with both $f(i)$ and $i-1$ in $\{m+1,\dots,n\}$, where $f$ is injective; hence $f(i)=i-1$.
6. Put $l=f(m+1)$; by 3 and 4, $k<l\le m$.

So $f=f_{k,l,m}$, and different triples give different functions.

**Counting.** $(k,l,m)\mapsto\{k,l,m+1\}$ is a bijection from triples with $1\le k<l\le m\le n-1$ onto the $3$-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (since $k<l<m+1\le n$). Hence
$$|\mathcal F|=\binom n3 .$$
(For example $n=3$: only $f=(1,1,2)$; $n=4$: four functions.) ∎

prompt: Suppose that $\mathcal S$ is a family of spheres (i.e., surfaces of balls of positive radius) in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, such that the intersection of any two contains at most one point. Prove that the set $M$ of those points that belong to at least two different spheres from $\mathcal S$ is countable.
answer: Each $x\in M$ is a tangency point of two spheres $S,T$ of $\mathcal S$. Code $x$ by a label (external/internal tangency) and two rational points: in $B(S),B(T)$ for external tangency, in the shell $B(S)\setminus\overline{B(T)}$ and in $B(T)$ for internal tangency ($T$ inside $S$). Since open balls of spheres in $\mathcal S$ are disjoint or nested, the code determines $x$.

solutions.title: Encode each point by rational points in balls
solutions.body:
For a sphere $S$ with centre $a$ and radius $r$ let $B(S)$ be the open ball and $\overline B(S)$ the closed ball.

**Fact.** Let $S\ne S'$ be spheres (centres $a,a'$, radii $r,r'$, $d=|a-a'|$) meeting in at most one point. Then either $d\ge r+r'$ — the open balls are disjoint and the closed balls meet in at most one point — or $d\le|r-r'|$ — the balls are nested, e.g. $B(S')\subseteq B(S)$ if $r'\le r$. Indeed, if $|r-r'|<d<r+r'$, a triangle with sides $d,r,r'$ exists, and rotating it about the line $aa'$ (possible as $n\ge2$) produces at least two common points. In particular, **any two open balls of (equal or distinct) spheres of $\mathcal S$ are disjoint or nested.**

For each $x\in M$ fix spheres $S\ne T$ in $\mathcal S$ through $x$; then $S\cap T=\{x\}$, so by the Fact either
- (E) $B(S)\cap B(T)=\varnothing$ and $\overline B(S)\cap\overline B(T)=\{x\}$ (external tangency), or
- (I) after renaming, $B(T)\subsetneq B(S)$ and $S\cap T=\{x\}$ (internal tangency).

Choose points with rational coordinates: in case (E), $u\in B(S)$, $v\in B(T)$; in case (I), $u\in B(S)\setminus\overline B(T)$ (a nonempty open shell) and $v\in B(T)$. Map $x\mapsto(\text{label},u,v)$, a map into the countable set $\{E,I\}\times\mathbb Q^n\times\mathbb Q^n$. We show it is injective; then $M$ is countable.

**Two points of type (E) with the same code.** Let $x,x'$ come from $(S,T)$ and $(S',T')$ with $u\in B(S)\cap B(S')$, $v\in B(T)\cap B(T')$. These pairs of balls intersect, so they are nested; by symmetry assume $B(S)\subseteq B(S')$.
- If $B(T)\subseteq B(T')$: $\{x\}=\overline B(S)\cap\overline B(T)\subseteq\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T')=\{x'\}$, so $x=x'$.
- If $B(T')\subseteq B(T)$: compare $B(S')$ and $B(T)$. $B(S')\subseteq B(T)$ is impossible ($u\in B(S)\subseteq B(S')$ but $B(S)\cap B(T)=\varnothing$), and so is $B(T)\subseteq B(S')$ ($v\in B(T')\subseteq B(T)$ but $B(S')\cap B(T')=\varnothing$); in particular $S'\ne T$. So $B(S')\cap B(T)=\varnothing$ and $\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T)$ has at most one point. Both $x\in\overline B(S)\cap\overline B(T)$ and $x'\in\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T')$ lie in $\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T)$; hence $x=x'$.

**Two points of type (I) with the same code.** Now $u\in(B(S)\setminus\overline B(T))\cap(B(S')\setminus\overline B(T'))$, $v\in B(T)\cap B(T')$. By symmetry $B(T)\subseteq B(T')$. The balls $B(T')$ and $B(S)$ both contain $v$, so they are nested; $B(S)\subseteq B(T')$ is impossible since $u\in B(S)$, $u\notin\overline B(T')$. Hence $B(T')\subsetneq B(S)$. Now $x\in\overline B(T)\subseteq\overline B(T')$ and $x\in S$, so $x\notin B(T')\subseteq B(S)$; thus $x\in T'$. The balls $B(S),B(S')$ share $u$, so they are nested:
- If $B(S)\subseteq B(S')$: $x'\in T'\subseteq\overline B(T')\subseteq\overline B(S)$ and $x'\in S'$, so $x'\notin B(S)$; hence $x'\in S$. So $x,x'\in T'\cap S$ with $T'\ne S$, and $x=x'$.
- If $B(S')\subseteq B(S)$: $x\in\overline B(T')\subseteq\overline B(S')$ and $x\in S$, so $x\notin B(S')$, i.e. $x\in S'$. So $x,x'\in T'\cap S'$ with $T'\ne S'$, and $x=x'$.

Hence the coding is injective and $M$ is countable. ∎

prompt:
Let $f:(0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ be a function that is zero except at the distinct points $a_1,a_2,\dots$. Let $b_n=f(a_n)$.

(a) Prove that if $\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n<\infty$, then $f$ is differentiable at at least one point $x\in(0,1)$.

(b) Prove that for any sequence of non-negative real numbers $(b_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ with $\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n=\infty$, there exists a sequence $(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ such that the function $f$ defined as above is nowhere differentiable.
answer: (a) Choose $c_n\to\infty$ with $\sum c_nb_n<\frac12$; the intervals $(a_n-c_nb_n,a_n+c_nb_n)$ have total length $<1$, and at any uncovered $x_0$ the difference quotients are $\le1/c_n$, so $f'(x_0)=0$. (b) Choose $\beta_n\le b_n$, $\beta_n\to0$, with block sums $\ge1$; place the $a_n$ so that each block's intervals of length $\beta_n$ cover $(0,1)$; then every $x_0$ has $a_n$ within $\beta_n$ with quotient $\ge1$.

solutions.title: Small covering intervals
solutions.body:
**Preliminary.** If $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$, then $f(x_0)=0$ and $f'(x_0)=0$. Indeed $f$ vanishes outside a countable set, so every interval contains points where $f=0$. If $f(x_0)>0$, then $f$ is not continuous at $x_0$. If $f(x_0)=0$, the difference quotient is $0$ along points $x\to x_0$ with $f(x)=0$, so $f'(x_0)=0$.

**(a)** If all $b_n=0$, $f\equiv0$. Otherwise let $B=\sum b_n>0$. Since the tails $\sum_{n\ge N}b_n\to0$, choose $N_1<N_2<\dots$ with $\sum_{n\ge N_k}b_n\le4^{-k}$, and put $c_n=1$ for $n<N_1$ and $c_n=2^k$ for $N_k\le n<N_{k+1}$. Then $c_n\to\infty$ and
$$\sum_nc_nb_n\le B+\sum_{k\ge1}2^k\sum_{n\ge N_k}b_n\le B+\sum_k2^{-k}=B+1 .$$
Replacing $c_n$ by $c_n/(4(B+1))$ we get $c_n\to\infty$ and $\sum c_nb_n\le\frac14$.

Let $I_n=(a_n-c_nb_n,\,a_n+c_nb_n)$ (empty if $b_n=0$). Their total length is $\le\frac12<1$, so they do not cover $(0,1)$: otherwise, for small $\delta>0$ the compact set $[\delta,1-\delta]$ would be covered by finitely many $I_n$, forcing $1-2\delta\le\frac12$. Take $x_0\in(0,1)$ in no $I_n$. Then $f(x_0)=0$ (if $x_0=a_n$, then $b_n=0$). For $x\ne x_0$: if $f(x)=0$ the difference quotient is $0$; if $x=a_n$ with $b_n>0$, then $|a_n-x_0|\ge c_nb_n$, so
$$\left|\frac{f(a_n)-f(x_0)}{a_n-x_0}\right|\le\frac{b_n}{c_nb_n}=\frac1{c_n}.$$
Given $\varepsilon>0$, only finitely many $n$ have $1/c_n\ge\varepsilon$, and the corresponding $a_n$ are at positive distance from $x_0$. So in a small neighbourhood of $x_0$ all difference quotients are $<\varepsilon$: $f'(x_0)=0$.

**(b)** Since $\sum b_n=\infty$, also $\sum\min(b_n,1)=\infty$, hence $\sum_{n\ge s}\min(b_n,\frac1k)\ge\frac1k\sum_{n\ge s}\min(b_n,1)=\infty$ for every $s,k$. So we can split $\mathbb N$ into consecutive finite blocks $J_1,J_2,\dots$ with $\sum_{n\in J_k}\beta_n\ge1$, where $\beta_n=\min(b_n,\frac1k)$ for $n\in J_k$. Thus $0\le\beta_n\le b_n$ and $\beta_n\le\frac1k$ on $J_k$.

Choose the $a_n$ block by block. In block $J_k$, list the $n$ with $\beta_n>0$ in order and lay consecutive closed intervals $[L_n,R_n]$ of length $\beta_n$ starting at $0$ ($L=0$, $R=\beta_n$, the next one starts where the previous ends), stopping once some $R_n\ge1$; as the lengths sum to $\ge1$, these intervals cover $[0,1]$. For each such $n$ pick $a_n\in(L_n,R_n)\cap(0,1)$ different from all previously chosen points (possible: a nonempty open interval is infinite). For all remaining $n$ pick any new point $a_n\in(0,1)$. The $a_n$ are distinct.

Let $x_0\in(0,1)$. If $f(x_0)>0$, $f$ is not differentiable at $x_0$ by the preliminary remark. If $f(x_0)=0$: for each $k$ some $n\in J_k$ has $x_0\in[L_n,R_n]$, so $|a_n-x_0|\le\beta_n\le\frac1k$, and $a_n\ne x_0$ because $f(a_n)=b_n\ge\beta_n>0$. Then
$$\frac{|f(a_n)-f(x_0)|}{|a_n-x_0|}\ge\frac{b_n}{\beta_n}\ge1 .$$
So there are points arbitrarily close to $x_0$ with difference quotient $\ge1$, contradicting $f'(x_0)=0$. Hence $f$ is nowhere differentiable. ∎

prompt:
a) Show that for any $m\in\mathbb N$ there exists a real $m\times m$ matrix $A$ such that $A^3=A+I$, where $I$ is the $m\times m$ identity matrix.

b) Show that $\det A>0$ for every real $m\times m$ matrix satisfying $A^3=A+I$.
answer: a) $A=\lambda I$ with $\lambda$ the real root of $\lambda^3=\lambda+1$. b) The eigenvalues are roots of $x^3-x-1$: one real root $\lambda_1>0$ and a non-real conjugate pair $\lambda_2,\overline{\lambda_2}$ of equal multiplicity, so $\det A=\lambda_1^\alpha|\lambda_2|^{2\beta}>0$.

solutions.title: Eigenvalues are roots of $x^3-x-1$
solutions.body:
Let $p(x)=x^3-x-1$.

**a)** $p$ is a real cubic, so it has a real root $\lambda$. Then $A=\lambda I$ satisfies $A^3-A-I=(\lambda^3-\lambda-1)I=0$.

**b)** *The roots of $p$.* $p'(x)=3x^2-1$, so $p$ has a local maximum at $-\frac1{\sqrt3}$ with value $-\frac1{3\sqrt3}+\frac1{\sqrt3}-1=\frac2{3\sqrt3}-1<0$ and a local minimum at $\frac1{\sqrt3}$ (even smaller). Hence $p<0$ on $(-\infty,\frac1{\sqrt3}]$, $p$ is increasing on $[\frac1{\sqrt3},\infty)$, and $p$ has exactly one real root $\lambda_1$, which is positive. The other two roots are a non-real conjugate pair $\lambda_2,\lambda_3=\overline{\lambda_2}$.

*Eigenvalues of $A$.* If $Av=\mu v$ with $v\ne0$ (over $\mathbb C$), then $0=(A^3-A-I)v=p(\mu)v$, so $p(\mu)=0$. Thus the characteristic polynomial $\chi_A$ (degree $m$, real coefficients) has all its roots among $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$. Since $\chi_A$ is real, the non-real roots $\lambda_2,\overline{\lambda_2}$ occur with the same multiplicity $\beta$; let $\alpha$ be the multiplicity of $\lambda_1$. Then
$$\det A=\lambda_1^{\alpha}\,\lambda_2^{\beta}\,\overline{\lambda_2}^{\,\beta}=\lambda_1^{\alpha}\,|\lambda_2|^{2\beta}>0,$$
because $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2\ne0$. ∎

prompt:
Does there exist a bijective map $\pi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ such that
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}<\infty\ ?$$
answer: **No.** For every $N$, at least $N$ of $\pi(N+1),\dots,\pi(3N)$ exceed $N$, so $\sum_{n=N+1}^{3N}\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}>\frac19$: the Cauchy criterion fails.

solutions.title: Blocks $N+1,\dots,3N$
solutions.body:
**No.** Let $\pi$ be any bijection of $\mathbb N$ and $N\in\mathbb N$. Among the $2N$ distinct numbers $\pi(N+1),\dots,\pi(3N)$ at most $N$ are $\le N$, so at least $N$ of them are $>N$. Hence
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{3N}\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}\ \ge\ \frac1{(3N)^2}\sum_{n=N+1}^{3N}\pi(n)\ >\ \frac1{9N^2}\cdot N\cdot N=\frac19 .$$
This holds for every $N$, so the partial sums of the positive series do not form a Cauchy sequence: the series diverges. ∎

solutions.title: Summation by parts
solutions.body:
Let $s_n=\pi(1)+\dots+\pi(n)$. The numbers $\pi(1),\dots,\pi(n)$ are distinct positive integers, so $s_n\ge1+2+\dots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2$. Abel summation (all terms are positive, so rearranging is fine) gives
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty s_n\left(\frac1{n^2}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\right)\ge\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{n(n+1)}2\cdot\frac{2n+1}{n^2(n+1)^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)}\ge\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n+1}=\infty .$$
(To justify the first equality for partial sums: $\sum_{n\le N}\frac{\pi(n)}{n^2}=\sum_{n<N}s_n\bigl(\frac1{n^2}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\bigr)+\frac{s_N}{N^2}\ge\sum_{n<N}s_n\bigl(\frac1{n^2}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\bigr)$.) So no such bijection exists. ∎

prompt:
Suppose that a function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfies the inequality
$$\left|\sum_{k=1}^n3^k\bigl(f(x+ky)-f(x-ky)\bigr)\right|\le1\tag{1}$$
for every positive integer $n$ and for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Prove that $f$ is a constant function.
answer: Subtracting (1) for $n-1$ from (1) for $n$ gives $|f(x+ny)-f(x-ny)|\le\frac2{3^n}$; with $x=\frac{u+v}2$, $y=\frac{v-u}{2n}$ this is $|f(v)-f(u)|\le\frac2{3^n}$ for all $n$.

solutions.title: Isolate the last term
solutions.body:
Fix $x,y$ and $n\ge2$. Applying (1) with $n$ and with $n-1$ and using the triangle inequality,
$$3^n\bigl|f(x+ny)-f(x-ny)\bigr|=\left|\sum_{k=1}^n3^k(\dots)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}3^k(\dots)\right|\le1+1=2 .$$
(For $n=1$, (1) itself gives $3|f(x+y)-f(x-y)|\le1$.) Hence
$$|f(x+ny)-f(x-ny)|\le\frac2{3^n}\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R,\ n\ge1 .$$
Given any $u,v\in\mathbb R$ and $n\ge1$, choose $x=\frac{u+v}2$ and $y=\frac{v-u}{2n}$, so that $x-ny=u$ and $x+ny=v$. Then $|f(v)-f(u)|\le\frac2{3^n}$ for every $n$; letting $n\to\infty$, $f(u)=f(v)$. So $f$ is constant. ∎

prompt:
Find all strictly monotonic functions $f:(0,+\infty)\to(0,+\infty)$ such that
$$f\!\left(\frac{x^2}{f(x)}\right)=x\quad\text{for all }x>0.$$
answer: $f(x)=Cx$ with any constant $C>0$. With $g(x)=f(x)/x$: $f^{-1}(x)=x/g(x)$, $g$ is constant on orbits, so $f^{(m)}(x)=x\,g(x)^m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$; monotonicity of $f^{(2m)}$ forces $g$ constant.

solutions.title: Iterate along orbits
solutions.body:
**Check.** For $f(x)=Cx$ ($C>0$): $f\bigl(\frac{x^2}{Cx}\bigr)=f\bigl(\frac xC\bigr)=x$, and $f$ is strictly increasing. We show there are no other solutions.

Let $f$ be a solution and $g(x)=\frac{f(x)}x>0$. The equation shows that $f$ is surjective; being strictly monotone it is injective, so $f$ is a bijection of $(0,\infty)$ and $f^{-1}$ is strictly monotone of the same type. The equation says
$$f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x^2}{f(x)}=\frac x{g(x)} .$$
Then $g\bigl(f^{-1}(x)\bigr)=\dfrac{x}{x/g(x)}=g(x)$, and replacing $x$ by $f(x)$: $g(f(x))=g(x)$. So $g$ is constant along each orbit of $f$.

**Claim:** $f^{(m)}(x)=x\,g(x)^m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ (with $f^{(-m)}=(f^{-1})^{(m)}$). For $m=0,1,-1$ this is clear. If it holds for $m\ge1$, then $f^{(m+1)}(x)=f^{(m)}(x)\,g\bigl(f^{(m)}(x)\bigr)=x\,g(x)^m\cdot g(x)$, using the invariance of $g$ on orbits; the negative direction is identical with $f^{-1}(z)=z/g(z)$.

**$g$ is constant.** $f^{(2)}=f\circ f$ is strictly increasing (a composition of two strictly increasing or two strictly decreasing maps), and so is $f^{(2m)}$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$. Suppose $0<a<b$ and $g(a)\ne g(b)$. Then for all $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$a\,g(a)^{2m}<b\,g(b)^{2m},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \left(\frac{g(a)}{g(b)}\right)^{2m}<\frac ba .$$
If $g(a)/g(b)>1$, let $m\to+\infty$; if $g(a)/g(b)<1$, let $m\to-\infty$. In both cases the left side tends to $+\infty$ — a contradiction. Hence $g\equiv C$ is constant, $C>0$, and $f(x)=Cx$.

**Answer: $f(x)=Cx$ for an arbitrary constant $C>0$.** ∎

prompt: Suppose that $2n$ points of an $n\times n$ grid are marked. Show that for some $k>1$ one can select $2k$ distinct marked points, say $a_1,\dots,a_{2k}$, such that $a_1$ and $a_2$ are in the same row, $a_2$ and $a_3$ are in the same column, $\dots$, $a_{2k-1}$ and $a_{2k}$ are in the same row, and $a_{2k}$ and $a_1$ are in the same column.
answer: Bipartite graph: rows and columns are the $2n$ vertices, marked points are the $2n$ edges. A graph with as many edges as vertices contains a cycle, and a cycle $r_1c_1r_2c_2\dots r_kc_k$ ($k\ge2$) gives the required marked points.

solutions.title: A cycle in the row–column graph
solutions.body:
Build a bipartite graph $G$: its vertices are the $n$ rows and the $n$ columns; join row $r$ and column $c$ by an edge iff the cell $(r,c)$ is marked. $G$ has $2n$ vertices and $2n$ edges, and no multiple edges.

**$G$ contains a cycle.** A graph without cycles (a forest) on $N$ vertices has at most $N-1$ edges: a forest with at least one edge has a vertex of degree $1$ (the end of a longest path), and deleting it removes one vertex and one edge, so induction on $N$ works. Since $G$ has $2n>2n-1$ edges, it has a cycle.

Because $G$ is bipartite and simple, the cycle has even length $2k$ with $k\ge2$; write it as
$$r_1,c_1,r_2,c_2,\dots,r_k,c_k,(r_1),$$
with distinct rows $r_i$ and distinct columns $c_i$; the edges are $r_ic_i$ and $c_ir_{i+1}$ (indices mod $k$), i.e. the marked cells $P_i=(r_i,c_i)$ and $Q_i=(r_{i+1},c_i)$. Take
$$a_1=Q_k=(r_1,c_k),\ a_2=P_1,\ a_3=Q_1,\ a_4=P_2,\ \dots,\ a_{2k-1}=Q_{k-1},\ a_{2k}=P_k .$$
Then $a_{2i-1}=Q_{i-1}=(r_i,c_{i-1})$ and $a_{2i}=P_i=(r_i,c_i)$ share row $r_i$; $a_{2i}=P_i$ and $a_{2i+1}=Q_i=(r_{i+1},c_i)$ share column $c_i$; finally $a_{2k}=(r_k,c_k)$ and $a_1=(r_1,c_k)$ share column $c_k$. The $2k$ points are distinct because they are distinct edges of the cycle, and $k>1$. ∎

solutions.title: Delete sparse lines, then walk
solutions.body:
We prove more generally: if at least $p+q$ cells of a $p\times q$ grid are marked, the required configuration exists.

Delete any row or column containing at most one marked point; this lowers $p+q$ by $1$ and the number of marked points by at most $1$, so the hypothesis persists. Repeat until every remaining row and column contains at least two marked points. The grid never becomes empty: a grid with a single row has at most $q<1+q$ cells, so the invariant "at least $p+q$ marked points" forces at least two rows and two columns at every stage.

Now walk: start at a marked point $b_1$, let $b_2$ be another marked point in its row, $b_3$ another marked point in the column of $b_2$, and so on, alternating row and column moves. By finiteness some point repeats; let $b_m=b_l$ ($l<m$) be the first repetition. If $m-l$ is even, $b_l,\dots,b_{m-1}$ (started at a row step or shifted by one) is an alternating closed sequence of distinct points. If $m-l$ is odd, $b_{l}=b_m$, $b_{l+1}$ and $b_{m-1}$ lie on one line, so dropping $b_l$ and joining $b_{m-1}$ directly to $b_{l+1}$ gives an alternating closed sequence of even length $m-l-1$. A closed alternating sequence needs at least $4$ points (two points in the same row are not in the same column), so $k\ge2$. ∎

prompt:
a) For each $1<p<\infty$ find a constant $c_p<\infty$ for which the following statement holds: If $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ is a continuously differentiable function satisfying $f(1)>f(-1)$ and $|f'(y)|\le1$ for all $y\in[-1,1]$, then there is an $x\in[-1,1]$ such that $f'(x)>0$ and
$$|f(y)-f(x)|\le c_p\bigl(f'(x)\bigr)^{1/p}|y-x|\quad\text{for all }y\in[-1,1].$$
b) Does such a constant also exist for $p=1$?
answer: a) $c_p=\frac{6p}{p-1}$ works: otherwise $\{f'>t\}\subseteq\{M|f'|>c_pt^{1/p}\}$, and the maximal inequality plus $\int|f'|<2\int f'^+$ and the layer-cake formula give $\int f'^+<\int f'^+$. b) **No**: for each $c$ there is an even $f'$ (equal to $-1$ near $0$, then a positive profile decaying like $x^{-1-\beta}$, $\beta<\frac1c$) for which every $x$ with $f'(x)>0$ violates the inequality.

solutions.title: Maximal inequality; an explicit counterexample for $p=1$
solutions.body:
Write $g=\max(f',0)$ and $h=\max(-f',0)$, so $f'=g-h$, $|f'|=g+h$.

**a)** We show that $c=c_p=\frac{6p}{p-1}$ works. Since $0<f(1)-f(-1)=\int_{-1}^1g-\int_{-1}^1h$, we get
$$\int_{-1}^1|f'|=\int g+\int h<2\int_{-1}^1g,\qquad \int_{-1}^1 g>0. \tag{i}$$
Suppose, for contradiction, that for every $x$ with $f'(x)>0$ there is $y_x\in[-1,1]$ with $|f(y_x)-f(x)|>c\,f'(x)^{1/p}|y_x-x|$ (so $y_x\ne x$).

*Covering lemma.* Let $\varphi=|f'|$ on $[-1,1]$ and $\varphi=0$ outside, and $\lambda>0$. If $E\subseteq[-1,1]$ is open in $[-1,1]$ and each $x\in E$ lies in a nondegenerate interval $I_x$ with $\int_{I_x}\varphi>\lambda|I_x|$, then $|E|\le\frac3\lambda\int\varphi$. Proof: enlarging $I_x$ slightly keeps the strict inequality and makes $x$ an interior point, so we may take $I_x$ open. For a compact $K\subseteq E$ finitely many $I_x$ cover $K$. Select greedily: take the longest, discard all intervals meeting it, repeat. The chosen intervals $I_1,\dots,I_s$ are disjoint, and every discarded interval lies in the concentric interval of triple length of a chosen one that is at least as long; hence $|K|\le3\sum|I_j|<\frac3\lambda\sum\int_{I_j}\varphi\le\frac3\lambda\int\varphi$. Taking the supremum over compact $K\subseteq E$ gives the claim.

*Level sets.* For $t\in(0,1]$ let $E_t=\{x:g(x)>t\}$, open in $[-1,1]$. For $x\in E_t$ the interval $I_x$ between $x$ and $y_x$ satisfies $\int_{I_x}\varphi\ge|f(y_x)-f(x)|>c\,t^{1/p}|I_x|$. By the lemma and (i),
$$|E_t|\le\frac{3}{c\,t^{1/p}}\int|f'|<\frac{6}{c\,t^{1/p}}\int_{-1}^1g\qquad(0<t\le1)$$
(if $E_t=\varnothing$ the strict bound holds trivially since $\int g>0$). Since $0\le g\le1$, the layer-cake formula gives
$$\int_{-1}^1g=\int_0^1|E_t|\,dt<\frac6c\int_{-1}^1g\int_0^1t^{-1/p}\,dt=\frac6c\cdot\frac p{p-1}\int_{-1}^1g=\int_{-1}^1g,$$
a contradiction. Hence $c_p=\frac{6p}{p-1}$ has the required property.

**b) No.** It suffices to refute every $c\ge1$ (a smaller constant is a stronger statement). Fix $c\ge1$, choose $0<\beta<\frac1c$, and a small $x_1>0$ such that $\bigl(\frac{1+x_1}{2x_1}\bigr)^{-\beta}<\frac14$. Put $D=\frac34x_1$ and
$$q(x)=\frac{2\beta D}{x+x_1}\left(\frac{x+x_1}{2x_1}\right)^{-\beta},\qquad H_q(x)=2D\left(\frac{x+x_1}{2x_1}\right)^{-\beta}\quad(x\ge x_1),$$
so that $H_q(x_1)=2D$, $H_q'=-q$ and $q(x)(x+x_1)=\beta H_q(x)$. Note $0<q\le q(x_1)=\frac{\beta D}{x_1}<1$. For $L>0$ define $g_L$ on $[0,1]$ by: $-1$ on $[0,\frac{x_1}2]$, linear from $-1$ to $0$ on $[\frac{x_1}2,x_1]$, and $\min\bigl(L(x-x_1),q(x)\bigr)$ on $[x_1,1]$; it is continuous with $|g_L|\le1$ and $\int_0^{x_1}g_L=-\frac{x_1}2-\frac{x_1}4=-D$. As $L\to\infty$, $\int_{x_1}^1g_L\to\int_{x_1}^1q=2D-H_q(1)>2D-\frac{2D}4>D$ (monotone convergence); fix $L$ with $\int_{x_1}^1g_L>D$. Extend $g=g_L$ evenly to $[-1,1]$ and let $f(x)=\int_0^xg$, an odd $C^1$ function with $|f'|\le1$ and $f(1)=-D+\int_{x_1}^1g>0$, so $f(1)>f(-1)=-f(1)$.

We have $f'(x)>0$ exactly for $|x|>x_1$. Let $x>x_1$ and $y=-x_1$; note $f(x_1)=-D$, $f(-x_1)=D$. Put $H(x)=D-f(x)=2D-\int_{x_1}^xg$. Since $g\le q$ on $[x_1,1]$, $H(x)\ge H_q(x)>0$, so
$$|f(y)-f(x)|=H(x)\ge H_q(x)=\frac{q(x)(x+x_1)}\beta>c\,q(x)(x+x_1)\ge c\,f'(x)\,|y-x|,$$
using $c\beta<1$ and $f'(x)=g(x)\le q(x)$. For $x<-x_1$ take $y=x_1$; by oddness of $f$ and evenness of $g$ the same computation applies. Thus no $x$ satisfies the required inequality with constant $c$, and **no constant exists for $p=1$.** ∎

prompt: Suppose that in a not necessarily commutative ring $R$ the square of any element is $0$. Prove that $abc+abc=0$ for any three elements $a,b,c$.
answer: $(a+b)^2=0$ gives $xy=-yx$ for all $x,y$; then $abc=-(bc)a=-b(ca)=(ca)b=c(ab)=-(ab)c=-abc$.

solutions.title: Anticommutativity
solutions.body:
For any $x,y\in R$: $0=(x+y)^2=x^2+xy+yx+y^2=xy+yx$, so $xy=-yx$. Applying this repeatedly (and associativity):
$$abc=a(bc)=-(bc)a=-b(ca)=(ca)b=c(ab)=-(ab)c=-abc .$$
Here we used $a(bc)=-(bc)a$, then $b(ca)=-(ca)b$, then $c(ab)=-(ab)c$. Hence $abc+abc=0$. ∎

prompt: We throw a die (which selects one of the numbers $1,2,\dots,6$ with equal probability) $n$ times. What is the probability that the sum of the values is divisible by $5$?
answer: $\dfrac15+\dfrac4{5\cdot6^n}$ if $5\mid n$, and $\dfrac15-\dfrac1{5\cdot6^n}$ otherwise.

solutions.title: Roots of unity filter
solutions.body:
Let $p_k$ be the probability that the sum is $k$, and $F(x)=\sum_kp_kx^k=\left(\dfrac{x+x^2+\dots+x^6}6\right)^n$ (the throws are independent). With $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/5}$, the filter $\frac15\sum_{j=0}^4\varepsilon^{jk}=[5\mid k]$ gives
$$P(5\mid\text{sum})=\sum_kp_{k}[5\mid k]=\frac15\sum_{j=0}^4F(\varepsilon^j).$$
$F(1)=1$. For $j=1,\dots,4$, $\varepsilon^j+\varepsilon^{2j}+\dots+\varepsilon^{5j}=0$ (a full set of 5th roots of unity), so $\varepsilon^j+\dots+\varepsilon^{6j}=\varepsilon^{6j}=\varepsilon^j$ and $F(\varepsilon^j)=\dfrac{\varepsilon^{jn}}{6^n}$. Now $\sum_{j=1}^4\varepsilon^{jn}$ equals $4$ if $5\mid n$ and $-1$ otherwise. Therefore
$$P=\begin{cases}\dfrac15+\dfrac4{5\cdot6^n},&5\mid n,\\[3mm]\dfrac15-\dfrac1{5\cdot6^n},&5\nmid n.\end{cases}$$
(Check $n=1$: $\frac15-\frac1{30}=\frac16$, only the throw $5$.) ∎

solutions.title: Group the outcomes in fives
solutions.body:
Consider the $6^n$ equally likely sequences of results. Every sequence other than $66\dots6$ has the form
$$\underbrace{6\dots6}_{k}\,X\,Y_1\dots Y_{n-k-1},\qquad X\in\{1,\dots,5\},$$
with $k$ and $Y_1,\dots,Y_{n-k-1}$ determined by the sequence. Group together the $5$ sequences that differ only in $X$. Within a group the sums run through $5$ consecutive integers, so exactly one is divisible by $5$. The $6^n-1$ sequences other than $6\dots6$ form $\frac{6^n-1}5$ groups, and the sequence $6\dots6$ has sum $6n$, divisible by $5$ iff $5\mid n$. Hence the number of favourable sequences is $\frac{6^n-1}5+1$ if $5\mid n$ and $\frac{6^n-1}5$ otherwise; dividing by $6^n$ gives the same answer:
$$\frac15+\frac4{5\cdot6^n}\ (5\mid n),\qquad\frac15-\frac1{5\cdot6^n}\ (5\nmid n).$$

prompt: Assume that $x_1,\dots,x_n\ge-1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^3=0$. Prove that $\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\le\dfrac n3$.
answer: For $x\ge-1$: $x^3-\frac34x+\frac14=(x+1)\left(x-\frac12\right)^2\ge0$; sum over $i$ and use $\sum x_i^3=0$.

solutions.title: A polynomial inequality valid for $x\ge-1$
solutions.body:
For every $x\ge-1$,
$$x^3-\frac34x+\frac14=(x+1)\Bigl(x-\frac12\Bigr)^2\ge0,$$
as one checks by expanding: $(x+1)(x^2-x+\frac14)=x^3-\frac34x+\frac14$. Summing over $x=x_1,\dots,x_n$:
$$0\le\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^3-\frac34\sum_{i=1}^nx_i+\frac n4=-\frac34\sum_{i=1}^nx_i+\frac n4,$$
so $\sum x_i\le\frac n3$. ∎

*Remark.* Equality requires every $x_i\in\{-1,\frac12\}$; with $a$ values $-1$ and $b$ values $\frac12$, $\sum x_i^3=0$ gives $b=8a$, so equality occurs exactly when $n=9a$ with $a$ of the $x_i$ equal to $-1$ and $8a$ equal to $\frac12$.

(The polynomial is found by looking for the tangent-line bound $x^3\ge\frac34x-\frac14$, which touches $x^3$ at $x=\frac12$ and holds with equality at the endpoint $x=-1$.)

prompt:
Prove that there exists no function $f:(0,+\infty)\to(0,+\infty)$ such that
$$f^2(x)\ge f(x+y)\bigl(f(x)+y\bigr)$$
for any $x,y>0$.
answer: The inequality gives $f(x)-f(x+y)\ge\frac{f(x)y}{f(x)+y}$; splitting $[x,x+1]$ into $n$ steps with $nf(x+1)\ge1$ yields $f(x+1)\le f(x)-\frac12$, so $f$ eventually becomes negative.

solutions.title: Force a fixed drop on every unit interval
solutions.body:
Suppose such an $f$ exists. Dividing by $f(x)+y>0$,
$$f(x+y)\le\frac{f(x)^2}{f(x)+y}<f(x),\qquad f(x)-f(x+y)\ge f(x)-\frac{f(x)^2}{f(x)+y}=\frac{f(x)\,y}{f(x)+y}. \tag{$*$}$$
In particular $f$ is strictly decreasing.

Fix $x>0$ and choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $nf(x+1)\ge1$. For $k=0,\dots,n-1$ apply $(*)$ at the point $x_k=x+\frac kn$ with $y=\frac1n$:
$$f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge\frac{f(x_k)}{nf(x_k)+1}\ge\frac1{2n},$$
because $t\mapsto\frac t{nt+1}$ is increasing and $f(x_k)\ge f(x+1)\ge\frac1n$, so the value is at least $\frac{1/n}{2}$. Adding these $n$ inequalities, $f(x)-f(x+1)\ge\frac12$.

This holds for every $x>0$, so $f(x+m)\le f(x)-\frac m2$ for all $m\in\mathbb N$. Taking $m>2f(x)$ gives $f(x+m)<0$, contradicting $f>0$. Hence no such function exists. ∎

prompt:
Let $S$ be the set of all words consisting of the letters $x,y,z$, and consider an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $S$ satisfying the following conditions: for arbitrary words $u,v,w\in S$

(i) $uu\sim u$;

(ii) if $v\sim w$, then $uv\sim uw$ and $vu\sim wu$.

Show that every word in $S$ is equivalent to a word of length at most $8$.
answer: Lemma: if $u$ contains all three letters, then for every $v$ there is $w$ with $uvw\sim u$. A square-free word $a=bcd$ of length $\ge9$ with $|b|=|d|=4$ has $b,d$ containing all letters; with $bcde\sim b$ and $def\sim d$: $a\sim bcdef\sim bcdedef\sim(bcde)(def)\sim bd$.

solutions.title: Absorb the middle of the word
solutions.body:
By (i) and (ii), any factor $vv$ inside a word can be replaced by $v$: $pvvq\sim pvq$. Below, $w$ may be the empty word (then $uvw$ means $uv$), and empty outer factors are simply omitted.

**Lemma.** If $u$ contains each of the letters $x,y,z$ and $v$ is any word, there is a word $w$ with $uvw\sim u$.

*Proof.* If $v$ is a single letter, say $x$, write $u=u_1xu_2$; then $u\,x\,u_2=u_1(xu_2)(xu_2)\sim u_1xu_2=u$, so $w=u_2$ works. In general let $v=a_1a_2\cdots a_k$ (letters). Each word $ua_1\cdots a_j$ still contains all letters, so by the single-letter case there are words $w_1,\dots,w_k$ with
$$ua_1w_1\sim u,\quad (ua_1)a_2w_2\sim ua_1,\quad\dots,\quad (ua_1\cdots a_{k-1})a_kw_k\sim ua_1\cdots a_{k-1}.$$
Multiplying on the right by (ii) and chaining:
$$uv\,w_kw_{k-1}\cdots w_1\sim ua_1\cdots a_{k-1}\,w_{k-1}\cdots w_1\sim\dots\sim ua_1w_1\sim u .$$
So $w=w_k\cdots w_1$ works. $\square$

**Main argument.** We show that every word $a$ of length $\ge9$ is equivalent to a shorter word; by induction, every word is then equivalent to one of length $\le8$.

If $a$ contains a factor $vv$, then $a\sim$ (the word with $vv$ replaced by $v$), which is shorter. So assume $a$ is *square-free*. Write $a=bcd$ where $b$ and $d$ are the first and last four letters ($c$ is nonempty). A square-free word of length $4$ contains all three letters: over two letters, say $x,y$, every word of length $4$ contains a square (avoiding $xx,yy$ forces alternation $xyxy$ or $yxyx$, which are squares). So $b$ and $d$ contain all of $x,y,z$.

By the Lemma there is $e$ with $b(cd)e\sim b$, and then $f$ with $d\,e\,f\sim d$. Now
$$a=bcd\ \sim\ bc(def)\ \sim\ bc(de)(de)f\ =\ (bcde)(def)\ \sim\ b(def)\ \sim\ bd,$$
using $d\sim def$, then $(de)(de)\sim de$, then $bcde\sim b$, then $def\sim d$ (each time with (ii)). The word $bd$ has length $8<|a|$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be a subset of $\mathbb Z_n=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ containing at most $\frac1{100}\ln n$ elements. Define the $r$th Fourier coefficient of $A$ for $r\in\mathbb Z_n$ by
$$f(r)=\sum_{s\in A}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}n\,sr\right).$$
Prove that there exists an $r\ne0$ such that $|f(r)|\ge\dfrac{|A|}2$.
answer: Pigeonhole: split the unit circle into $6$ arcs of angle $\frac\pi3$; the $n$ vectors $\bigl(e^{2\pi ia_jt/n}\bigr)_{j=1}^k$, $t=0,\dots,n-1$, fall into $6^k<n$ classes, and $r=t_2-t_1$ for two in the same class gives $\operatorname{Re}f(r)\ge\frac k2$.

solutions.title: Pigeonhole on the torus
solutions.body:
(We assume $n\ge2$, so that some $r\ne0$ exists.) Let $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}$. If $k=0$, any $r\ne0$ works. Let $k\ge1$; then $k\le\frac{\ln n}{100}$ gives
$$6^k=e^{k\ln6}\le n^{\ln6/100}<n .$$
Divide the unit circle into $6$ half-open arcs of angle $\frac\pi3$. For $t=0,1,\dots,n-1$ consider the $k$-tuple
$$\Bigl(\exp\tfrac{2\pi ia_1t}n,\ \dots,\ \exp\tfrac{2\pi ia_kt}n\Bigr),$$
and classify it by which arc each coordinate lies in. There are $6^k<n$ classes and $n$ tuples, so two of them, for $t_1<t_2$, are in the same class. Let $r=t_2-t_1\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$, so $r\ne0$ in $\mathbb Z_n$. For each $j$, the points $\exp\frac{2\pi ia_jt_1}n$ and $\exp\frac{2\pi ia_jt_2}n$ lie on a common arc of angle $\frac\pi3$, so the angle between them is less than $\frac\pi3$ and
$$\operatorname{Re}\exp\frac{2\pi ia_jr}n=\cos\Bigl(\frac{2\pi a_jt_2}n-\frac{2\pi a_jt_1}n\Bigr)>\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12 .$$
Summing over $j$,
$$|f(r)|\ge\operatorname{Re}f(r)>\frac k2=\frac{|A|}2.\ \blacksquare$$

prompt:
Is it true that if $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is

a) monotone increasing,

b) monotone decreasing,

then there exists an $x\in[0,1]$ for which $f(x)=x$?
answer: a) Yes; b) No

solutions.title: Supremum argument for (a), explicit counterexample for (b)
solutions.body:
**a) Yes.** Let $f$ be increasing (non-decreasing) and put
$$A=\{x\in[0,1]:\ f(x)\ge x\}.$$
Since $f(0)\ge 0$, we have $0\in A$, so $A$ is non-empty and bounded; let $a=\sup A\in[0,1]$.

* For every $x\in A$ we have $x\le a$, hence $x\le f(x)\le f(a)$. So $f(a)$ is an upper bound of $A$, and therefore $a\le f(a)$.
* Applying $f$ to $a\le f(a)$ gives $f(a)\le f(f(a))$, i.e. the point $f(a)\in[0,1]$ belongs to $A$. Hence $f(a)\le \sup A=a$.

Together, $f(a)=a$: the point $a$ is a fixed point. (Continuity is not needed.)

**b) No.** Define
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}1-\dfrac x2, & 0\le x\le \tfrac12,\\[2mm] \dfrac12-\dfrac x2, & \tfrac12<x\le 1.\end{cases}$$
On $[0,\tfrac12]$ the values lie in $[\tfrac34,1]$, on $(\tfrac12,1]$ they lie in $[0,\tfrac14)$; so $f$ maps $[0,1]$ into $[0,1]$, it is decreasing on each piece, and it jumps down at $\tfrac12$, so it is decreasing on $[0,1]$.

There is no fixed point: for $x\le\tfrac12$ we have $f(x)\ge\tfrac34>x$, and for $x>\tfrac12$ we have $f(x)<\tfrac14<x$.

**Answer: a) Yes; b) No.** ∎

prompt: Let $p(x)=x^5+x$ and $q(x)=x^5+x^2$. Find all pairs $(w,z)$ of complex numbers with $w\ne z$ for which $p(w)=p(z)$ and $q(w)=q(z)$.
answer: $(w,z)=\left(\frac{1\pm\sqrt3\,i}{2},\frac{1\mp\sqrt3\,i}{2}\right)$ and $\left(\frac{1\pm\sqrt7\,i}{2},\frac{1\mp\sqrt7\,i}{2}\right)$ (four ordered pairs).

solutions.title: Divide by $w-z$ and use symmetric functions
solutions.body:
Since $w\ne z$ we may divide the differences by $w-z$. Write
$$h(w,z)=\frac{w^5-z^5}{w-z}=w^4+w^3z+w^2z^2+wz^3+z^4 .$$
Then
$$\frac{p(w)-p(z)}{w-z}=h(w,z)+1,\qquad \frac{q(w)-q(z)}{w-z}=h(w,z)+(w+z).$$
So the conditions are equivalent to
$$h(w,z)+1=0\quad\text{and}\quad h(w,z)+w+z=0 .$$
Subtracting gives $w+z=1$.

Let $s=w+z$ and $c=wz$. Express $h$ through $s,c$:
$$w^4+z^4=(s^2-2c)^2-2c^2,\qquad w^3z+wz^3=c(s^2-2c),\qquad w^2z^2=c^2,$$
so $h=s^4-3s^2c+c^2$. With $s=1$ the condition $h=-1$ becomes
$$1-3c+c^2=-1\iff c^2-3c+2=0\iff c\in\{1,2\}.$$

* $c=1$: $w,z$ are the roots of $t^2-t+1=0$, i.e. $\frac{1\pm\sqrt3\,i}{2}$.
* $c=2$: $w,z$ are the roots of $t^2-t+2=0$, i.e. $\frac{1\pm\sqrt7\,i}{2}$.

In both cases the two roots are distinct, so $w\ne z$. Conversely, every such pair has $w+z=1$ and $h(w,z)=-1$, so both divided differences vanish, i.e. $p(w)=p(z)$ and $q(w)=q(z)$.

**Answer:** $(w,z)=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt3 i}{2},\frac{1-\sqrt3 i}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{1-\sqrt3 i}{2},\frac{1+\sqrt3 i}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{1+\sqrt7 i}{2},\frac{1-\sqrt7 i}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{1-\sqrt7 i}{2},\frac{1+\sqrt7 i}{2}\right)$. ∎

prompt:
$A$ and $B$ are square complex matrices of the same size and
$$\operatorname{rank}(AB-BA)=1.$$
Show that $(AB-BA)^2=0$.
answer: $C=AB-BA$ has rank 1, so $C=uv^{T}$ and $C^2=(v^Tu)\,C=(\operatorname{tr}C)\,C=0$ because $\operatorname{tr}C=0$.

solutions.title: Write the rank-one matrix as $uv^T$
solutions.body:
Let $C=AB-BA$. A matrix of rank $1$ can be written as $C=uv^{T}$ with non-zero column vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^n$ (all columns of $C$ are multiples of one non-zero column $u$; collect the multipliers in $v$).

Then
$$C^2=u\,(v^{T}u)\,v^{T}=(v^{T}u)\,C .$$
The scalar $v^Tu=\sum_i u_iv_i$ is exactly the trace of $uv^T=C$. But
$$\operatorname{tr}C=\operatorname{tr}(AB)-\operatorname{tr}(BA)=0 ,$$
since $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ for all square matrices. Hence $C^2=0\cdot C=0$. ∎

solutions.title: Eigenvalues and Jordan form
solutions.body:
Again let $C=AB-BA$. Since $\operatorname{rank}C=1$, the kernel of $C$ has dimension $n-1$, so $0$ is an eigenvalue of geometric (hence also algebraic) multiplicity at least $n-1$. The remaining eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $\lambda=\operatorname{tr}C=0$. So all eigenvalues of $C$ are $0$ and $C$ is nilpotent.

In the Jordan normal form of $C$ the number of Jordan blocks equals $\dim\ker C=n-1$, so there are $n-1$ blocks of total size $n$: one block of size $2$ and $n-2$ blocks of size $1$. The square of a nilpotent Jordan block of size at most $2$ is zero, so $C^2=0$. ∎

prompt:
a) Show that if $(x_i)$ is a decreasing sequence of positive numbers then
$$\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right)^{1/2}\le \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}.$$

b) Show that there is a constant $C$ so that if $(x_i)$ is a decreasing sequence of positive numbers then
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt m}\left(\sum_{i=m}^\infty x_i^2\right)^{1/2}\le C\sum_{i=1}^\infty x_i .$$
answer: (a) Expand the square and keep only terms $j\le i$, using $x_j/\sqrt j\ge x_i/\sqrt i$. (b) Apply (a) to each tail, swap the sums, and bound $\sum_{m=1}^{i}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m(i+1-m)}}$ by a constant ($4$, or even $\pi$).

solutions.title: Expand the square; then swap the order of summation
solutions.body:
**a)** All terms are positive, so
$$\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\right)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\frac{x_j}{\sqrt j}\ \ge\ \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\sum_{j=1}^{i}\frac{x_j}{\sqrt j},$$
where we dropped the terms with $j>i$. For $j\le i$ we have $x_j\ge x_i$ and $\frac1{\sqrt j}\ge\frac1{\sqrt i}$, so $\sum_{j=1}^i\frac{x_j}{\sqrt j}\ge i\cdot\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}=\sqrt i\,x_i$. Therefore
$$\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\right)^2\ge\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\cdot\sqrt i\,x_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 ,$$
and taking square roots gives (a).

**b)** We may assume $\sum x_i<\infty$ (otherwise there is nothing to prove). Fix $m$. The tail $x_m,x_{m+1},\dots$ is again decreasing and positive, so by (a) for every $N\ge m$
$$\left(\sum_{i=m}^N x_i^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sum_{i=m}^N\frac{x_i}{\sqrt{i-m+1}}\le\sum_{i=m}^\infty\frac{x_i}{\sqrt{i-m+1}} ;$$
letting $N\to\infty$, the same bound holds for the infinite tail. Summing over $m$ and exchanging the order of summation (all terms are non-negative):
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac1{\sqrt m}\left(\sum_{i=m}^\infty x_i^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sum_{m=1}^\infty\sum_{i=m}^\infty\frac{x_i}{\sqrt m\sqrt{i-m+1}}=\sum_{i=1}^\infty x_i\,S_i,\qquad S_i=\sum_{m=1}^{i}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}\sqrt{i+1-m}} .$$
It remains to bound $S_i$ by a constant. The summand is symmetric under $m\leftrightarrow i+1-m$, and for $m\le\frac{i+1}2$ we have $i+1-m\ge\frac{i+1}2$. Hence, with $K=\lfloor\frac{i+1}2\rfloor$,
$$S_i\le 2\sum_{m=1}^{K}\frac{1}{\sqrt m\,\sqrt{(i+1)/2}}\le\frac{2}{\sqrt{(i+1)/2}}\cdot2\sqrt K\le 4,$$
using $\sum_{m=1}^K\frac1{\sqrt m}\le\sum_{m=1}^K 2(\sqrt m-\sqrt{m-1})=2\sqrt K$ (because $\frac1{\sqrt m}\le\frac{2}{\sqrt m+\sqrt{m-1}}$) and $K\le\frac{i+1}2$. (The factor 2 may count a middle term twice; that only makes the bound larger.)

Thus the inequality holds with $C=4$. ∎

solutions.title: A sharper constant from an integral
solutions.body:
Part (a) and the reduction of (b) to bounding $S_i=\sum_{m=1}^{i}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m(i+1-m)}}$ are as in the first solution.

The function $h(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x(i+1-x)}}$ is convex on $(0,i+1)$ (its logarithm $-\frac12\ln x-\frac12\ln(i+1-x)$ is convex, and the exponential of a convex function is convex). For a convex function the value at the midpoint of an interval is at most the average over the interval, so
$$h(m)\le\int_{m-1/2}^{m+1/2}h(x)\,dx\qquad(1\le m\le i).$$
Summing,
$$S_i\le\int_{1/2}^{i+1/2}h(x)\,dx<\int_0^{i+1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x(i+1-x)}}=\pi ,$$
where the last integral is computed with $x=(i+1)\sin^2\theta$, $dx=2(i+1)\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$, giving $\int_0^{\pi/2}2\,d\theta=\pi$.

So the inequality in (b) holds with $C=\pi$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring of characteristic zero (not necessarily commutative). Let $e$, $f$ and $g$ be idempotent elements of $R$ satisfying $e+f+g=0$. Show that $e=f=g=0$.

($R$ is of characteristic zero means that, if $a\in R$ and $n$ is a positive integer, then $na\ne0$ unless $a=0$. An idempotent $x$ is an element satisfying $x=x^2$.)
answer: From $g^2=g$ get $ef+fe=2g$; commuting with $e$ gives $3(ef-fe)=0$, so $ef=fe=g$; then $e+2ef=0=f+2ef$, so $e=f$ and $3e=0$.

solutions.title: Square $g=-(e+f)$ and commute with $e$
solutions.body:
Throughout we use: if $na=0$ for a positive integer $n$, then $a=0$.

**Step 1.** Since $g=-(e+f)$,
$$g=g^2=(e+f)^2=e^2+ef+fe+f^2=e+f+ef+fe=-g+ef+fe ,$$
so
$$ef+fe=2g. \tag{1}$$

**Step 2: $e$ and $f$ commute.** Multiply (1) by $e$ on the left and on the right:
$$ef+efe=2eg,\qquad efe+fe=2ge .$$
Subtracting, $ef-fe=2(eg-ge)$. Now $eg=e(-e-f)=-e-ef$ and $ge=-e-fe$, so $eg-ge=-(ef-fe)$. Hence $ef-fe=-2(ef-fe)$, i.e. $3(ef-fe)=0$, and therefore $ef=fe$.

**Step 3.** Now (1) reads $2ef=2g$, so $ef=g$ and the hypothesis becomes
$$e+f+ef=0. \tag{2}$$
Multiplying (2) by $e$ on the left gives $e+ef+ef=0$, i.e. $e=-2ef$; multiplying by $f$ on the left gives $fe+f+fef=ef+f+ef=0$ (using $fe=ef$, $f^2=f$), i.e. $f=-2ef$. Thus $e=f$.

**Step 4.** With $f=e$: $e=-2ef=-2e^2=-2e$, so $3e=0$ and $e=0$. Then $f=e=0$ and $g=-(e+f)=0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ be an increasing differentiable function for which $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=\infty$ and $f'$ is bounded. Let $F(x)=\int_0^x f$. Define the sequence $(a_n)$ inductively by
$$a_0=1,\qquad a_{n+1}=a_n+\frac{1}{f(a_n)},$$
and the sequence $(b_n)$ simply by $b_n=F^{-1}(n)$. Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}(a_n-b_n)=0$.
answer: By the mean value theorem $F(a_{k+1})-F(a_k)=1+d_k$ with $0\le d_k\le\frac{f(a_{k+1})-f(a_k)}{f(a_k)}$; summing shows $0<F(a_n)-F(b_n)=o(f(a_n))$, and another mean value step with $f'\le B$ turns this into $0<a_n-b_n<2\varepsilon$.

solutions.title: Compare $F(a_n)$ with $n$ via the mean value theorem
solutions.body:
**Preliminaries.** $F'=f>0$, so $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing; $F(0)=0$ and $F(x)\ge f(0)x\to\infty$, so $b_n=F^{-1}(n)$ is well defined for $n\ge0$, and $b_n\to\infty$ (as $F$ is bounded on bounded sets). Let $B$ be a bound for $f'$, so $f(u)-f(v)\le B(u-v)$ for $u\ge v$.

The sequence $(a_n)$ is increasing. It is unbounded: otherwise $a_n\to L$ and $a_{n+1}-a_n=1/f(a_n)\ge1/f(L)>0$, impossible. Hence $a_n\to\infty$ and $f(a_n)\to\infty$.

**Step 1.** By the mean value theorem there is $\xi_k\in(a_k,a_{k+1})$ with
$$F(a_{k+1})-F(a_k)=f(\xi_k)(a_{k+1}-a_k)=\frac{f(\xi_k)}{f(a_k)} .$$
Since $f$ is increasing, $f(a_k)\le f(\xi_k)\le f(a_{k+1})$, so
$$F(a_{k+1})-F(a_k)=1+d_k,\qquad 0\le d_k\le\frac{f(a_{k+1})-f(a_k)}{f(a_k)} .$$
Summing over $k=0,\dots,n-1$ and using $F(b_n)=n$:
$$F(a_n)-F(b_n)=F(1)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}d_k. \tag{1}$$
As $F(1)>0$ and $d_k\ge0$, we get $F(a_n)>F(b_n)$, hence $a_n>b_n$.

**Step 2: the right side of (1) is $o(f(a_n))$.** Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $K$ with $f(a_K)>2/\varepsilon$. For $n>K$,
$$\sum_{k=K}^{n-1}d_k\le\frac{1}{f(a_K)}\sum_{k=K}^{n-1}\bigl(f(a_{k+1})-f(a_k)\bigr)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}f(a_n).$$
The remaining part $F(1)+\sum_{k<K}d_k$ is a constant, which is $<\frac\varepsilon2 f(a_n)$ for large $n$ because $f(a_n)\to\infty$. Hence for all large $n$
$$F(a_n)-F(b_n)<\varepsilon f(a_n). \tag{2}$$

**Step 3: back to $a_n-b_n$.** By the mean value theorem, $F(a_n)-F(b_n)=f(\zeta)(a_n-b_n)$ for some $\zeta\in(b_n,a_n)$, and $f(\zeta)\ge f(b_n)$. Also $f(a_n)\le f(b_n)+B(a_n-b_n)$. Inserting into (2):
$$f(b_n)(a_n-b_n)<\varepsilon f(b_n)+\varepsilon B(a_n-b_n),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \bigl(f(b_n)-\varepsilon B\bigr)(a_n-b_n)<\varepsilon f(b_n).$$
Since $b_n\to\infty$, $f(b_n)\to\infty$, so for large $n$ we have $f(b_n)>2\varepsilon B$ and therefore
$$0<a_n-b_n<\frac{\varepsilon f(b_n)}{f(b_n)-\varepsilon B}<2\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $a_n-b_n\to0$. ∎

prompt:
a) Show that the unit square can be partitioned into $n$ smaller squares if $n$ is large enough.

b) Let $d\ge2$. Show that there is a constant $N(d)$ such that, whenever $n\ge N(d)$, a $d$-dimensional unit cube can be partitioned into $n$ smaller cubes.
answer: Cutting one cube into $a^d$ equal cubes adds $a^d-1$ pieces; $2^d-1$ and $(2^d-1)^d-1$ are coprime, and every large integer is a non-negative combination of two coprime numbers.

solutions.title: Refinements plus a Frobenius-coin lemma
solutions.body:
Part (a) is the case $d=2$ of (b), so we prove (b) for any $d\ge2$.

**Lemma.** If $a,b$ are coprime positive integers, then every integer $m\ge a(b-1)$ can be written as $m=ax+by$ with integers $x,y\ge0$.

*Proof.* The numbers $0,a,2a,\dots,(b-1)a$ are pairwise incongruent modulo $b$ (as $\gcd(a,b)=1$), so they form a complete residue system; choose $x\in\{0,\dots,b-1\}$ with $ax\equiv m\pmod b$. Then $m-ax\ge m-a(b-1)\ge0$ is divisible by $b$, and $y=(m-ax)/b\ge0$ works. $\square$

**Refinement.** Given a dissection of the cube into $k$ cubes, pick any one of them and cut it into $a^d$ equal cubes (divide each of its edges into $a$ equal parts). This gives a dissection into $k+(a^d-1)$ cubes. Starting from the unit cube itself ($k=1$) and refining repeatedly (each time some cube of the current dissection), we can reach
$$1+x(a_1^d-1)+y(a_2^d-1)\qquad\text{pieces, for all }x,y\ge0,$$
for any fixed $a_1,a_2\ge2$.

**Coprime increments.** Take $a_1=2$ and $a_2=2^d-1$ (which is $\ge3$ for $d\ge2$). Put $P=2^d-1$ and $R=(2^d-1)^d-1=P^d-1$. A common divisor of $P$ and $R$ divides $P^d$ and $P^d-1$, hence divides $1$; so $\gcd(P,R)=1$.

By the lemma every $m\ge P(R-1)$ is of the form $xP+yR$ with $x,y\ge0$, so the cube can be dissected into $n=1+m$ cubes for every
$$n\ge N(d):=1+P(R-1).$$
All pieces are smaller than the unit cube because $n\ge2$. (For $d=2$: $P=3$, $R=8$, so every $n\ge22$ works; in fact every $n\ge6$ is possible for the square.) ∎

prompt:
Let $f$ be continuous and nowhere monotone on $[0,1]$. Show that the set of points on which $f$ attains local minima is dense in $[0,1]$.

(A function is nowhere monotone if there exists no interval where the function is monotone. A set is dense if each non-empty open interval contains at least one element of the set.)
answer: In any interval find $p<q\le r<s$ with $f(p)>f(q)$ and $f(r)<f(s)$; the minimum of $f$ on $[p,s]$ is attained at an interior point, which is a local minimum.

solutions.title: Minimum on a well-chosen subinterval
solutions.body:
Let $(u,v)\subseteq[0,1]$ be a non-empty open interval. Choose $u<\alpha<c<\beta<v$.

Since $f$ is not monotone on $[\alpha,c]$, it is in particular not non-decreasing there: there are $\alpha\le p<q\le c$ with $f(p)>f(q)$. Since $f$ is not non-increasing on $[c,\beta]$, there are $c\le r<s\le\beta$ with $f(r)<f(s)$.

By the extreme value theorem the continuous function $f$ attains its minimum on $[p,s]$ at some point $t$. Because $q,r\in[p,s]$,
$$f(t)\le f(q)<f(p)\quad\text{and}\quad f(t)\le f(r)<f(s),$$
so $t\ne p$ and $t\ne s$, i.e. $t\in(p,s)$. Then $f(t)\le f(x)$ for all $x$ in the open neighbourhood $(p,s)$ of $t$, so $f$ has a local minimum at $t$, and $t\in(p,s)\subset(u,v)$.

So every non-empty open interval contains a local minimum point: these points are dense. ∎

prompt: Let $p(z)$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with complex coefficients. Prove that there exist at least $n+1$ complex numbers $z$ for which $p(z)$ is $0$ or $1$.
answer: (For $n\ge1$.) A root of $p$ or of $p-1$ of multiplicity $m$ is a root of $p'$ of multiplicity $m-1$; counting, $2n-(|S_0|+|S_1|)\le\deg p'=n-1$.

solutions.title: Count multiplicities against the roots of $p'$
solutions.body:
For $n=0$ the statement is false ($p\equiv 5$ takes neither value), so we assume $n\ge1$, as intended.

Let $S_0=\{z:p(z)=0\}$ and $S_1=\{z:p(z)=1\}$; they are disjoint. For a polynomial $h$ and $c\in\mathbb C$ let $\mu(h,c)$ be the multiplicity of $c$ as a root of $h$ ($0$ if $h(c)\ne0$). Since $p$ and $p-1$ both have degree $n$,
$$\sum_{c\in S_0}\mu(p,c)=n,\qquad\sum_{c\in S_1}\mu(p-1,c)=n. \tag{1}$$

If $c$ is a root of $h$ of multiplicity $m\ge1$, then $c$ is a root of $h'$ of multiplicity exactly $m-1$ (write $h=(z-c)^mg$ with $g(c)\ne0$; then $h'=(z-c)^{m-1}(mg+(z-c)g')$ and the second factor is $mg(c)\ne0$ at $c$). Both $p$ and $p-1$ have derivative $p'$, hence
$$\mu(p',c)=\mu(p,c)-1\ (c\in S_0),\qquad \mu(p',c)=\mu(p-1,c)-1\ (c\in S_1).$$
Since $n\ge1$, $p'$ is a non-zero polynomial of degree $n-1$, so the total multiplicity of its roots in $S_0\cup S_1$ is at most $n-1$:
$$n-1\ \ge\sum_{c\in S_0\cup S_1}\mu(p',c)=\sum_{c\in S_0}(\mu(p,c)-1)+\sum_{c\in S_1}(\mu(p-1,c)-1)=2n-|S_0|-|S_1| ,$$
using (1). Hence $|S_0|+|S_1|\ge n+1$: there are at least $n+1$ distinct points where $p$ takes the value $0$ or $1$. ∎

prompt:
Suppose the graph of a polynomial of degree 6 is tangent to a straight line at 3 points $A_1,A_2,A_3$, where $A_2$ lies between $A_1$ and $A_3$.

a) Prove that if the lengths of the segments $A_1A_2$ and $A_2A_3$ are equal, then the areas of the figures bounded by these segments and the graph of the polynomial are equal as well.

b) Let $k=\dfrac{A_2A_3}{A_1A_2}$, and let $K$ be the ratio of the areas of the appropriate figures. Prove that
$$\frac27k^5<K<\frac72k^5.$$

solutions.title: Factor the difference from the tangent line
solutions.body:
Let the line be $\ell(x)=mx+t$ and the polynomial $p$, of degree $6$, and let $x_1<x_2<x_3$ be the abscissas of $A_1,A_2,A_3$. Tangency at $A_i$ means $p(x_i)=\ell(x_i)$ and $p'(x_i)=m$, so each $x_i$ is (at least) a double root of the degree-6 polynomial $p-\ell$. Hence
$$p(x)-\ell(x)=c\,(x-x_1)^2(x-x_2)^2(x-x_3)^2,\qquad c\ne0 .$$
This does not change sign, so the figure bounded by the segment $A_iA_{i+1}$ and the graph is the region between the line and the graph over $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, with area $|c|\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}(x-x_1)^2(x-x_2)^2(x-x_3)^2\,dx$.

Lengths on the line are proportional to horizontal projections: $A_iA_{i+1}=(x_{i+1}-x_i)\sqrt{1+m^2}$. Shift coordinates so that $x_2=0$, and put $x_1=-u$, $x_3=v$ with $u,v>0$; then $k=v/u$.

**a)** If $u=v$, the integrand $x^2(x^2-u^2)^2$ is even, so $\int_{-u}^0=\int_0^u$ and the two areas are equal.

**b)** Direct integration (expand the polynomial, or substitute $x=-us$ resp. $x=vs$) gives
$$\int_{-u}^{0}(x+u)^2x^2(x-v)^2\,dx=\frac{u^7}{210}\,(7k^2+7k+2),\qquad \int_{0}^{v}(x+u)^2x^2(x-v)^2\,dx=\frac{u^7k^5}{210}\,(2k^2+7k+7).$$
To see the first one, substitute $x=-us$ ($0\le s\le1$): then $x+u=u(1-s)$, $x=-us$, $x-v=-u(s+k)$, and
$$\int_{-u}^{0}(x+u)^2x^2(x-v)^2\,dx=u^7\int_0^1 s^2(1-s)^2(s^2+2ks+k^2)\,ds .$$
With $\int_0^1 s^a(1-s)^b\,ds=\frac{a!\,b!}{(a+b+1)!}$ the three pieces are $\frac{4!\,2!}{7!}=\frac1{105}$, $2k\cdot\frac{3!\,2!}{6!}=\frac{k}{30}$ and $k^2\cdot\frac{2!\,2!}{5!}=\frac{k^2}{30}$, which add up to $\frac{2+7k+7k^2}{210}$.
