Assume the statement for $n$, and let $a_1\le\dots\le a_{n+1}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}ia_i=0$. Then $a_{n+1}\ge0$: otherwise all $a_i<0$ and the weighted sum would be negative. Put $b_i=a_i+\frac{2a_{n+1}}n$ for $i\le n$. The $b_i$ are still nondecreasing, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^nib_i=\sum_{i=1}^nia_i+\frac{2a_{n+1}}n\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}2=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}ia_i=0 .$$
By the induction hypothesis,
$$0\le\sum_{i=1}^nb_i[ix]=\sum_{i=1}^na_i[ix]+a_{n+1}\cdot\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^n[ix].$$
Summing $[ix]+[(n+1-i)x]\le[(n+1)x]$ over $i=1,\dots,n$ gives $\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^n[ix]\le[(n+1)x]$. Since $a_{n+1}\ge0$,
$$0\le\sum_{i=1}^na_i[ix]+a_{n+1}[(n+1)x]=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}a_i[ix].\ ∎$$

solutions.title: Abel summation
solutions.body:
Let $P_k=\sum_{j=1}^k[jx]$. Summing $[jx]+[(k-j)x]\le[kx]$ over $j=1,\dots,k-1$ gives $2P_{k-1}\le(k-1)[kx]=(k-1)(P_k-P_{k-1})$. Hence $(k+1)P_{k-1}\le(k-1)P_k$, i.e.
$$\frac{P_{k-1}}{(k-1)k}\le\frac{P_k}{k(k+1)} .$$
So $\frac{P_k}{k(k+1)}$ is nondecreasing in $k$.

Let $\tau=\frac{2P_n}{n(n+1)}$, $w_i=[ix]-\tau i$ and $W_k=\sum_{i\le k}w_i=P_k-\tau\frac{k(k+1)}2$. Then $W_n=0$, and by monotonicity $W_k=\frac{k(k+1)}2\Big(\frac{2P_k}{k(k+1)}-\frac{2P_n}{n(n+1)}\Big)\le0$. Since $\sum ia_i=0$, Abel summation gives
$$\sum_{i=1}^na_i[ix]=\sum_{i=1}^na_iw_i=a_nW_n-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k)W_k=-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k)W_k\ge0,$$
because $a_{k+1}-a_k\ge0$ and $W_k\le0$. ∎

prompt: In $\mathbb R^3$ some $n$ points are coloured. In every step, if four coloured points lie on the same line, Vojtěch can colour any other point on this line. He observes that he can colour any point $P\in\mathbb R^3$ in a finite number of steps (possibly depending on $P$). Find the minimal value of $n$ for which this could happen.

solutions.title: Cubic surfaces and six planes
solutions.body:
**Lower bound $n\ge20$.** The polynomials in $x,y,z$ of degree at most $3$ form a vector space of dimension $\binom{6}{3}=20$. If $n\le19$, the $n$ linear conditions $p(A)=0$ (for the coloured points $A$) have a nonzero solution $p$.

Every point Vojtěch can colour is also a zero of $p$. Indeed, if $p$ vanishes at four distinct points of a line $\{A+tv\}$, then $t\mapsto p(A+tv)$ is a polynomial of degree $\le3$ in $t$ with four roots, hence identically zero. So $p$ vanishes on the whole line. But a nonzero polynomial does not vanish everywhere in $\mathbb R^3$, so some point can never be coloured.

**Construction with $20$ points.** Take six planes $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_6$ in general position:
* any two meet in a line $\ell_{ij}=\alpha_i\cap\alpha_j$;
* any three meet in exactly one point;
* no four share a point.

Colour the $\binom63=20$ triple points $\alpha_i\cap\alpha_j\cap\alpha_k$.

1. **Each line $\ell_{ij}$:** it contains the four distinct triple points $\alpha_i\cap\alpha_j\cap\alpha_k$, $k\ne i,j$, so every point of $\ell_{ij}$ can be coloured.
2. **Each plane $\alpha_i$:** let $P\in\alpha_i$ not lie on any $\ell_{ij}$. Choose a line $m\subset\alpha_i$ through $P$ that is not parallel to any of the five lines $\ell_{ij}$ ($j\ne i$) and avoids the finitely many triple points in $\alpha_i$. Then $m$ meets the five lines in five distinct points. They are distinct because two of them coinciding would be a triple point. All five can be coloured by step 1, so $P$ can be coloured.
3. **Any point $P$:** if $P$ lies on some $\alpha_i$, use step 2. Otherwise choose a line through $P$ that is not parallel to any $\alpha_i$ and meets none of the fifteen lines $\ell_{ij}$; this excludes finitely many planes of directions. It meets the six planes in six distinct points, which can be coloured by step 2, so $P$ can be coloured.

Hence $20$ points suffice, and the minimum is $n=20$. **Answer: 20.** ∎

prompt:
Compute the integral
$$\iint\limits_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{1-e^{-xy}}{xy}\right)^2e^{-x^2-y^2}\,dx\,dy .$$

solutions.title: Differentiate with respect to a parameter (official)
solutions.body:
For $0\le\varrho\le1$ let
$$F(\varrho)=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}\Big(\frac{1-e^{-\varrho xy}}{xy}\Big)^2e^{-x^2-y^2}dx\,dy$$
(the integrand is continuous, with value $\varrho^2e^{-x^2-y^2}$ where $xy=0$). We need $F(1)$.

**A Gaussian integral.** For $|t|<1$, complete the square:
$$\iint e^{-x^2-2txy-y^2}dx\,dy=\iint e^{-(x+ty)^2-(1-t^2)y^2}dx\,dy=\sqrt\pi\cdot\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{1-t^2}}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{1-t^2}} .$$

**Derivatives.** Let $f$ be the integrand. Then
$$\partial_\varrho f=\frac{2e^{-\varrho xy}-2e^{-2\varrho xy}}{xy}e^{-x^2-y^2},\qquad\partial_\varrho^2f=\big(4e^{-2\varrho xy}-2e^{-\varrho xy}\big)e^{-x^2-y^2}.$$
For $0\le\varrho\le1-\varepsilon$, we have $2\varrho|xy|\le\varrho(x^2+y^2)$, so
$$|\partial^2_\varrho f|\le6e^{2\varrho|xy|-x^2-y^2}\le6e^{-\varepsilon(x^2+y^2)},$$
which is integrable. Also $f$ and $\partial_\varrho f$ vanish at $\varrho=0$, so they are bounded by the same function. Hence we may differentiate under the integral sign on $[0,1)$. Using the Gaussian integral with $t=\varrho$ and $t=\varrho/2$,
$$F''(\varrho)=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{1-\varrho^2}}-\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\varrho^2/4}} .$$
Since $F'(0)=F(0)=0$,
$$F'(\varrho)=4\pi\arcsin\varrho-4\pi\arcsin\frac\varrho2 ,$$
$$F(\varrho)=4\pi\Big[\varrho\arcsin\varrho+\sqrt{1-\varrho^2}-1-\varrho\arcsin\frac\varrho2-\sqrt{4-\varrho^2}+2\Big].$$

**Passing to $\varrho=1$.** For every fixed $u=xy$, the function $\varrho\mapsto\frac{1-e^{-\varrho u}}u$ is nonnegative and nondecreasing on $[0,1]$: its $\varrho$-derivative is $e^{-\varrho u}>0$. So the integrand increases with $\varrho$, and by the monotone convergence theorem $F(1)=\lim_{\varrho\to1^-}F(\varrho)$. Hence
$$F(1)=4\pi\Big[\frac\pi2-1-\frac\pi6-\sqrt3+2\Big]=\frac{4\pi^2}3-4(\sqrt3-1)\pi\approx3.9603 .$$
**Answer: $\frac{4\pi^2}{3}-4(\sqrt3-1)\pi$.**

solutions.title: Write the square as a double integral
solutions.body:
For every real $u$,
$$\Big(\frac{1-e^{-u}}u\Big)^2=\Big(\int_0^1e^{-us}ds\Big)^2=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1e^{-u(s+t)}\,ds\,dt$$
(for $u=0$ both sides equal $1$). Put $u=xy$ and integrate over $\mathbb R^2$. Everything is nonnegative, so Tonelli's theorem lets us swap the integrals. Using the Gaussian integral $\iint e^{-x^2-2\tau xy-y^2}=\frac\pi{\sqrt{1-\tau^2}}$ with $\tau=\frac{s+t}2<1$ (for almost every $(s,t)$):
$$I=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac{\pi\,ds\,dt}{\sqrt{1-\frac{(s+t)^2}4}} .$$
The sum $w=s+t$ of the two coordinates has density $w$ on $[0,1]$ and $2-w$ on $[1,2]$. Hence
$$I=\pi\int_0^1\frac{w\,dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}}+\pi\int_1^2\frac{(2-w)\,dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}} .$$
Since $\int\frac{w\,dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}}=-4\sqrt{1-w^2/4}$ and $\int\frac{dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}}=2\arcsin\frac w2$:
* the first integral is $4-2\sqrt3$;
* the second is $4\big(\frac\pi2-\frac\pi6\big)-2\sqrt3=\frac{4\pi}3-2\sqrt3$.

So
$$I=\pi\Big(\frac{4\pi}3+4-4\sqrt3\Big)=\frac{4\pi^2}3-4(\sqrt3-1)\pi\approx3.96025,$$
which agrees with a direct numerical evaluation. ∎

prompt:
Let $\{a_n\}_{n=0}^\infty$ be a sequence given recursively by $a_0=1$ and
$$a_{n+1}=\frac{7a_n+\sqrt{45a_n^2-36}}{2},\qquad n=0,1,\dots$$
Show that the following statements hold for all positive integers $n$:

a) $a_n$ is a positive integer.

b) $a_na_{n+1}-1$ is the square of an integer.
answer: Squaring $2a_{n+1}-7a_n=\sqrt{45a_n^2-36}$ gives $a_{n+1}^2-7a_na_{n+1}+a_n^2+9=0$; by Vieta $a_{n+1}=7a_n-a_{n-1}$ (so all terms are integers), and $(a_n+a_{n+1})^2=9(a_na_{n+1}-1)$.

solutions.title: Quadratic relation and Vieta jumping
solutions.body:
**The sequence is increasing.** If $a_n\ge1$, then $45a_n^2-36>0$, so $a_{n+1}$ is defined and $2a_{n+1}-7a_n=\sqrt{45a_n^2-36}\ge0$, hence $a_{n+1}\ge\frac72a_n>a_n\ge1$. By induction all $a_n$ are defined, positive and $a_0<a_1<a_2<\cdots$. Also $a_1=\frac{7+3}{2}=5$.

**A quadratic relation.** Squaring $2a_{n+1}-7a_n=\sqrt{45a_n^2-36}$:
$$4a_{n+1}^2-28a_na_{n+1}+49a_n^2=45a_n^2-36\iff a_{n+1}^2-7a_na_{n+1}+a_n^2+9=0.\tag{1}$$

**a)** Fix $n\ge1$. By (1) for $n$ and for $n-1$ (the latter written as $a_{n-1}^2-7a_na_{n-1}+a_n^2+9=0$, since (1) is symmetric in its two variables), both $a_{n+1}$ and $a_{n-1}$ are roots of the quadratic
$$t^2-7a_n\,t+(a_n^2+9)=0 .$$
They are different ($a_{n-1}<a_n<a_{n+1}$), so they are the two roots, and by Vieta's formulas
$$a_{n+1}+a_{n-1}=7a_n,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad a_{n+1}=7a_n-a_{n-1}\quad(n\ge1).$$
Since $a_0=1$ and $a_1=5$ are integers, induction shows that every $a_n$ is an integer, and it is positive by the first paragraph. (The sequence is $1,5,34,233,1597,\dots$)

**b)** By (1), $a_{n+1}^2+a_n^2=7a_na_{n+1}-9$, hence
$$(a_n+a_{n+1})^2=7a_na_{n+1}-9+2a_na_{n+1}=9\,(a_na_{n+1}-1),$$
so
$$a_na_{n+1}-1=\left(\frac{a_n+a_{n+1}}{3}\right)^2 .$$
The left side is an integer and $q=\frac{a_n+a_{n+1}}3$ is rational. A rational number whose square is an integer is itself an integer (if $q=u/v$ in lowest terms with $v>1$, then $u^2/v^2$ is not an integer since $\gcd(u^2,v^2)=1$). Hence $q$ is an integer and $a_na_{n+1}-1=q^2$ is a perfect square. (Examples: $a_1a_2-1=169=13^2$, $a_2a_3-1=7921=89^2$.) ∎

prompt:
A triplet of polynomials $u,v,w\in\mathbb R[x,y,z]$ is called *smart* if there exist polynomials $P,Q,R\in\mathbb R[x,y,z]$ such that the following polynomial identity holds:
$$u^{2019}P+v^{2019}Q+w^{2019}R=2019 .$$

a) Is the triplet of polynomials
$$u=x+2y+3,\qquad v=y+z+2,\qquad w=x+y+z$$
smart?

b) Is the triplet of polynomials
$$u=x+2y+3,\qquad v=y+z+2,\qquad w=x+y-z$$
smart?

(Answer both parts, e.g. "yes, no".)
answer: No, yes

solutions.title: Common zero vs. a linear relation
solutions.body:
**a) No.** The three polynomials have a common zero: solving $x+2y+3=0$, $y+z+2=0$, $x+y+z=0$ gives $x=2$, $y=-\frac52$, $z=\frac12$ (check: $2-5+3=0$, $-\frac52+\frac12+2=0$, $2-\frac52+\frac12=0$). Substituting this point into a supposed identity $u^{2019}P+v^{2019}Q+w^{2019}R=2019$ gives $0=2019$, a contradiction. So the triplet is not smart.

**b) Yes.** Now
$$u-v-w=(x+2y+3)-(y+z+2)-(x+y-z)=1 .$$
Let $N=3\cdot2018+1=6055$ and raise this identity to the $N$-th power using the multinomial theorem:
$$1=(u-v-w)^N=\sum_{n_1+n_2+n_3=N}\frac{N!}{n_1!\,n_2!\,n_3!}(-1)^{n_2+n_3}\,u^{n_1}v^{n_2}w^{n_3}.$$
In every term at least one exponent is $\ge2019$: otherwise $n_1+n_2+n_3\le3\cdot2018<N$. Assign each term to one variable whose exponent is $\ge2019$ (say the first such among $u,v,w$) and factor out $u^{2019}$, $v^{2019}$ or $w^{2019}$ respectively. Collecting the terms, we get polynomials $P_0,Q_0,R_0$ (even with integer coefficients) such that
$$u^{2019}P_0+v^{2019}Q_0+w^{2019}R_0=1 .$$
Multiplying by $2019$, the polynomials $P=2019P_0$, $Q=2019Q_0$, $R=2019R_0$ work, so the triplet is smart.

**Answer: a) no, b) yes.** ∎

prompt:
For an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $M$ with integer entries we define a sequence $\mathcal S_M=\{M_i\}_{i=0}^\infty$ by the recurrence
$$M_0=M,\qquad M_{i+1}=(M_i^T)^{-1}M_i,\quad i=0,1,\dots$$
Find the smallest integer $n\ge2$ for which there exists a normal $n\times n$ matrix $M$ with integer entries such that its sequence $\mathcal S_M$ is non-constant and has period $P=7$, i.e., $M_{i+7}=M_i$ for all $i=0,1,\dots$

($M^T$ means the transpose of a matrix $M$. A square matrix $M$ is called normal if $M^TM=MM^T$ holds.)

solutions.title: Eigenvalues, then signed permutation matrices
solutions.body:
**Step 1: $M$ must be orthogonal.** A real normal matrix is unitarily diagonalizable: $M=UDU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ (all $\lambda_j\ne0$ since $M$ is invertible). As $M$ is real, $M^T=M^*=U\bar DU^*$, so
$$M_1=(M^T)^{-1}M=U\,\bar D^{-1}D\,U^*=U D_1U^*,\qquad D_1=\operatorname{diag}\big(\lambda_j/\bar\lambda_j\big).$$
$M_1$ is again real and of the same form, so by induction $M_i=UD_iU^*$ where the entries of $D_{i+1}$ are $\mu/\bar\mu$ for the entries $\mu$ of $D_i$. Every number $\mu/\bar\mu$ has modulus $1$, so for $i\ge1$ all diagonal entries of $D_i$ have modulus $1$ and $M_i$ is unitary. Periodicity gives $M=M_0=M_7$, hence $M$ is unitary; being real, it is **orthogonal**: $M^T=M^{-1}$.

**Step 2: the sequence is $M_i=M^{2^i}$.** If $M_i$ is orthogonal, then $(M_i^T)^{-1}=M_i$ and $M_{i+1}=M_i^2$ is orthogonal too. Hence $M_i=M^{2^i}$ for all $i$. The conditions become
- period 7: $M^{2^7}=M$, i.e. (as $M$ is invertible) $M^{127}=I$;
- non-constant: $M_1\ne M_0$, i.e. $M^2\ne M$, i.e. $M\ne I$.

**Step 3: integer orthogonal matrices.** Each column of $M$ is an integer vector of length $1$, so it has exactly one entry $\pm1$ and zeros elsewhere; distinct columns are orthogonal, so the nonzero entries lie in distinct rows. Thus $M$ is a *signed permutation matrix*: $Me_j=\varepsilon_je_{\sigma(j)}$ with $\varepsilon_j=\pm1$ and a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Then $M^k$ is a signed permutation matrix with permutation $\sigma^k$.

**Step 4: lower bound.** From $M^{127}=I$ we get $\sigma^{127}=\mathrm{id}$, so the order of $\sigma$ divides the prime $127$. If $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$, then $M$ is diagonal with entries $\pm1$, so $M^2=I$ and $M=M^{127}(M^2)^{-63}=I$, which is excluded. Hence $\sigma$ has order $127$. The order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths, so $\sigma$ has a cycle of length $127$, forcing $n\ge127$.

**Step 5: construction for $n=127$.** Let $M$ be the permutation matrix of the cycle $e_1\mapsto e_2\mapsto\cdots\mapsto e_{127}\mapsto e_1$. It has integer entries, is orthogonal (hence normal and invertible), and $M_i=M^{2^i}$. Since $M$ has order $127$, $M_i=M_j$ iff $2^i\equiv2^j\pmod{127}$ iff $i\equiv j\pmod 7$ (the order of $2$ modulo $127$ is $7$, as $2^7=128\equiv1$). So the sequence has period exactly $7$ and is non-constant.

(The eigenvalue view: $\lambda\mapsto\lambda/\bar\lambda$ acts as $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^2$ on the unit circle, so period $P$ forces $\lambda^{2^P-1}=1$; for $P=7$, $2^P-1=127$ is prime.)

**Answer: $n=127$.** ∎

prompt:
Determine the largest constant $K\ge0$ such that
$$\frac{a^a(b^2+c^2)}{(a^a-1)^2}+\frac{b^b(c^2+a^2)}{(b^b-1)^2}+\frac{c^c(a^2+b^2)}{(c^c-1)^2}\ge K\left(\frac{a+b+c}{abc-1}\right)^2$$
holds for all positive real numbers $a,b,c$ such that $ab+bc+ca=abc$.

solutions.title: Power series and weighted AM–GM
solutions.body:
The condition says $\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c=1$; in particular $a,b,c>1$, so $a^a,b^b,c^c>1$.

**Upper bound $K\le18$.** For $a=b=c=3$ the condition holds, the left side equals $3\cdot\frac{27\cdot18}{26^2}=\frac{1458}{676}$ and $\left(\frac{a+b+c}{abc-1}\right)^2=\frac{81}{676}$. So $K\le\frac{1458}{81}=18$.

**The inequality with $K=18$.**

*Step 1: $abc\ge3(a+b+c)$.* By $(x+y+z)^2\ge3(xy+yz+zx)$ with $x=\frac1a,y=\frac1b,z=\frac1c$:
$$1=\Big(\tfrac1a+\tfrac1b+\tfrac1c\Big)^2\ge3\Big(\tfrac1{ab}+\tfrac1{bc}+\tfrac1{ca}\Big)=\frac{3(a+b+c)}{abc}.$$
In particular $abc\ge27>1$.

*Step 2: reduction.* Using $b^2+c^2\ge2bc=\frac{2abc}{a}$ and the analogous bounds,
$$\text{LHS}\ge2abc\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}.$$
We will show
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}\ge\frac{abc}{(abc-1)^2}.\tag{$*$}$$
Then, with Step 1,
$$\text{LHS}\ge\frac{2(abc)^2}{(abc-1)^2}\ge\frac{2\cdot9(a+b+c)^2}{(abc-1)^2}=18\left(\frac{a+b+c}{abc-1}\right)^2 .$$

*Step 3: proof of $(*)$.* For $0<x<1$, differentiating $\frac1{1-x}=\sum_{k\ge0}x^k$ gives $\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}=\sum_{k\ge1}kx^k$. With $x=a^{-a}\in(0,1)$:
$$\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}=\frac1a\cdot\frac{a^{-a}}{(1-a^{-a})^2}=\frac1a\sum_{k\ge1}k\,a^{-ak}.$$
Hence
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}=\sum_{k\ge1}k\left(\frac1a\,a^{-ak}+\frac1b\,b^{-bk}+\frac1c\,c^{-ck}\right).$$
Since the weights $\frac1a,\frac1b,\frac1c$ are positive with sum $1$, the weighted AM–GM inequality gives
$$\frac1a\,a^{-ak}+\frac1b\,b^{-bk}+\frac1c\,c^{-ck}\ge\big(a^{-ak}\big)^{1/a}\big(b^{-bk}\big)^{1/b}\big(c^{-ck}\big)^{1/c}=(abc)^{-k}.$$
Therefore the sum is at least $\sum_{k\ge1}k\,(abc)^{-k}=\frac{(abc)^{-1}}{(1-(abc)^{-1})^2}=\frac{abc}{(abc-1)^2}$, which is $(*)$.

Equality throughout requires $a=b=c$, i.e. $a=b=c=3$, where it indeed holds.

**Answer: $K=18$.** ∎

prompt:
a) Is it true that for every non-empty set $A$ and every associative operation $*\colon A\times A\to A$ the conditions
$$x*x*y=y\qquad\text{and}\qquad y*x*x=y\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in A$$
imply commutativity of $*$?

b) Is it true that for every non-empty set $A$ and every associative operation $*\colon A\times A\to A$ the condition
$$x*x*y=y\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in A$$
implies commutativity of $*$?

(Answer both parts, e.g. "yes, no".)
answer: Yes, no

solutions.title: Identity element / a two-element counterexample
solutions.body:
**a) Yes.** Fix $x$ and put $e=x*x$. The two conditions say $e*y=y$ and $y*e=y$ for every $y$, so $e$ is a two-sided identity. A two-sided identity is unique (if $e,e'$ are identities, $e=e*e'=e'$), so $x*x=e$ for **every** $x\in A$.

Now let $x,y\in A$. Applying this to the element $x*y$ (and using associativity freely) gives $x*y*x*y=e$. Multiply on the left by $x$ and on the right by $y$:
$$x*x*y*x*y*y=x*e*y\ \Longrightarrow\ e*(y*x)*e=x*y\ \Longrightarrow\ y*x=x*y .$$
So $*$ is commutative.

(The official solution reaches the same conclusion by substituting $y\mapsto y*x*y$ into the first condition to get $x=y*x*y$, and then multiplying by $y$.)

**b) No.** Let $A=\{a,b\}$ with $a\ne b$ and define $x*y=y$ for all $x,y$ (so $a*a=a$, $b*b=b$, $a*b=b$, $b*a=a$). It is associative: $(x*y)*z=z=x*(y*z)$. It satisfies $x*x*y=y$ for all $x,y$. But $a*b=b\ne a=b*a$, so it is not commutative. (Note that $y*x*x=x\ne y$ in general, so the second condition of part a) fails, as it must.)

**Answer: a) yes, b) no.** ∎

prompt:
Find all twice differentiable functions $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$f''(x)\cos(f(x))\ge(f'(x))^2\sin(f(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R.$$
answer: Only the constant functions: the condition says $g=\sin f$ satisfies $g''\ge0$, and a bounded convex function on $\mathbb R$ is constant, which forces $f$ to be constant.

solutions.title: The inequality says $\sin f$ is convex
solutions.body:
**Constants work:** if $f\equiv C$, both sides are $0$.

**No other solutions.** Let $g(x)=\sin(f(x))$. Then $g'=f'\cos f$ and
$$g''=f''\cos f-(f')^2\sin f,$$
so the condition is exactly $g''\ge0$ on $\mathbb R$: $g$ is convex. A differentiable convex function lies above its tangent lines:
$$g(x)\ge g(y)+g'(y)(x-y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R .$$
If $g'(y_0)\ne0$ for some $y_0$, letting $x\to+\infty$ (if $g'(y_0)>0$) or $x\to-\infty$ (if $g'(y_0)<0$) makes the right side tend to $+\infty$, contradicting $|g|\le1$. Hence $g'\equiv0$ and $g\equiv c$ is constant.

So $\sin(f(x))=c$ for all $x$, i.e. $f(\mathbb R)$ is contained in the set $\{t:\sin t=c\}$, which is discrete (its points are isolated). Since $f$ is continuous, $f(\mathbb R)$ is connected, and a connected subset of a discrete set is a single point. Hence $f$ is constant.

**Answer: exactly the constant functions $f\equiv C$, $C\in\mathbb R$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $p$ be an even non-negative continuous function with $\int_{\mathbb R}p(x)\,dx=1$ and let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $\xi_1,\xi_2,\dots,\xi_n$ be independent identically distributed random variables with density function $p$. Define
$$X_0=0,\quad X_1=X_0+\xi_1,\quad X_2=X_1+\xi_2,\quad\dots,\quad X_n=X_{n-1}+\xi_n .$$
Prove that the probability that all the random variables $X_1,X_2,\dots,X_{n-1}$ lie between $X_0$ and $X_n$ equals $\frac1n$.
answer: Write $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n,-\xi_1,\dots,-\xi_n$ around a circle; the event for the $n$ cyclic shifts $(\xi_{m+1},\dots,\xi_n,-\xi_1,\dots,-\xi_m)$ happens for exactly one shift almost surely (where the closed walk attains its maximum or minimum), and all shifts have the same distribution because $p$ is even, so $n\cdot P=1$.

solutions.title: Cyclic shifts of a closed walk
solutions.body:
For $n=1$ the statement is trivial, so let $n\ge2$. For a vector $y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ let $I(y)=1$ if all partial sums $y_1,\ y_1+y_2,\ \dots,\ y_1+\dots+y_{n-1}$ lie strictly between $0$ and $y_1+\dots+y_n$, and $I(y)=0$ otherwise. We want $\mathbb E\,I(\xi)$, where $\xi=(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n)$. (Ties have probability $0$, see below, so "between" may be read strictly or not.)

**The closed walk.** Let $c_1,\dots,c_{2n}=\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n,-\xi_1,\dots,-\xi_n$, extended $2n$-periodically, and $t_j=c_1+\dots+c_j$ ($t_0=0$). Since $c_1+\dots+c_{2n}=0$, $(t_j)$ is $2n$-periodic. With $S=t_n=\xi_1+\dots+\xi_n$ one checks $t_{n+j}=S-t_j$ for $0\le j\le n$, and then by periodicity
$$t_{j+n}=S-t_j\qquad\text{for all }j.\tag{1}$$
For $0\le m\le n-1$ let $\xi^{(m)}=(c_{m+1},\dots,c_{m+n})=(\xi_{m+1},\dots,\xi_n,-\xi_1,\dots,-\xi_m)$; its partial sums are $u_j=t_{m+j}-t_m$ ($1\le j\le n$).

**Claim 1.** $I(\xi^{(m)})=1$ iff $t_m$ is a strict maximum or a strict minimum of the $2n$ values $t_m,t_{m+1},\dots,t_{m+2n-1}$ (one full period).

*Proof.* Let $D=u_n=t_{m+n}-t_m$. By (1), for $1\le j\le n-1$, $t_{m+n+j}-t_m=(S-t_{m+j})-(S-t_{m+n})=D-u_j$. So the $2n-1$ differences $t_{m+i}-t_m$ ($1\le i\le 2n-1$) are $u_1,\dots,u_{n-1},\ D,\ D-u_1,\dots,D-u_{n-1}$. They are all positive iff $D>0$ and $0<u_j<D$ for all $j$; all negative iff $D<0$ and $D<u_j<0$ for all $j$. Together this is exactly $I(\xi^{(m)})=1$. $\square$

**Claim 2.** Almost surely $t_0,\dots,t_{2n-1}$ are pairwise distinct. Indeed $t_i$ is the sum of $\xi_l$ over $l\in A_i$, where $A_i=\{1,\dots,i\}$ for $0\le i\le n$ and $A_i=\{i-n+1,\dots,n\}$ for $n<i<2n$. These $2n$ sets are distinct (the prefixes contain $1$ or are empty; the sets for $i>n$ are nonempty and miss $1$). So $t_i-t_j=\sum_l\varepsilon_l\xi_l$ with $\varepsilon_l\in\{-1,0,1\}$ not all zero, say $\varepsilon_{l_0}\ne0$. Conditionally on the other $\xi_l$, this equals $\pm\xi_{l_0}$ plus a constant, which is $0$ with probability $0$ because $\xi_{l_0}$ has a density. $\square$

**Exactly one shift works.** On the almost sure event of Claim 2, one period of the walk has a unique maximum position $j^+$ and a unique minimum position $j^-$ in $\mathbb Z/2n$. By (1), the shift $j\mapsto j+n$ turns $t$ into $S-t$, so it maps the maximum to the minimum: $j^-\equiv j^++n\pmod{2n}$. Hence exactly one of $j^+,j^-$ lies in $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, and by Claim 1
$$\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}I(\xi^{(m)})=1\qquad\text{almost surely.}$$

**All shifts have the same law.** Since $p$ is even, $-\xi_l$ also has density $p$; by independence, $\xi^{(m)}=(\xi_{m+1},\dots,\xi_n,-\xi_1,\dots,-\xi_m)$ consists of $n$ independent variables with density $p$, i.e. it has the same distribution as $\xi$. So $\mathbb E\,I(\xi^{(m)})=\mathbb E\,I(\xi)$ for each $m$.

Taking expectations, $n\,\mathbb E\,I(\xi)=1$, i.e. the required probability is $\frac1n$. ∎

(The official solution phrases the counting step via Raney's cycle lemma for the circular sequence $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n,-\xi_1,\dots,-\xi_n$.)

prompt:
Let $D=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0,\ \operatorname{Re}z>0\}$. Let $n\ge1$ and let $a_1,\dots,a_n\in D$ be distinct complex numbers. Define
$$f(z)=z\cdot\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{z-a_j}{z-\overline{a_j}} .$$
Prove that $f'$ has at least one root in $D$.
answer: The $2n$ roots $b_k$ of $f'$ satisfy $\sum 1/b_k=2\sum1/a_j$, so some root lies in the upper half-plane; and $\operatorname{Re}\frac{f'}{f}<0$ on $\{\operatorname{Re}z\le0<\operatorname{Im}z\}$, so that root lies in $D$.

solutions.title: Sum of reciprocals of the critical points + logarithmic derivative
solutions.body:
Write $f=g/h$ with $g(z)=z\prod_j(z-a_j)$ (degree $n+1$) and $h(z)=\prod_j(z-\bar a_j)$ (degree $n$), and let $N=g'h-gh'$, so $f'=N/h^2$.

**The roots of $f'$.** $N$ has degree $2n$ with leading coefficient $(n+1)-n=1$. It has no common root with $h$: if $h(w)=0$ then $w=\bar a_k$, $N(w)=-g(w)h'(w)$, and $g(w)\ne0$ (as $\operatorname{Im}w<0$ while the roots $0,a_j$ of $g$ have $\operatorname{Im}\ge0$), $h'(w)\ne0$ (the $\bar a_j$ are distinct). So the roots of $f'$ are exactly the $2n$ roots $b_1,\dots,b_{2n}$ of $N$ (with multiplicity). Also $N(0)=g'(0)h(0)=\prod(-a_j)\prod(-\bar a_j)\ne0$, so all $b_k\ne0$.

**Step 1: $\sum_k\frac1{b_k}=2\sum_j\frac1{a_j}$.** For a polynomial with nonzero roots, $\sum 1/b_k=-N'(0)/N(0)$. Near $0$ write $f(z)=Az\,\varphi(z)$ with $A=\prod_j(a_j/\bar a_j)$ and $\varphi(z)=\prod_j\frac{1-z/a_j}{1-z/\bar a_j}=1+cz+O(z^2)$, $c=\sum_j\big(\frac1{\bar a_j}-\frac1{a_j}\big)$. Then $f(z)=A(z+cz^2+O(z^3))$, so $f'(z)=A(1+2cz+O(z^2))$ and $\frac{f''(0)}{f'(0)}=2c$. On the other hand $\log f'=\log N-2\log h$ gives
$$\frac{f''(0)}{f'(0)}=\frac{N'(0)}{N(0)}-2\frac{h'(0)}{h(0)}=\frac{N'(0)}{N(0)}+2\sum_j\frac1{\bar a_j}.$$
Hence $\frac{N'(0)}{N(0)}=2c-2\sum_j\frac1{\bar a_j}=-2\sum_j\frac1{a_j}$, and $\sum_k\frac1{b_k}=2\sum_j\frac1{a_j}$.

**Step 2: some root lies in the upper half-plane.** For $a\in D$, $\operatorname{Im}\frac1a=-\frac{\operatorname{Im}a}{|a|^2}<0$. By Step 1, $\sum_k\operatorname{Im}\frac1{b_k}<0$, so some $b=b_k$ has $\operatorname{Im}\frac1b<0$, i.e. $\operatorname{Im}b>0$.

**Step 3: no root with $\operatorname{Re}z\le0<\operatorname{Im}z$.** Let $\operatorname{Re}z\le0$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Then $f(z)$ is finite and nonzero (the zeros $0,a_j$ and poles $\bar a_j$ of $f$ are not in this region), so $f'(z)=0$ iff $\frac{f'}{f}(z)=0$, where
$$\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}=\frac1z+\sum_j\left(\frac1{z-a_j}-\frac1{z-\bar a_j}\right).$$
Using $\operatorname{Re}\frac1w=\frac{\operatorname{Re}w}{|w|^2}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(z-a_j)=\operatorname{Re}(z-\bar a_j)=\operatorname{Re}z-\operatorname{Re}a_j<0$:
$$\operatorname{Re}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}=\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{|z|^2}+\sum_j(\operatorname{Re}z-\operatorname{Re}a_j)\left(\frac1{|z-a_j|^2}-\frac1{|z-\bar a_j|^2}\right).$$
The first term is $\le0$. Since $|z-\bar a_j|^2-|z-a_j|^2=4\operatorname{Im}z\operatorname{Im}a_j>0$, each bracket is positive and each summand is negative ($n\ge1$). Hence $\operatorname{Re}\frac{f'}{f}(z)<0$, so $f'(z)\ne0$.

**Conclusion.** The root $b$ from Step 2 has $\operatorname{Im}b>0$, and by Step 3 it cannot have $\operatorname{Re}b\le0$. Thus $\operatorname{Re}b>0$, i.e. $b\in D$. ∎

prompt:
Assume that a real polynomial $P(x)$ has no real roots. Prove that the polynomial
$$Q(x)=P(x)+\frac{P''(x)}{2!}+\frac{P^{(4)}(x)}{4!}+\dots$$
also has no real roots.
answer: By Taylor's formula $Q(x)=\frac{P(x+1)+P(x-1)}{2}$; $P$ has constant sign on $\mathbb R$, hence so does $Q$.

solutions.title: Taylor expansion at $x\pm1$
solutions.body:
A polynomial equals its (finite) Taylor expansion, so for every real $x$
$$P(x+1)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{P^{(k)}(x)}{k!},\qquad P(x-1)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\frac{P^{(k)}(x)}{k!}$$
(the sums are finite since $P^{(k)}=0$ for $k>\deg P$). Adding, the odd terms cancel:
$$\frac{P(x+1)+P(x-1)}{2}=\sum_{k\ \text{even}}\frac{P^{(k)}(x)}{k!}=Q(x).$$
A real polynomial without real roots is continuous and never zero, so by the intermediate value theorem it has constant sign; say $P(t)>0$ for all real $t$ (otherwise replace $P$ by $-P$, which replaces $Q$ by $-Q$). Then for every real $x$,
$$Q(x)=\frac{P(x+1)+P(x-1)}2>0,$$
so $Q$ has no real roots. ∎

prompt:
Let $n\ge1$. Assume that $A$ is a real $n\times n$ matrix which satisfies the equality
$$A^7+A^5+A^3+A-I=0 .$$
Show that $\det(A)>0$.
answer: Every eigenvalue is a root of $w(x)=x^7+x^5+x^3+x-1$; $w$ is strictly increasing, so its only real root is positive, and non-real eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs, so $\det A=\lambda_0^{k}\prod|\lambda_j|^{2k_j}>0$.

solutions.title: Eigenvalues are roots of $w$
solutions.body:
Let $w(x)=x^7+x^5+x^3+x-1$, so $w(A)=0$. If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ (over $\mathbb C$), then $0=w(A)v=w(\lambda)v$, so every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ is a root of $w$.

**Real roots of $w$.** $w'(x)=7x^6+5x^4+3x^2+1>0$, so $w$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$ and has at most one real root. Since $w(0)=-1<0<3=w(1)$, it has exactly one real root $\lambda_0$, and $\lambda_0\in(0,1)$. In particular $0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**The determinant.** $\det A$ is the product of the $n$ eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity (roots of the characteristic polynomial). The characteristic polynomial has real coefficients, so its non-real roots come in conjugate pairs $\mu,\bar\mu$ with equal multiplicities. Every real eigenvalue equals $\lambda_0$. Therefore
$$\det A=\lambda_0^{\,k}\prod_{j}(\mu_j\bar\mu_j)^{k_j}=\lambda_0^{\,k}\prod_j|\mu_j|^{2k_j}>0,$$
because $\lambda_0>0$ and every $\mu_j\ne0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a given continuous function. Find the limit
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)\sum_{k=0}^n\int_0^1x^k(1-x)^{n-k}f(x)\,dx .$$
answer: The limit is $f(0)+f(1)$: the kernel $K_n(x)=(n+1)\sum_k x^k(1-x)^{n-k}$ is symmetric, has total integral $\sum_k\binom nk^{-1}\to2$, and tends to $0$ uniformly away from the endpoints.

solutions.title: An approximate identity concentrated at both endpoints
solutions.body:
Let $K_n(x)=(n+1)\sum_{k=0}^nx^k(1-x)^{n-k}\ge0$; the quantity is $\int_0^1K_nf$. Note $K_n(1-x)=K_n(x)$.

**Total mass.** By the Beta integral $\int_0^1x^k(1-x)^{n-k}dx=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}$,
$$\int_0^1K_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{k!\,(n-k)!}{n!}=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^{-1}.$$
The terms $k=0,n$ give $2$, the terms $k=1,n-1$ give $\frac2n$, and for $2\le k\le n-2$ we have $\binom nk\ge\binom n2$, so these at most $n$ terms contribute at most $\frac{2n}{n(n-1)}$. Hence $\int_0^1K_n\to2$, and by symmetry $\int_0^{1/2}K_n=\int_{1/2}^1K_n\to1$.

**Concentration.** For $\delta\in(0,\frac12)$ and $x\in[\delta,1-\delta]$, each term satisfies $x^k(1-x)^{n-k}\le\max(x,1-x)^n\le(1-\delta)^n$, so $0\le K_n(x)\le(n+1)^2(1-\delta)^n\to0$ uniformly on $[\delta,1-\delta]$. Consequently $\int_0^{\delta}K_n\to1$ and $\int_{1-\delta}^1K_n\to1$.

**The limit.** Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $\delta$ with $|f(x)-f(0)|<\varepsilon$ on $[0,\delta]$ and $|f(x)-f(1)|<\varepsilon$ on $[1-\delta,1]$; let $\|f\|=\max|f|$. Then
$$\Big|\int_0^1K_nf-f(0)\!\int_0^\delta\!K_n-f(1)\!\int_{1-\delta}^1\!K_n\Big|\le\varepsilon\int_0^1K_n+\|f\|\int_\delta^{1-\delta}K_n .$$
(estimate $f-f(0)$ on $[0,\delta]$, $f-f(1)$ on $[1-\delta,1]$, and $f$ on the middle part). As $n\to\infty$, $\int_0^\delta K_n\to1$, $\int_{1-\delta}^1K_n\to1$, $\int_0^1K_n\to2$ and $\int_\delta^{1-\delta}K_n\to0$, hence
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Big|\int_0^1K_nf-f(0)-f(1)\Big|\le2\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)\sum_{k=0}^n\int_0^1x^k(1-x)^{n-k}f(x)\,dx=f(0)+f(1).$$
**Answer: $f(0)+f(1)$.** ∎

solutions.title: Summing the geometric series (official approach)
solutions.body:
For $x\ne\frac12$, $\sum_{k=0}^nx^k(1-x)^{n-k}=\frac{x^{n+1}-(1-x)^{n+1}}{x-(1-x)}=\frac{x^{n+1}-(1-x)^{n+1}}{2x-1}$.

**Lemma.** If $c\in(0,1)$ and $g$ is continuous on $[c,1]$, then $(n+1)\int_c^1x^ng(x)\,dx\to g(1)$.

*Proof.* $(n+1)\int_c^1x^n\,dx=1-c^{n+1}\to1$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, take $\eta>0$ with $|g(x)-g(1)|<\varepsilon$ on $[1-\eta,1]$. Then $\big|(n+1)\int_c^1x^n(g-g(1))\big|\le\varepsilon+(n+1)(1-\eta)^n\cdot2\max|g|$, which is $<2\varepsilon$ for large $n$. $\square$

Split $[0,1]$ into $[0,\frac14]$, $[\frac14,\frac34]$, $[\frac34,1]$.
- On $[\frac14,\frac34]$, every term is at most $(\frac34)^n$, so that part is at most $(n+1)^2(\frac34)^n\max|f|\to0$.
- On $[\frac34,1]$, the contribution is $(n+1)\int_{3/4}^1\frac{x^{n+1}f(x)}{2x-1}dx-(n+1)\int_{3/4}^1\frac{(1-x)^{n+1}f(x)}{2x-1}dx$. The first term is $(n+1)\int_{3/4}^1x^n\,g(x)\,dx$ with $g(x)=\frac{x f(x)}{2x-1}$ continuous on $[\frac34,1]$, so it tends to $g(1)=f(1)$ by the lemma; the second is at most $(n+1)(\frac14)^{n+1}\cdot2\max|f|\to0$.
- On $[0,\frac14]$, the substitution $x\mapsto1-x$ turns the integral into the previous case with $f(1-x)$ in place of $f(x)$, so it tends to $f(0)$.

Adding up, the limit is $f(0)+f(1)$. ∎

prompt:
In a box there are $31$, $41$ and $59$ stones coloured, respectively, red, green and blue. Three players, having t-shirts of these three colours, play the following game. They sequentially make one of two moves:

(I) either remove three stones of one colour from the box,

(II) or replace two stones of different colours by two stones of the third colour.

The game ends when all the stones in the box have the same colour and the winner is the player whose t-shirt has this colour. Assuming that the players play optimally, is it possible to decide whether the game ends and who will win, depending on who the starting player is?
answer: Yes. Invariants mod 3 show that the game can only end with red stones, so Red wins if it ends. If Red starts, Green and Blue can keep the game going forever (it never ends); if Green or Blue starts, Red wins.

solutions.title: Invariants mod 3, then strategies
solutions.body:
Write positions as $(r,g,b)$ (numbers of red, green, blue stones); the players move in a fixed cyclic order. While the game is not over, at least two colours are present, so a move of type (II) is always available. Green and Blue can never win (see below), so for them "optimal" means preventing Red's win, i.e. keeping the game going forever.

**Invariants.** A move (I) changes one count by $-3$; a move (II) changes the counts by $-1,-1,+2$, i.e. each count by $-1\pmod 3$. Hence:
1. The differences $r-g$ and $g-b$ modulo $3$ never change. Initially $r-g=-10\equiv2$ and $g-b=-18\equiv0$, so always $g\equiv b$ and $r\equiv g+2\pmod3$.
2. The total $T=r+g+b$ only drops by $3$ (moves (I)), so $T\equiv131\equiv2\pmod3$ and $T\ge2$.
3. If $i$ moves of type (I) and $j$ of type (II) have been made, then $T=131-3i$ and $r\equiv31-j\equiv1-j\pmod3$. So the number of moves made so far satisfies
$$i+j\equiv\frac{131-T}{3}+1-r\pmod 3, \tag{$\dagger$}$$
i.e. **the position determines whose turn it is.**

**Only Red can win.** A one-colour position $(0,T,0)$ would have $g-b=T\equiv2\not\equiv0$, and $(0,0,T)$ would have $g-b\equiv1$; both are impossible. So if the game ends, the box contains only red stones and Red wins.

**Small positions.** By invariant 1 the only non-final position with $T=2$ is $(0,1,1)$, whose only move is (II) green+blue$\to$red, giving $(2,0,0)$. The positions with $T=5$ are $(5,0,0),(2,3,0),(2,0,3),(0,1,4),(0,4,1),(3,1,1),(1,2,2)$; the only one in which every colour has at most $2$ stones is $(1,2,2)$, and by $(\dagger)$ at $(1,2,2)$ the number of moves made is $\equiv42\equiv0$: it is always **the starting player's turn** there.

**Case 1: Green or Blue starts — Red wins.** Red's strategy: if some colour has at least $3$ stones, remove three of them; otherwise make any move. Suppose it is Red's turn and no colour has $\ge3$ stones. Then $T\le6$, so $T\in\{2,5\}$. $T=5$ would mean the position $(1,2,2)$, where it is the starting player's turn, not Red's. So $T=2$, the position is $(0,1,1)$, and Red's only move ends the game with Red winning. Thus each of Red's turns either ends the game or decreases $T$ by $3$; since $T$ never increases and stays $\ge2$, the game ends after at most $43$ of Red's turns, and by the above Red is the winner.

**Case 2: Red starts — the game can be kept going forever.** Let $X_1$ be the player moving right after Red and $X_2$ the player moving right before Red. Call a position *dangerous* if Red can end the game from it in one move. A move ending the game produces $(t,0,0)$, so it is (I) from $(t,3,0)$ or $(t,0,3)$, or (II) from $(t-2,1,1)$. Thus the dangerous positions are exactly $(t,3,0)$, $(t,0,3)$, $(s,1,1)$.

$X_1$ and $X_2$ use only moves of type (II) and keep the following invariant: the game is not over, $T\ge5$, at Red's turn the position is not dangerous, and at $X_2$'s turn the position is not of the form $(s,1,1)$. It holds at the start: $(31,41,59)$, Red to move.

*Red's move.* Red cannot end the game. If $T\ge8$, after Red's move $T\ge5$. If $T=5$, it is Red's (the starter's) turn, so by $(\dagger)$ $r\equiv1$ and the position is $(1,2,2)$, where no colour has $3$ stones; so Red makes a move (II) and $T$ stays $5$.

*$X_1$'s move* (from any non-final position with $T\ge5$) to a non-final position not of the form $(s,1,1)$:
- if $(g,b)=(1,1)$ or $(2,2)$: then $r=T-2g\ge1$; play red+green$\to$blue, reaching $(r-1,0,3)$ with $r-1\ge2$, or $(r-1,1,4)$;
- otherwise, if $g,b\ge1$: play green+blue$\to$red, reaching $(r+2,g-1,b-1)$, which is final only if $g=b=1$ and of the form $(s,1,1)$ only if $g=b=2$ — both excluded;
- otherwise one of $g,b$ is $0$, say $b=0$ (the case $g=0$ is symmetric), and $r,g\ge1$: play red+green$\to$blue, reaching $(r-1,g-1,2)$, not of the form $(s,1,1)$ and not final (a blue-only position is impossible).

*$X_2$'s move* (from a non-final position, $T\ge5$, not $(s,1,1)$) to a non-final, non-dangerous position:
- if $r,g\ge1$: red+green$\to$blue gives $(r-1,g-1,b+2)$; as $b+2\ge2$ it could only be dangerous as $(t,0,3)$, i.e. if $(g,b)=(1,1)$, which is excluded; it is not final;
- if $r\ge1$, $g=0$ (so $b\ge1$): red+blue$\to$green gives $(r-1,2,b-1)$, neither dangerous nor final;
- if $r=0$: then $g\equiv b\equiv1\pmod 3$ and $g,b\ge1$, $(g,b)\ne(1,1)$; green+blue$\to$red gives $(2,g-1,b-1)$, which is dangerous only for $(g,b)\in\{(4,1),(1,4)\}$ (note $(2,2)$ violates $g\equiv1$). But $(0,4,1)$ and $(0,1,4)$ have $T=5$, and by $(\dagger)$ the number of moves made there is $\equiv43\equiv1$, so it is $X_1$'s turn, not $X_2$'s.

So the invariant is preserved forever and the game never ends. (For instance, from $(1,2,2)$ the play cycles $(1,2,2)\to(0,1,4)\to(2,0,3)\to(1,2,2)$, or via $(0,4,1)\to(2,3,0)$, or $(3,1,1)\to(2,0,3)$.)

**Answer: yes — if Red starts, the game (with best play by Green and Blue) never ends; if Green or Blue starts, Red wins.** (A computer search over all positions confirms this.) ∎

prompt:
Determine whether there exists a differentiable function $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$f(0)=f(1)=1,\qquad|f'(x)|\le2\ \text{for all }x\in[0,1]\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left|\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac12 .$$
answer: No

solutions.title: Squeeze above $|2x-1|$
solutions.body:
Suppose such $f$ exists. For $x\in(0,1)$, the mean value theorem on $[0,x]$ gives $c\in(0,x)$ with $\frac{f(x)-1}{x}=f'(c)\ge-2$, so $f(x)\ge1-2x$. On $[x,1]$ it gives $d\in(x,1)$ with $\frac{f(x)-1}{x-1}=f'(d)\le2$; as $x-1<0$, $f(x)\ge1+2(x-1)=2x-1$. Together (also at $x=0,1$)
$$f(x)\ge|2x-1|\qquad(0\le x\le1).$$
Hence
$$\frac12=\int_0^1|2x-1|\,dx\le\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\le\left|\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac12,$$
so $\int_0^1\big(f(x)-|2x-1|\big)dx=0$. The integrand is continuous ($f$ is differentiable, hence continuous) and nonnegative, so it vanishes identically: $f(x)=|2x-1|$ on $[0,1]$. But this function is not differentiable at $x=\frac12$, a contradiction.

**Answer: no, such a function does not exist.** ∎

prompt: For any given pair of positive integers $m>n$ find all $a\in\mathbb R$ for which the polynomial $x^m-ax^n+1$ can be expressed as a quotient of two nonzero polynomials with real nonnegative coefficients.
answer: Exactly the $a$ with $a<m\,n^{-n/m}(m-n)^{n/m-1}=\dfrac{m}{n^{n/m}(m-n)^{(m-n)/m}}$, i.e. exactly when $x^m-ax^n+1$ has no positive root.

solutions.title: Positive roots vs. telescoping $u^K-v^K$
solutions.body:
Let $f(x)=x^m-ax^n+1$ and $a^*=m\,n^{-n/m}(m-n)^{n/m-1}=\big(\tfrac mn\big)^{n/m}\big(\tfrac m{m-n}\big)^{(m-n)/m}$.

**$a\le0$ works:** $f=f/1$ has nonnegative coefficients. From now on $a>0$.

**If $a\ge a^*$, impossible.** $f'(x)=x^{n-1}(mx^{m-n}-an)$ vanishes at $x_0=(an/m)^{1/(m-n)}>0$, and
$$f(x_0)=1-x_0^n\big(a-x_0^{m-n}\big)=1-a\,\frac{m-n}{m}\,x_0^n .$$
Since $a\,x_0^n=a\big(\tfrac{an}{m}\big)^{n/(m-n)}=a^{m/(m-n)}\big(\tfrac nm\big)^{n/(m-n)}$,
$$f(x_0)\le0\iff a^{m/(m-n)}\ge\frac{m}{m-n}\Big(\frac mn\Big)^{n/(m-n)}\iff a\ge\Big(\frac m{m-n}\Big)^{(m-n)/m}\Big(\frac mn\Big)^{n/m}=a^* .$$
As $f(0)=1>0$, for $a\ge a^*$ the polynomial $f$ has a root $\beta\in(0,x_0]$. If $f=P/Q$ with nonzero $P,Q$ having nonnegative coefficients, then $P=fQ$ gives $P(\beta)=0$; but a nonzero polynomial with nonnegative coefficients is positive at every $\beta>0$. Contradiction.

**If $0<a<a^*$, possible.** For a positive integer $N$ let $K=mnN$, $u=x^m+1$, $v=ax^n$, and
$$P=u^K-v^K,\qquad Q=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}u^{K-1-j}v^j .$$
Then $P=(u-v)Q=fQ$, so $f=P/Q$, and $Q\ne0$ has nonnegative coefficients (as $a>0$). In $P=(x^m+1)^K-a^Kx^{nK}$ the only possibly negative coefficient is that of $x^{nK}=x^{m\cdot n^2N}$, which equals $\binom{K}{n^2N}-a^K$. So it suffices to find $N$ with
$$\binom{K}{k}\ge a^K,\qquad K=mnN,\ k=n^2N .$$
*Binomial estimate.* Let $\theta=k/K=n/m\in(0,1)$. In the expansion $1=(\theta+(1-\theta))^K=\sum_j\binom Kj\theta^j(1-\theta)^{K-j}$ the ratio of consecutive terms is $\frac{(K-j)k}{(j+1)(K-k)}$, which is $>1$ for $j<k$ and $<1$ for $j\ge k$; so the term $j=k$ is the largest of the $K+1$ terms and is at least $\frac1{K+1}$. Hence
$$\binom Kk\ge\frac{1}{K+1}\Big(\theta^{-\theta}(1-\theta)^{-(1-\theta)}\Big)^K=\frac{(a^*)^K}{K+1},$$
since $\theta^{-\theta}(1-\theta)^{-(1-\theta)}=(m/n)^{n/m}(m/(m-n))^{(m-n)/m}=a^*$. Because $a<a^*$ and $(K+1)^{1/K}\to1$, we get $(a^*)^K/(K+1)\ge a^K$ for all large $N$. Then $P$ has nonnegative coefficients, as required.

(The official solution reaches the same limit $\binom{K}{k}^{1/K}\to a^*$ via Stirling's formula.)

**Answer: $a<m\,n^{-n/m}(m-n)^{n/m-1}$ (all such real $a$, including all $a\le0$).** ∎

prompt:
Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be given real numbers with $0<m\le x_i\le M$ for each $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $X$ be the discrete random variable uniformly distributed on $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$. The mean $\mu$ and the variance $\sigma^2$ of $X$ are defined as
$$\mu(X)=\frac{x_1+\dots+x_n}{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma^2(X)=\frac{(x_1-\mu(X))^2+\dots+(x_n-\mu(X))^2}{n}.$$
By $X^2$ denote the discrete random variable uniformly distributed on $\{x_1^2,\dots,x_n^2\}$. Prove that
$$\sigma^2(X)\ge\left(\frac{m}{2M^2}\right)^2\sigma^2(X^2).$$
answer: In fact $\sigma^2(X^2)\le4M^2\sigma^2(X)$, because $(x_i^2-x_j^2)^2=(x_i+x_j)^2(x_i-x_j)^2\le4M^2(x_i-x_j)^2$; and $\frac{m^2}{4M^4}\cdot4M^2=\frac{m^2}{M^2}\le1$.

solutions.title: Pairwise form of the variance
solutions.body:
For any numbers $y_1,\dots,y_n$ with mean $\bar y$,
$$\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j}(y_i-y_j)^2=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j}\big(y_i^2+y_j^2-2y_iy_j\big)=2\cdot\frac1n\sum_iy_i^2-2\bar y^2=2\sigma^2(Y).$$
Apply it to $y_i=x_i^2$. Since $0<x_i,x_j\le M$,
$$(x_i^2-x_j^2)^2=(x_i+x_j)^2(x_i-x_j)^2\le4M^2(x_i-x_j)^2,$$
so
$$\sigma^2(X^2)=\frac1{2n^2}\sum_{i,j}(x_i^2-x_j^2)^2\le4M^2\cdot\frac{1}{2n^2}\sum_{i,j}(x_i-x_j)^2=4M^2\sigma^2(X).$$
Therefore, using $m\le M$,
$$\left(\frac m{2M^2}\right)^2\sigma^2(X^2)\le\frac{m^2}{4M^4}\cdot4M^2\,\sigma^2(X)=\frac{m^2}{M^2}\,\sigma^2(X)\le\sigma^2(X).$$
∎ (The proved inequality $\sigma^2(X)\ge\frac{1}{4M^2}\sigma^2(X^2)$ is even stronger than required.)

solutions.title: Variance as a minimum
solutions.body:
For any random variable $Y$ and constant $c$, $\mathbb E(Y-c)^2=\sigma^2(Y)+(\mathbb EY-c)^2\ge\sigma^2(Y)$. Take $Y=X^2$ and $c=\mu^2$ with $\mu=\mu(X)\in[m,M]$:
$$\sigma^2(X^2)\le\mathbb E\big(X^2-\mu^2\big)^2=\mathbb E\big[(X+\mu)^2(X-\mu)^2\big]\le(2M)^2\,\mathbb E(X-\mu)^2=4M^2\sigma^2(X).$$
As in the first solution, $\frac{m^2}{4M^4}\sigma^2(X^2)\le\frac{m^2}{M^2}\sigma^2(X)\le\sigma^2(X)$. ∎

prompt:
A function $f\colon\mathbb Z^+\to\mathbb R$ is called multiplicative if for every $a,b\in\mathbb Z^+$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$ we have $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$. Let $g$ be the multiplicative function given by
$$g(p^\alpha)=\alpha p^{\alpha-1},$$
where $\alpha\in\mathbb Z^+$ and $p>0$ is a prime. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that
$$g(n)+1=g(n+1).$$
answer: $g(13^2)=26$, $g(3^3)=27$ and $g=1$ on squarefree numbers; take $n=169x$, $n+1=27y$ with $x=77+1053t$, $y=482+6591t$ squarefree, which happens for a positive proportion of $t$ (e.g. $n=13013$).

solutions.title: Two prime powers and squarefree values of linear forms
solutions.body:
**Values of $g$.** For a squarefree $x=p_1\cdots p_r$, $g(x)=\prod g(p_i)=\prod 1\cdot p_i^0=1$. Also $g(13^2)=2\cdot13=26$ and $g(3^3)=3\cdot3^2=27$. Hence, by multiplicativity,
$$g(169x)=26\ \text{ if $x$ is squarefree and }13\nmid x,\qquad g(27y)=27\ \text{ if $y$ is squarefree and }3\nmid y .$$
So it suffices to find infinitely many such pairs with $169x+1=27y$; then $n=169x$ satisfies $g(n)+1=27=g(n+1)$.

**A family of solutions.** $169\cdot77+1=13014=27\cdot482$, and for $t\ge0$ put
$$x_t=77+1053t,\qquad y_t=482+6591t\qquad(1053=27\cdot39,\ 6591=169\cdot39).$$
Then $169x_t+1=13014+177957t=27y_t$. Moreover $x_t\equiv77\equiv12\pmod{13}$ and $y_t\equiv482\equiv2\pmod3$, so $13\nmid x_t$ and $3\nmid y_t$; also $x_t\equiv2\pmod 3$ and $y_t\equiv1\pmod{13}$. (For $t=0$: $x_0=77=7\cdot11$, $y_0=482=2\cdot241$ are squarefree, giving $g(13013)=26$, $g(13014)=27$.)

**Infinitely many $t$ with $x_t,y_t$ both squarefree.** Fix a large $X$ and count $t\in\{0,1,\dots,X-1\}$ for which $p^2\mid x_t$ or $p^2\mid y_t$ for some prime $p$.
- $p=3$ and $p=13$ never occur, by the congruences above.
- For $p\notin\{3,13\}$, $p\nmid1053\cdot6591=3^5\cdot13^4$, so $p^2\mid x_t$ holds for $t$ in a single residue class modulo $p^2$; the number of such $t<X$ is at most $X/p^2+1$. The same holds for $y_t$.
- Only primes with $p^2\le y_{X-1}<6591X$, i.e. $p<\sqrt{6591X}$, can occur.

Hence the number of bad $t$ is at most
$$\sum_{p<\sqrt{6591X},\ p\ne3,13}2\Big(\frac X{p^2}+1\Big)\le2X\Big(\frac14+\sum_{k\ge5\ \text{odd}}\frac1{k^2}\Big)+2\sqrt{6591X}.$$
Since $\sum_{k\ \text{odd}}\frac1{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2}8$, the bracket equals $\frac14+\frac{\pi^2}8-1-\frac19<0.373$. So at least $0.254X-2\sqrt{6591X}$ values $t<X$ are good, and this tends to infinity with $X$.

Each good $t$ gives $n=169x_t$ with $g(n)+1=g(n+1)$, and different $t$ give different $n$. ∎

(The official solution uses a theorem of Prachar on the density of squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions; the elementary count above suffices.)

prompt:
Let $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a continuously differentiable function. Prove that
$$\left|f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac12\max_{x\in[0,1]}|f'(x)| .$$
answer: $f(1)-\int_0^1f=\int_0^1xf'(x)\,dx$ (integration by parts), and $\left|\int_0^1xf'\right|\le\max|f'|\int_0^1x\,dx=\frac12\max|f'|$.

solutions.title: Integration by parts
solutions.body:
Since $f$ is $C^1$, integration by parts gives
$$\int_0^1x\,f'(x)\,dx=\big[x f(x)\big]_0^1-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx .$$
Let $K=\max_{[0,1]}|f'|$ (it exists, $f'$ being continuous on a compact interval). Then
$$\left|f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|=\left|\int_0^1xf'(x)\,dx\right|\le\int_0^1x\,|f'(x)|\,dx\le K\int_0^1x\,dx=\frac K2 .$$
∎ (Equality holds for $f(x)=x$.)

solutions.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini (official approach)
solutions.body:
Write $f(x)=f(0)+\int_0^xf'(y)\,dy$ and $f(1)=f(0)+\int_0^1f'(y)\,dy$. Then
$$f(1)-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=\int_0^1f'(y)\,dy-\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^xf'(y)\,dy\,dx .$$
Swapping the order of integration in the double integral (the region is $0\le y\le x\le1$),
$$\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^xf'(y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1f'(y)\int_y^1dx\,dy=\int_0^1f'(y)(1-y)\,dy .$$
Hence $f(1)-\int_0^1f=\int_0^1f'(y)\big(1-(1-y)\big)dy=\int_0^1y\,f'(y)\,dy$, and the estimate finishes as in the first solution: $\left|\int_0^1yf'(y)\,dy\right|\le\max|f'|\cdot\frac12$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A,B$ be two complex nonsingular $n\times n$ matrices such that
$$A^2B-2ABA+BA^2=0 .$$
Prove that the matrix $AB^{-1}A^{-1}B-I_n$ is nilpotent. (Here $I_n$ denotes the $n\times n$ identity matrix. A matrix $X$ is called nilpotent if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $X^k=0$.)
answer: The condition says $A$ commutes with $AB-BA$; from this, if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $X=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B$ then so is $2-\frac1\lambda$. This Möbius map is $u\mapsto u+1$ in the coordinate $u=\frac1{\lambda-1}$, so a finite spectrum forces $\lambda=1$; hence $X-I$ is nilpotent.

solutions.title: Eigenvalues are permuted by $\lambda\mapsto 2-1/\lambda$
solutions.body:
Let $X=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B$ and $C=AB-BA$. The hypothesis reads $A(AB-BA)-(AB-BA)A=0$, i.e. $AC=CA$; hence also $A^{-1}C=CA^{-1}$.

It suffices to show that $1$ is the only eigenvalue of $X$: then the characteristic polynomial of $X-I$ is $t^n$, and $(X-I)^n=0$ by Cayley–Hamilton.

**Lemma.** If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $X$, then $\mu=\frac{2\lambda-1}{\lambda}$ is also an eigenvalue of $X$.

*Proof.* $X$ is invertible, so $\lambda\ne0$, and $X-\lambda I$ is singular. Hence so is
$$BA^{-1}(X-\lambda I)=A^{-1}B-\lambda BA^{-1}.$$
We rewrite this using $C$: $\lambda A^{-1}(BA-AB)A^{-1}=\lambda A^{-1}B-\lambda BA^{-1}$, so
$$A^{-1}B-\lambda BA^{-1}=-\lambda A^{-1}CA^{-1}+(1-\lambda)A^{-1}B=-\lambda A^{-2}C+(1-\lambda)A^{-1}B,$$
using $CA^{-1}=A^{-1}C$. Multiplying on the left by the invertible matrix $\frac1\lambda B^{-1}A$:
$$\frac1\lambda B^{-1}A\big(-\lambda A^{-2}C+(1-\lambda)A^{-1}B\big)=-B^{-1}A^{-1}C+\frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda}I=B^{-1}A^{-1}BA-I+\frac{1-\lambda}\lambda I=Y-\mu I,$$
where $Y=B^{-1}A^{-1}BA$ and we used $-B^{-1}A^{-1}(AB-BA)=-I+B^{-1}A^{-1}BA$. So $Y-\mu I$ is singular, i.e. $\mu$ is an eigenvalue of $Y$. Finally $Y=A^{-1}XA$ is similar to $X$, so $\mu$ is an eigenvalue of $X$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** Let $\varphi(\lambda)=2-\frac1\lambda$. Note $\varphi(\lambda)-1=\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}$, so for $\lambda\ne1$ also $\varphi(\lambda)\ne1$ and
$$\frac1{\varphi(\lambda)-1}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-1}=\frac1{\lambda-1}+1 .$$
Suppose $X$ had an eigenvalue $\lambda_0\ne1$. By the lemma, $\lambda_k=\varphi^k(\lambda_0)$ are eigenvalues for all $k\ge0$, all $\ne1$, and $\frac1{\lambda_k-1}=\frac1{\lambda_0-1}+k$ are pairwise distinct. So $X$ would have infinitely many eigenvalues — impossible. Hence every eigenvalue of $X$ equals $1$, and $X-I_n=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B-I_n$ is nilpotent. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $G$ be a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices. Let $d_i$ be the degree of its $i$-th vertex, $i=1,\dots,n$. Denote $\Delta=\max d_i$. Prove that if
$$\sum_{i=1}^nd_i^2>n\Delta(n-\Delta)$$
then $G$ contains a triangle. (A graph is called simple if there are no loops and no multiple edges between any pair of vertices.)
answer: If $G$ is triangle-free, adjacent vertices have disjoint neighbourhoods, so $d_i+d_j\le n$ on every edge and $\sum d_i^2=\sum_{ij\in E}(d_i+d_j)\le n|E|$; and $|E|\le\Delta(n-\Delta)$ because the neighbourhood of a max-degree vertex is independent.

solutions.title: Contrapositive: two counting bounds
solutions.body:
Assume $G$ has no triangle; we show $\sum d_i^2\le n\Delta(n-\Delta)$. Let $E$ be the edge set and $e=|E|$.

**Step 1: $\sum_id_i^2=\sum_{ij\in E}(d_i+d_j)$.** Each vertex $i$ appears in exactly $d_i$ edges and contributes $d_i$ to the right side for each of them, i.e. $d_i\cdot d_i$ in total.

**Step 2: $d_i+d_j\le n$ for every edge $ij$.** The neighbourhoods $N(i)$ and $N(j)$ are disjoint: a common neighbour $k$ would give a triangle $ijk$. Hence $d_i+d_j=|N(i)|+|N(j)|\le n$. With Step 1: $\sum_id_i^2\le n\,e$.

**Step 3: $e\le\Delta(n-\Delta)$.** Let $v$ have degree $\Delta$. No two vertices of $N(v)$ are adjacent (that would form a triangle with $v$), so every edge has at least one endpoint in $W=V\setminus N(v)$, a set of $n-\Delta$ vertices. Counting each edge from an endpoint in $W$,
$$e\le\sum_{w\in W}d_w\le(n-\Delta)\Delta .$$

Combining, $\sum_id_i^2\le ne\le n\Delta(n-\Delta)$. So if $\sum d_i^2>n\Delta(n-\Delta)$, $G$ must contain a triangle. ∎

(The bound is sharp: for the complete bipartite graph $K_{\Delta,\Delta}$ with $n=2\Delta$, $\sum d_i^2=2\Delta\cdot\Delta^2=n\Delta(n-\Delta)$.)

prompt:
Let $p>2$ be a prime and let
$$\mathcal A=\{n\in\mathbb N:\ 2p\mid n\ \text{and}\ p^2\nmid n\ \text{and}\ n\mid 3^n-1\}.$$
Prove that
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{|\mathcal A\cap[1,k]|}{k}\le\frac{2\log3}{p\log p}.$$
answer: Write $n=pr$; Fermat gives $3^n\equiv3^r\pmod p$, so $l=\operatorname{ord}_p3$ divides $r$. Thus every $n\in\mathcal A$ is a multiple of $pl$, and $3^l>p$ gives $l>\frac{\log p}{\log3}$, so the density is at most $\frac1{pl}<\frac{\log3}{p\log p}$.

solutions.title: Order of 3 modulo $p$
solutions.body:
If $p=3$, no $n$ with $3\mid n$ divides $3^n-1$ (which is $\equiv2\pmod3$), so $\mathcal A=\emptyset$ and there is nothing to prove. Let $p\ge5$ and let $l$ be the multiplicative order of $3$ modulo $p$.

**Every $n\in\mathcal A$ is a multiple of $pl$.** Let $n\in\mathcal A$ and write $n=pr$ (possible as $p\mid n$). Since $p\mid n\mid3^n-1$, we have $3^n\equiv1\pmod p$. By Fermat's little theorem $3^p\equiv3\pmod p$, so
$$3^n=(3^p)^r\equiv3^r\pmod p,$$
hence $3^r\equiv1\pmod p$ and $l\mid r$. Therefore $pl\mid n$.

**Size of $l$.** $p\mid3^l-1$ and $3^l-1>0$, so $p\le3^l-1<3^l$, i.e. $l>\frac{\log p}{\log 3}$.

**Density.** $\mathcal A\cap[1,k]$ is contained in the set of multiples of $pl$ in $[1,k]$, which has at most $\frac k{pl}$ elements. Hence
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{|\mathcal A\cap[1,k]|}{k}\le\frac1{pl}<\frac{\log3}{p\log p}\le\frac{2\log3}{p\log p}.$$
∎ (Neither the condition $p^2\nmid n$ nor the evenness of $n$ is needed for this bound; the official solution uses them to get $3^{r/2}\equiv\pm1\pmod p$, which leads to the factor $2$.)

prompt:
Suppose that $f\colon[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and that
$$\left(\int_{-1}^1e^xf(x)\,dx\right)^2\ge\left(\int_{-1}^1f(x)\,dx\right)\left(\int_{-1}^1e^{2x}f(x)\,dx\right).$$
Prove that there exists a point $c\in(-1,1)$ such that $f(c)=0$.
answer: If $f$ had no zero, WLOG $f>0$ on $(-1,1)$; then $t\mapsto\int(e^x-t)^2f\,dx$ is a positive quadratic, so its discriminant is negative: $\left(\int e^xf\right)^2<\int f\int e^{2x}f$ (strict Cauchy–Schwarz), a contradiction.

solutions.title: Strict Cauchy–Schwarz via a quadratic in $t$
solutions.body:
Suppose $f(x)\ne0$ for all $x\in(-1,1)$. By the intermediate value theorem $f$ has constant sign on $(-1,1)$; replacing $f$ by $-f$ (which does not change the hypothesis, both sides being quadratic in $f$) we may assume $f>0$ on $(-1,1)$, hence $f\ge0$ on $[-1,1]$.

For every real $t$, the function $(e^x-t)^2f(x)$ is continuous, nonnegative, and positive on $(-1,1)$ except possibly at the single point $x=\ln t$. Hence
$$0<\int_{-1}^1(e^x-t)^2f(x)\,dx=t^2\int_{-1}^1f-2t\int_{-1}^1e^xf+\int_{-1}^1e^{2x}f\qquad\text{for all }t\in\mathbb R.$$
The leading coefficient $\int f$ is positive, so a quadratic that is positive for all real $t$ has negative discriminant:
$$\left(\int_{-1}^1e^xf\right)^2<\left(\int_{-1}^1f\right)\left(\int_{-1}^1e^{2x}f\right),$$
contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $f(c)=0$ for some $c\in(-1,1)$. ∎

(Equivalently: by Cauchy–Schwarz for $e^x\sqrt f$ and $\sqrt f$, $(\int e^xf)^2\le\int f\int e^{2x}f$, with equality only if $e^x\sqrt f$ is a constant multiple of $\sqrt f$, which is impossible when $f>0$ on $(-1,1)$.)

prompt:
A real $2024\times2024$ matrix $A$ is called *nice* if $(Av,v)=1$ for every vector $v\in\mathbb R^{2024}$ with unit norm.

a) Prove that the only nice matrix such that all of its eigenvalues are real is the identity matrix.

b) Find an example of a nice non-identity matrix.
answer: Nice $\iff A+A^T=2I\iff A=I+B$ with $B^T=-B$. a) $B$ has purely imaginary eigenvalues, so real eigenvalues force them to be $0$, and a normal (skew-symmetric) matrix with only zero eigenvalues is $0$. b) $A=I+E_{12}-E_{21}$.

solutions.title: Symmetric part equals $I$
solutions.body:
**Nice means $A=I+B$ with $B$ skew-symmetric.** Since $(Av,v)=v^TAv=v^TA^Tv$, we get $v^T(A+A^T)v=2$ for all unit $v$, hence $v^TSv=0$ for all $v$, where $S=A+A^T-2I$ is symmetric (scale $v$). A symmetric matrix with vanishing quadratic form is zero, by polarization: $2u^TSw=(u+w)^TS(u+w)-u^TSu-w^TSw=0$. So $A+A^T=2I$, i.e. $B=A-I$ satisfies $B^T=-B$. Conversely, if $B^T=-B$ then $v^TBv=(v^TBv)^T=v^TB^Tv=-v^TBv$, so $v^TBv=0$ and $(Av,v)=|v|^2=1$ for unit $v$: $A=I+B$ is nice.

**a)** Let $A$ be nice with real eigenvalues; then $B=A-I$ has real eigenvalues. For a skew-symmetric real $B$ and $Bz=\lambda z$ ($z\in\mathbb C^{2024}$, $z\ne0$):
conjugating and transposing $Bz=\lambda z$ gives $\bar z^TB^T=\bar\lambda\bar z^T$, i.e. $\bar z^TB=-\bar\lambda\bar z^T$. Hence
$$\lambda\,\bar z^Tz=\bar z^TBz=-\bar\lambda\,\bar z^Tz,$$
and since $\bar z^Tz=|z|^2>0$, $\lambda=-\bar\lambda$ is purely imaginary. Being also real, every eigenvalue of $B$ is $0$; so $B$ is nilpotent and hence so is $B^2=-B^TB$. But $B^TB$ is symmetric, hence diagonalizable, and nilpotent, so $B^TB=0$. Then $|Bv|^2=v^TB^TBv=0$ for all $v$, i.e. $B=0$ and $A=I$. (And $I$ is indeed nice.)

**b)** Take $B=E_{12}-E_{21}$ (entry $1$ at position $(1,2)$, $-1$ at $(2,1)$, zeros elsewhere), which is skew-symmetric and nonzero. Then
$$A=I+E_{12}-E_{21}$$
is nice and $A\ne I$; indeed $(Av,v)=|v|^2+v_1v_2-v_2v_1=1$ for unit $v$. (Its eigenvalues $1\pm i$ are not all real, consistent with a).) ∎

prompt:
Let $a_1>0$ and for $n\ge1$ define
$$a_{n+1}=a_n+\frac1{a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n}.$$
Prove that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n^2}{\ln n}=2$.
answer: With $S_n=a_1+\dots+a_n$: $a_n\to\infty$, $\frac{S_n}{a_n}-\frac{S_{n-1}}{a_{n-1}}=1-\frac1{a_na_{n-1}}\to1$ so $\frac{S_n}{na_n}\to1$ (Cesàro), hence $n(a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2)=\frac{na_n}{S_n}\big(1+\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\big)\to2$, and Stolz–Cesàro gives $a_n^2/\ln n\to2$.

solutions.title: Cesàro and Stolz–Cesàro
solutions.body:
Let $S_n=a_1+\dots+a_n$, so $a_{n+1}-a_n=\frac1{S_n}>0$: the sequence is positive and increasing.

**Step 1: $a_n\to\infty$.** If $a_n\le L$ for all $n$, then $S_n\le nL$ and $a_{n+1}-a_n\ge\frac1{nL}$, so $a_{n+1}-a_1\ge\frac1L\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k\to\infty$, a contradiction. Being increasing and unbounded, $a_n\to\infty$.

**Step 2: $\frac{S_n}{na_n}\to1$.** For $n\ge2$, using $a_n-a_{n-1}=\frac1{S_{n-1}}$,
$$\frac{S_n}{a_n}-\frac{S_{n-1}}{a_{n-1}}=\frac{S_{n-1}+a_n}{a_n}-\frac{S_{n-1}}{a_{n-1}}=1-S_{n-1}\frac{a_n-a_{n-1}}{a_na_{n-1}}=1-\frac1{a_na_{n-1}}\longrightarrow1 .$$
By Cesàro's theorem (the averages of a convergent sequence converge to the same limit), $\frac1n\sum_{k=2}^n\Big(\frac{S_k}{a_k}-\frac{S_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\Big)=\frac1n\Big(\frac{S_n}{a_n}-1\Big)\to1$, i.e. $\frac{S_n}{na_n}\to1$.

**Step 3: $n(a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2)\to2$.** We have $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=1+\frac1{a_nS_n}\to1$ and
$$n\,(a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2)=n\,\frac{a_{n+1}+a_n}{S_n}=\frac{na_n}{S_n}\Big(1+\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\Big)\longrightarrow1\cdot2=2 .$$

**Step 4: Stolz–Cesàro.** The sequence $v_n=\ln n$ is strictly increasing and unbounded, and since $n\ln(1+\frac1n)\to1$,
$$\frac{a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2}{\ln(n+1)-\ln n}=\frac{n(a_{n+1}^2-a_n^2)}{n\ln(1+\frac1n)}\longrightarrow2 .$$
By the Stolz–Cesàro theorem, $\lim\frac{a_n^2}{\ln n}=2$. ∎

prompt:
Let $(b_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a sequence of positive integers satisfying $b_n=d\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k\right)$ for all $n\ge1$. (By $d(m)$ we denote the number of positive divisors of $m$.)

a) Prove that $(b_n)_{n\ge0}$ is unbounded.

b) Prove that there are infinitely many $n$ such that $b_n>b_{n+1}$.
answer: With $s_n=\sum_{k<n}b_k$: $s_{n+1}=s_n+d(s_n)$. a) By CRT choose $x$ with $p_j^C\mid x+j$ ($1\le j\le C$); the walk cannot jump over $[x+1,x+C]$, giving $d(s_n)>C$. b) If $b$ were eventually nondecreasing, each value $a$ would be taken on an arithmetic progression with difference $a$ of numbers with exactly $a$ divisors; such progressions have length $<a^8$ (CRT + Mertens), while $b_n\ll n^{1/19}$ since $d(m)\ll m^{1/20}$ — too few values for too many indices.

solutions.title: Crossing a block of highly divisible numbers; progressions with constant divisor count
solutions.body:
Let $s_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k$, so $s_0=0$, $s_1=b_0\ge1$, $s_{n+1}=s_n+b_n$, the sequence $(s_n)$ is strictly increasing, and $b_n=d(s_n)$ for $n\ge1$. Let $p_1<p_2<\dots$ be the primes.

**a)** Suppose $b_n\le C$ for all $n$. By the Chinese remainder theorem there is a positive integer $x$ with $x\equiv-j\pmod{p_j^{\,C}}$ for $j=1,\dots,C$; then $p_j^C\mid x+j$ and $d(x+j)\ge C+1$ for $1\le j\le C$. Let $n$ be the least index with $s_n>x$; $n\ge1$ as $s_0=0$. Then $s_{n-1}\le x$ and $s_n=s_{n-1}+b_{n-1}\le x+C$, so $s_n\in[x+1,x+C]$ and $b_n=d(s_n)\ge C+1$, a contradiction.

**b)** We need three facts.

*Fact 1 ($d(m)\le C_\delta m^\delta$ for each $\delta>0$).* $\frac{d(m)}{m^\delta}=\prod_{p^v\Vert m}\frac{v+1}{p^{v\delta}}$. If $p\ge2^{1/\delta}$, then $p^{v\delta}\ge2^v\ge v+1$, so the factor is $\le1$. For each of the finitely many $p<2^{1/\delta}$ the factor is at most $c_\delta=\sup_{v\ge0}(v+1)2^{-v\delta}<\infty$. Hence $d(m)\le c_\delta^{\,2^{1/\delta}}m^\delta$.

*Fact 2 (growth).* By Fact 1 with $\delta=\frac1{20}$, $d(m)\le Cm^{1/20}$. Let $\psi(t)=t^{19/20}$; $\psi'$ is decreasing, so by the mean value theorem, for $n\ge1$,
$$\psi(s_{n+1})-\psi(s_n)\le(s_{n+1}-s_n)\psi'(s_n)=d(s_n)\cdot\tfrac{19}{20}s_n^{-1/20}\le C .$$
Thus $s_n^{19/20}\le s_1^{19/20}+Cn$, so $s_n\le C'n^{20/19}$ and $b_n=d(s_n)\le C s_n^{1/20}\le B\,n^{1/19}$ for all $n\ge1$, with a constant $B$.

*Fact 3 (progressions).* For $a\ge1$ call an arithmetic progression $s,s+a,\dots,s+(L-1)a$ of positive integers *$a$-uniform* if all its terms have exactly $a$ divisors. **Claim:** there is a constant $C_1$ such that every $a$-uniform progression has length $L\le C_1a^8$.

*Proof.* Fix a prime $p$, let $\ell=v_p(a)$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_{\ell+1}$ be the $\ell+1$ smallest primes not dividing $a$; put $B_p=\prod_jq_j^{\,p}$. Since $\gcd(B_p,a)=1$, any $B_p$ consecutive terms of the progression run through all residues modulo $B_p$; by CRT one of them, $t$, satisfies $t\equiv q_j^{\,p-1}\pmod{q_j^{\,p}}$ for all $j$, so $v_{q_j}(t)=p-1$ and $p^{\ell+1}\mid d(t)$, whence $d(t)\ne a$. Therefore $L<B_p$ for **every** prime $p$. (In particular $L$ is bounded for each fixed $a$.)

Now let $a$ be large. We have $\omega(a)\le\log_2a$ and $\ell\le\log_2a$, and among the first $m=\ell+1+\omega(a)\le3\log_2a$ primes at least $\ell+1$ do not divide $a$, so $q_j\le p_m$. By Chebyshev's estimate $p_m=O(m\log m)$, so $p_m\le(\log a)^2$ for large $a$, and $\log B_p\le2p(\ell+1)\log\log a$. Suppose $B_p>a^8$ for every prime $p\le x:=\log a$. Then $\ell_p+1>\frac{4\log a}{p\log\log a}$ for all $p\le x$ (with $\ell_p=v_p(a)$), and multiplying by $\log p$ and summing,
$$\sum_{p\le x}(\ell_p+1)\log p>\frac{4\log a}{\log\log a}\sum_{p\le x}\frac{\log p}{p}\ge\frac{4\log a}{\log\log a}\,(\log\log a-c_0)$$
by Mertens' theorem $\sum_{p\le x}\frac{\log p}p=\log x+O(1)$. The left side is $\sum_p\ell_p\log p+\theta(x)\le\log a+2x=3\log a$ (as $\prod p^{\ell_p}\mid a$, and Chebyshev's bound $\theta(x)\le x\log4$). This gives $3>4\big(1-\frac{c_0}{\log\log a}\big)$, false for large $a$. So for large $a$ some $p\le\log a$ has $B_p\le a^8$, hence $L<a^8$; together with the boundedness for each small $a$ this proves the claim. $\square$

*Conclusion.* Suppose, for contradiction, that $b_n\le b_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge N$ (with $N\ge1$). For each value $a$, the indices $n\ge N$ with $b_n=a$ form a block of consecutive integers $n_0,\dots,n_0+L-1$; along it $s_{n_0+i}=s_{n_0}+ia$ and $d(s_{n_0+i})=b_{n_0+i}=a$, so this is an $a$-uniform progression and $L\le C_1a^8$. For $M>N$, all $b_n$ with $N\le n\le M$ are at most $BM^{1/19}$ by Fact 2, so
$$M-N+1\le\sum_{a\le BM^{1/19}}C_1a^8\le C_1\big(BM^{1/19}\big)^9=C_2\,M^{9/19},$$
which fails for large $M$. Hence $b_n>b_{n+1}$ for infinitely many $n$. ∎

(The official solution proves the sharper bound $L\ll_\varepsilon a^{1+\varepsilon}$ with the same CRT idea; any polynomial bound suffices, because $b_n$ grows slower than every power of $n$.)

prompt: Let $a\ge2$ be an integer. Prove that there exists a positive integer $b$ with the following property: For each positive integer $n$, there is a prime number $p=p(a,b,n)$ such that $a^n+b$ is divisible by $p$ but not divisible by $p^2$.
answer: If $a$ is a power of $2$, take $b=10$ (then $2\,\|\,a^n+10$, except $a=2,n=1$ where $3\,\|\,12$). Otherwise let $q$ be an odd prime factor of $a$: if $q\,\|\,a$ take $b=a$; if $q^2\mid a$ take $b=q$.

solutions.title: Case analysis on the prime factors of $a$
solutions.body:
We write $p\,\|\,N$ for "$p\mid N$ but $p^2\nmid N$".

**Case 1: $a=2^m$, $m\ge1$.** Take $b=10$. Then $a^n+10=2\,(2^{mn-1}+5)$.
- If $mn\ge2$, then $2^{mn-1}$ is even, so $2^{mn-1}+5$ is odd and $2\,\|\,a^n+10$.
- If $mn=1$ (i.e. $a=2$, $n=1$): $a^n+10=12=4\cdot3$ and $3\,\|\,12$.

**Case 2: $a$ has an odd prime factor $q$.**
- If $q\,\|\,a$, take $b=a$. Then $a^n+a=a\,(a^{n-1}+1)$. For $n\ge2$, $a^{n-1}+1\equiv1\pmod q$; for $n=1$ it equals $2$, not divisible by the odd prime $q$. In both cases $q\nmid a^{n-1}+1$, and together with $q\,\|\,a$ this gives $q\,\|\,a^n+a$.
- If $q^2\mid a$, take $b=q$. Then $a^n+q\equiv q\pmod{q^2}$ for every $n\ge1$, so $q\mid a^n+q$ but $q^2\nmid a^n+q$, i.e. $q\,\|\,a^n+q$.

In every case $b$ works for all positive integers $n$. ∎

prompt:
Find all real numbers $x>1$ that satisfy the equality
$$\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{x}\right\rfloor=n-\left\lfloor\frac nx\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\frac nx\rfloor}{x}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\frac nx\rfloor}{x}\right\rfloor}{x}\right\rfloor+\dots$$
for all positive integers $n$.

Here, $\lfloor t\rfloor$ is the integer part of $t$, i.e. the integer such that $\lfloor t\rfloor\le t<\lfloor t\rfloor+1$.

solutions.title: Reduce to a two-term identity
solutions.body:
Let $f(m)=\lfloor m/x\rfloor$ and $R(n)=n-f(n)+f(f(n))-\cdots$. Since $x>1$, $f(m)<m$ for $m\ge1$ and $f(0)=0$, so the alternating sum is finite. Clearly
$$R(n)=n-R(f(n))\qquad(n\ge1),\qquad R(0)=0 .$$

**Reduction.** Suppose the equality $\lfloor\frac{n+1}x\rfloor=R(n)$ holds for all $n\ge1$. It also holds for $n=0$ ($\lfloor\frac1x\rfloor=0=R(0)$). Applying it to $m=f(n)\ge0$,
$$\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{x}\right\rfloor=n-R(f(n))=n-\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/x\rfloor+1}{x}\right\rfloor .\tag{1}$$
Conversely, if (1) holds for all $n\ge1$, then by strong induction $\lfloor\frac{n+1}x\rfloor=R(n)$ for all $n$: indeed $m=f(n)<n$, so by induction $R(m)=\lfloor\frac{m+1}x\rfloor$ and $R(n)=n-R(m)=\lfloor\frac{n+1}x\rfloor$ by (1). So the problem is equivalent to (1) for all $n\ge1$.

**Necessity: $x=\varphi$.** Divide (1) by $n$ and let $n\to\infty$; since $\lfloor t\rfloor=t+O(1)$, the left side tends to $\frac1x$ and the right side to $1-\frac1{x^2}$. So $\frac1x+\frac1{x^2}=1$, i.e. $x^2-x-1=0$, whose only root $>1$ is $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $x=\varphi$; recall $\frac1\varphi=\varphi-1$, $\frac1{\varphi^2}=1-\frac1\varphi$ and $1+\frac1\varphi=\varphi$. Fix $n\ge1$ and write $\frac n\varphi=m+\varepsilon$ with $m=\lfloor\frac n\varphi\rfloor$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$ ($\varepsilon\ne0$ as $\varphi$ is irrational). Then
$$\frac{n+1}\varphi=m+\varepsilon+\frac1\varphi,\qquad\frac{m+1}\varphi=\frac{n/\varphi-\varepsilon+1}{\varphi}=\frac n{\varphi^2}+\frac{1-\varepsilon}\varphi=n-m-\varepsilon+\frac{1-\varepsilon}\varphi .$$
So (1) is equivalent to
$$\Big\lfloor\varepsilon+\tfrac1\varphi\Big\rfloor+\Big\lfloor\tfrac1\varphi-\varphi\varepsilon\Big\rfloor=0\qquad\Big(\text{using }\tfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varphi}-\varepsilon=\tfrac1\varphi-\varepsilon\big(1+\tfrac1\varphi\big)\Big).$$
Put $u=\varepsilon+\frac1\varphi\in(\frac1\varphi,1+\frac1\varphi)$; then $\frac1\varphi-\varphi\varepsilon=\frac1\varphi+1-\varphi u=\varphi(1-u)$. Note $u\ne1$: otherwise $\frac n\varphi-m=1-\frac1\varphi$, i.e. $(n+1)(\varphi-1)=m+1$, impossible since $\varphi$ is irrational.
- If $u<1$: $\lfloor u\rfloor=0$ and $0<\varphi(1-u)<\varphi\big(1-\frac1\varphi\big)=\varphi-1<1$, so the sum is $0+0=0$.
- If $u>1$: $\lfloor u\rfloor=1$ and $-1=-\varphi\cdot\frac1\varphi<\varphi(1-u)<0$, so the sum is $1+(-1)=0$.

Hence (1) holds for every $n\ge1$, and $x=\varphi$ satisfies the equality for all $n$ (a computer check for $n<20000$ agrees).

**Answer: $x=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$.** ∎

prompt:
Let us call a sequence $(b_1,b_2,\dots)$ of positive integers *fast-growing* if $b_{n+1}\ge b_n+2$ for all $n\ge1$. Also, for a sequence $a=(a(1),a(2),\dots)$ of real numbers and a sequence $b=(b_1,b_2,\dots)$ of positive integers, let us denote
$$S(a,b)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\big|a(b_n)+a(b_n+1)+\dots+a(b_{n+1}-1)\big| .$$

1. Do there exist two fast-growing sequences $b=(b_1,b_2,\dots)$, $c=(c_1,c_2,\dots)$ such that for every sequence $a=(a(1),a(2),\dots)$, if all the series
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty a(n),\qquad S(a,b)\qquad\text{and}\qquad S(a,c)$$
are convergent, then the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty|a(n)|$ is also convergent?

2. Do there exist three fast-growing sequences $b=(b_1,b_2,\dots)$, $c=(c_1,c_2,\dots)$, $d=(d_1,d_2,\dots)$ such that for every sequence $a=(a(1),a(2),\dots)$, if all the series
$$S(a,b),\qquad S(a,c)\qquad\text{and}\qquad S(a,d)$$
are convergent, then the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty|a(n)|$ is also convergent?

(Answer both parts, e.g. "yes, no".)
answer: No, yes

solutions.title: Counterexamples for two groupings; pairs, pairs and triples
solutions.body:
Call $\{b_n,b_n+1,\dots,b_{n+1}-1\}$ the $n$-th *$b$-group*; groups are disjoint blocks of consecutive integers of length $\ge2$.

**Part 1: No.** Let $b,c$ be fast-growing.

*Case 1: from some index on, all steps are exactly $2$ in both sequences* ($b_{n+1}=b_n+2$, $c_{n+1}=c_n+2$ for $n\ge n_0$). Take $a(n)=\frac{(-1)^n}n$. Then $\sum a(n)$ converges (alternating series), $\sum|a(n)|=\sum\frac1n=\infty$, and for $n\ge n_0$ each $b$-group is a pair $\{k,k+1\}$ with $|a(k)+a(k+1)|=\frac1{k(k+1)}$; since the $b_n$ are distinct, $S(a,b)\le(\text{finitely many terms})+\sum_k\frac1{k(k+1)}<\infty$, and likewise $S(a,c)<\infty$.

*Case 2: otherwise,* say $b_{n+1}\ge b_n+3$ for infinitely many $n$ (the case of $c$ is symmetric). For such $n$ with $b_n\ge c_1$, the numbers $b_n,b_n+1,b_n+2$ lie in one $b$-group. If $b_n+1$ is not a term of $c$, then $b_n$ and $b_n+1$ lie in the same $c$-group; if $b_n+1=c_k$, then $b_n+1,b_n+2$ lie in the same $c$-group (as $c_{k+1}\ge c_k+2$). Either way we get a pair $(i,i+1)$ lying in a common $b$-group and a common $c$-group, and pairs coming from different $n$ are disjoint. So there are infinitely many disjoint such pairs $(i_k,i_k+1)$, $k=1,2,\dots$, with $i_1<i_2<\cdots$. Put
$$a(i_k)=\tfrac1k,\qquad a(i_k+1)=-\tfrac1k,\qquad a(n)=0\ \text{otherwise}.$$
Every $b$-group and every $c$-group contains each pair entirely or not at all, so all group sums are $0$ and $S(a,b)=S(a,c)=0$. The partial sums of $\sum a(n)$ are $0$ or $\frac1k$, so it converges (to $0$); but $\sum|a(n)|=2\sum\frac1k=\infty$.

So no two fast-growing sequences have the required property.

**Part 2: Yes.** Take $b_n=2n-1$, $c_n=2n$, $d_n=3n-2$; the groups are the pairs $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\dots$, the pairs $\{2,3\},\{4,5\},\dots$ and the triples $\{1,2,3\},\{4,5,6\},\dots$. Consider a triple $x=a(3k+1)$, $y=a(3k+2)$, $z=a(3k+3)$. The pairs $\{3k+1,3k+2\}$ and $\{3k+2,3k+3\}$ are a $b$-group and a $c$-group (in some order, depending on the parity of $k$), and $\{3k+1,3k+2,3k+3\}$ is a $d$-group. By the triangle inequality
$$|x|\le|x+y+z|+|y+z|,\qquad|z|\le|x+y+z|+|x+y|,\qquad|y|\le|x+y|+|x|,$$
so
$$|x|+|y|+|z|\le3|x+y+z|+2|x+y|+2|y+z|\le3\big(|x+y+z|+|x+y|+|y+z|\big).$$
Summing over $k\ge0$ (each group occurs at most once), $\sum_n|a(n)|\le3\big(S(a,b)+S(a,c)+S(a,d)\big)<\infty$.

**Answer: 1. no; 2. yes.** ∎

(The official solution uses $a(n)=(-1)^n/n$ in Case 1 and claims the pair sums vanish; they are not zero but $\frac1{k(k+1)}$ in absolute value, which is still summable.)

prompt:
Let $n\ge2$ be an integer, and let $A$ be an $n\times n$ real matrix with minimal polynomial $x^n+x-1$. Show that
$$\operatorname{tr}\big((nA^{n-1}+I)^{-1}A^{n-2}\big)=0 .$$
Here, $\operatorname{tr}(B)=\sum_{i=1}^nb_{ii}$ denotes the trace of the matrix $B=(b_{ij})_{i,j=1}^n$.
answer: With $\alpha(z)=z^n+z-1$ (distinct roots $\lambda_k$, the eigenvalues of $A$) the trace is $\sum_k\frac{\lambda_k^{n-2}}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)}$, and $\sum_k\frac{g(\lambda_k)}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)}=0$ for every polynomial $g$ of degree $\le n-2$ (Lagrange interpolation).

solutions.title: Lagrange interpolation identity
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha(z)=z^n+z-1$.

**The eigenvalues.** The minimal polynomial has degree $n$, so it equals the characteristic polynomial, and the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ of $A$ (over $\mathbb C$) are the roots of $\alpha$. They are distinct: a common root of $\alpha$ and $\alpha'(z)=nz^{n-1}+1$ would satisfy $z^n=-z/n$, hence $0=\alpha(z)=\frac{n-1}nz-1$, so $z=\frac n{n-1}>0$; but then $\alpha'(z)>0$, a contradiction. Hence $\alpha'(\lambda_k)\ne0$, and $A$ is diagonalizable: $A=S\Lambda S^{-1}$, $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_k)$.

**The trace.** $nA^{n-1}+I=S\operatorname{diag}(\alpha'(\lambda_k))S^{-1}$ is invertible, and
$$\operatorname{tr}\big((nA^{n-1}+I)^{-1}A^{n-2}\big)=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{\lambda_k^{n-2}}{n\lambda_k^{n-1}+1}=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{\lambda_k^{n-2}}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)} .$$

**Lemma.** If $\alpha$ is monic of degree $n$ with distinct roots $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ and $g$ is a polynomial of degree $\le n-2$, then $\sum_k\frac{g(\lambda_k)}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)}=0$.

*Proof.* By Lagrange interpolation (the unique polynomial of degree $\le n-1$ through the $n$ points $(\lambda_k,g(\lambda_k))$ is $g$ itself),
$$g(x)=\sum_{k=1}^ng(\lambda_k)\prod_{j\ne k}\frac{x-\lambda_j}{\lambda_k-\lambda_j},\qquad \prod_{j\ne k}(\lambda_k-\lambda_j)=\alpha'(\lambda_k).$$
Comparing coefficients of $x^{n-1}$: the right side gives $\sum_kg(\lambda_k)/\alpha'(\lambda_k)$, the left side gives $0$ since $\deg g\le n-2$. $\square$

Applying the lemma with $g(x)=x^{n-2}$ shows that the trace is $0$. ∎

solutions.title: Logarithmic derivatives (official approach)
solutions.body:
As in the first solution, the trace equals $\sum_k\frac{\lambda_k^{n-2}}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)}=\frac1{n(n-1)}\sum_k\frac{\alpha''(\lambda_k)}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)}$, because $\alpha''(z)=n(n-1)z^{n-2}$. So it suffices to show $\sum_k\frac{\alpha''(\lambda_k)}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)}=0$ for a polynomial $\alpha$ of degree $n$ with distinct roots $\lambda_k$.

For a polynomial $P=c\prod_j(z-z_j)$ we have $\frac{P'}{P}=\sum_j\frac1{z-z_j}$ away from the roots. Let $w_1,\dots,w_{n-1}$ be the roots of $\alpha'$; none of them is a root of $\alpha$ (the roots of $\alpha$ are simple). Then
$$\sum_k\frac{\alpha''(\lambda_k)}{\alpha'(\lambda_k)}=\sum_k\sum_j\frac1{\lambda_k-w_j}=-\sum_j\sum_k\frac1{w_j-\lambda_k}=-\sum_j\frac{\alpha'(w_j)}{\alpha(w_j)}=0,$$
since $\alpha'(w_j)=0$. ∎

prompt: Let $x_0=a$, $x_1=b$, $x_2=c$ for given numbers $a,b,c\in\mathbb R$, and let $x_{n+2}=\dfrac{x_n+x_{n-1}}{2}$ for $n\ge1$. Show that the sequence $(x_n)_{n=0}^\infty$ converges, and find its limit.
answer: $\lim x_n=\dfrac{a+2b+2c}{5}$: the differences satisfy $x_{n+4}-x_{n+3}=-\frac14(x_n-x_{n-1})$, so the sequence is Cauchy, and $x_{n+1}+x_n+\frac12x_{n-1}$ is invariant (equal to $c+b+\frac a2$).

solutions.title: Contracting differences and an invariant
solutions.body:
**Convergence.** Let $d_n=x_n-x_{n-1}$ ($n\ge1$). For $n\ge1$,
$$x_{n+4}-x_{n+3}=\frac{x_{n+2}+x_{n+1}}2-\frac{x_{n+1}+x_n}2=\frac{x_{n+2}-x_n}2=\frac12\Big(\frac{x_n+x_{n-1}}2-x_n\Big)=-\frac14(x_n-x_{n-1}),$$
i.e. $d_{n+4}=-\frac14d_n$. Hence $|d_n|\le D\cdot4^{-n/4}$ for all $n\ge1$, where $D=4\max(|d_1|,|d_2|,|d_3|,|d_4|)$, so $\sum|d_n|<\infty$. Thus $x_n=x_0+\sum_{k\le n}d_k$ converges.

**An invariant.** Let $y_n=x_{n+1}+x_n+\frac12x_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$. Then
$$y_{n+1}=x_{n+2}+x_{n+1}+\tfrac12x_n=\tfrac12x_n+\tfrac12x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}+\tfrac12x_n=x_{n+1}+x_n+\tfrac12x_{n-1}=y_n,$$
so $y_n=y_1=c+b+\frac a2$ for all $n$.

**The limit.** If $x_n\to L$, then $y_n\to L+L+\frac L2=\frac52L$, so $\frac52L=c+b+\frac a2$ and
$$L=\frac{a+2b+2c}{5}.$$
∎

solutions.title: Characteristic roots
solutions.body:
The recurrence $x_{k+3}=\frac12x_{k+1}+\frac12x_k$ ($k\ge0$) has characteristic polynomial $2t^3-t-1=(t-1)(2t^2+2t+1)$ with distinct roots $1$ and $\rho,\bar\rho=\frac{-1\pm i}2$, $|\rho|=\frac1{\sqrt2}<1$. Hence $x_k=L+\beta\rho^k+\bar\beta\bar\rho^k$ for some constants, and $x_k\to L$ because $\rho^k\to0$.

To find $L$, let $Q_k=2x_{k+2}+2x_{k+1}+x_k$. Using $2x_{k+3}=x_{k+1}+x_k$,
$$Q_{k+1}=2x_{k+3}+2x_{k+2}+x_{k+1}=(x_{k+1}+x_k)+2x_{k+2}+x_{k+1}=Q_k,$$
so $Q_k$ is constant. With $k=0$ it equals $2c+2b+a$, and in the limit it equals $5L$. So $L=\frac{a+2b+2c}5$. ∎

prompt: Let $A,B$ be two $n\times n$ complex matrices of the same rank, and let $k\in\mathbb N$. Prove that $A^{k+1}B^k=A$ if and only if $B^{k+1}A^k=B$.
answer: From $A^{k+1}B^k=A$: $\ker B\subseteq\ker A$, so $\ker A=\ker B$, and $\operatorname{rank}A^2=\operatorname{rank}A$, so $\mathbb C^n=\operatorname{Im}A\oplus\ker A$. In such a basis $A=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}B_1&0\\B_3&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $A_1^kB_1^k=I$, which gives $B^{k+1}A^k=B$; the converse is symmetric.

solutions.title: Block decomposition along $\operatorname{Im}A\oplus\ker A$
solutions.body:
The statement is symmetric in $A$ and $B$, so it suffices to show: if $A^{k+1}B^k=A$, then $B^{k+1}A^k=B$. (We take $k\ge1$; for $k=0$ both identities are trivially true.) Let $r=\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$.

**$\ker A=\ker B$.** If $Bx=0$ then $Ax=A^{k+1}B^kx=0$. So $\ker B\subseteq\ker A$, and both have dimension $n-r$; hence they are equal.

**$\mathbb C^n=\operatorname{Im}A\oplus\ker A$.** From $r=\operatorname{rank}(A^{k+1}B^k)\le\operatorname{rank}A^{k+1}\le\operatorname{rank}A^2\le\operatorname{rank}A=r$ we get $\operatorname{rank}A^2=r$, so $\ker A^2$ (which contains $\ker A$) has the same dimension as $\ker A$: $\ker A^2=\ker A$. If $x\in\ker A\cap\operatorname{Im}A$, $x=Ay$, then $A^2y=0$, so $y\in\ker A$ and $x=0$. Since the dimensions add up to $n$, the sum is direct and equals $\mathbb C^n$.

**Block form.** Choose a basis consisting of a basis of $\operatorname{Im}A$ followed by a basis of $\ker A=\ker B$. $A$ maps $\operatorname{Im}A$ into itself, injectively (its kernel meets $\operatorname{Im}A$ trivially), and kills $\ker A$; $B$ kills $\ker A$. Hence
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}B_1&0\\B_3&0\end{pmatrix},$$
with $A_1$ an invertible $r\times r$ matrix. By induction $B^j=\begin{pmatrix}B_1^j&0\\B_3B_1^{j-1}&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $j\ge1$.

**Conclusion.** $A^{k+1}B^k=\begin{pmatrix}A_1^{k+1}B_1^k&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=A$ gives $A_1^{k+1}B_1^k=A_1$, i.e. $A_1^kB_1^k=I_r$ ($A_1$ invertible). Hence $A_1^k$ and $B_1^k$ are inverse to each other, so also $B_1^kA_1^k=I_r$. Now
$$B^{k+1}A^k=\begin{pmatrix}B_1^{k+1}&0\\B_3B_1^k&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A_1^k&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}B_1\,(B_1^kA_1^k)&0\\B_3\,(B_1^kA_1^k)&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}B_1&0\\B_3&0\end{pmatrix}=B .$$
∎

prompt:
Evaluate the integral
$$\int_0^\infty\frac{\log(x+2)}{x^2+3x+2}\,dx .$$

solutions.title: Substitution $x+1=1/t$
solutions.body:
Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm, and $x^2+3x+2=(x+1)(x+2)$. Substitute $x+1=\frac1t$, $t\in(0,1]$, $dx=-\frac{dt}{t^2}$. Then $x+2=\frac{1+t}t$ and $(x+1)(x+2)=\frac{1+t}{t^2}$, so
$$\int_0^\infty\frac{\ln(x+2)}{(x+1)(x+2)}\,dx=\int_0^1\ln\frac{1+t}{t}\cdot\frac{t^2}{1+t}\cdot\frac{dt}{t^2}=\int_0^1\frac{\ln(1+t)}{1+t}\,dt-\int_0^1\frac{\ln t}{1+t}\,dt .$$
The first integral is $\big[\frac12\ln^2(1+t)\big]_0^1=\frac12\ln^22$. For the second, expand $\frac1{1+t}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kt^k$ and use $\int_0^1t^k\ln t\,dt=-\frac1{(k+1)^2}$ (termwise integration is justified since the partial sums of the alternating series are bounded by $1$ and $|\ln t|$ is integrable):
$$-\int_0^1\frac{\ln t}{1+t}\,dt=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^k}{(k+1)^2}=1-\frac1{4}+\frac19-\dots=\frac{\pi^2}{12}.$$
Hence the integral equals
$$\frac{\pi^2}{12}+\frac{\ln^22}{2}\approx1.062694 .$$
(Numerical integration confirms this value.) ∎

solutions.title: Differentiation under the integral sign (official approach)
solutions.body:
